A founder in São Paulo wants an R&D team in Bologna. The product is software with a hardware edge. The talent they need is in Emilia-Romagna: embedded engineers, mechatronics people, data scientists from the local university. They have no Italian company and no wish to spend a long time building one.

This is a scenario, not a case study. It shows the path and the decisions in the order they usually come.

## Decision 1: Own entity or Employer of Record

The founder can open an Italian subsidiary. That means a legal entity, a registered office, a bank account, accounting, payroll, and local advisers. It makes sense when the team will be large and stay for years.

The alternative is an Employer of Record (EOR). The EOR is the legal employer in Italy. The founder directs the daily work. The EOR handles the contract, payroll, social contributions, and compliance.

For a first team of a few engineers, with a product that is still changing, the EOR is usually the faster and lighter route. The founder can move to their own entity later, once the team and the plan are stable.

## Decision 2: Who to hire first

Most founders start with a technical lead. This person knows the local market, can interview candidates, and will shape the team's habits. Hire for judgment, not only for skills.

The founder should write down what the team will own. A vague brief attracts vague candidates. A clear one, such as "own the firmware for our sensor line", attracts people who want that job.

## Decision 3: Where the people come from

There are two pools. The first is people already living in Italy. They can start quickly and need no relocation. The second is people from abroad, including Brazilians who want to move to Italy and who may have Italian family ties.

Hiring locally is simpler. Hiring from abroad adds immigration and relocation steps, and these take time. A founder who wants speed should start with the local pool and add international hires later.

## Decision 4: The employment contract

Italian employment is governed by national collective agreements. The sector decides which one applies. For an engineering team, the right agreement sets minimum pay, notice periods, leave, and other terms.

The founder does not need to master this. They do need to know that the contract is not a blank page. The EOR applies the correct agreement and tells the founder what it means for the offer. Ask for this before you make any offer.

## Decision 5: Pay and the real cost

The salary in the offer is not the cost to the company. Employer contributions and other mandatory items sit on top. A founder who budgets only for the salary will be surprised.

Ask the EOR for the full cost of each role, in writing, before the offer goes out. Compare it with the budget in your own currency. Currency moves can matter for a Brazilian company paying in euros, so leave some margin.

## Decision 6: How the team works with Brazil

Bologna and São Paulo share part of the working day, but not all of it. Pick a fixed overlap for meetings and keep the rest of the day free for deep work. Write down decisions, because not everyone is online at the same time.

Plan at least one visit in each direction. A team that has met in person works better remotely afterward.

## Decision 7: Intellectual property

R&D work produces things the company wants to own. The founder should make sure the contract and the company's internal rules deal with inventions, code, and designs. This is a conversation to have with the EOR and a local lawyer, before the first day and not after.

## The path in order

1. Define the team's purpose and the first role.
2. Choose EOR or own entity.
3. Get the full cost and the applicable collective agreement for the role.
4. Recruit, starting with the technical lead.
5. Sign the contract through the EOR and set up payroll.
6. Onboard the person with a clear first goal.
7. Add roles as the work proves itself.
8. Review at a set point whether to keep the EOR or move to an own entity.

## What goes wrong

The common mistakes are simple. Founders hire before they know the full cost. They treat the contract as a formality. They give the local lead no authority. They expect the team to behave like the one at home.

Avoid these, and Bologna is a good place to build.

You want to build a team in Italy. You do not want to spend your first months on paperwork. This plan shows the milestones in order, so you know what to decide, what to delay and what to hand off.

The plan assumes you start without an Italian entity. You can hire through an Employer of Record (EOR) while you test the market. You open your own entity later, when the business justifies it.

## Early weeks: decide what you are building

Before you talk to any candidate, answer a few questions in writing.

- Which roles do you need in Italy, and why Italy?
- Do these people sell, build, support or manage?
- Will they work from home, from a coworking space or from your future office?
- Who in your company owns the Italian relationship?

The last question matters most. Italian hires need a named contact on your side. Without one, small issues pile up. Pick a manager and give them time for this.

Also decide your hiring route now. An EOR employs the person on your behalf. You direct the daily work. The EOR handles the contract, payroll, social contributions and compliance. This lets you hire fast without a local entity.

## Early to middle weeks: prepare the offer

Italian employment is shaped by national collective agreements (CCNL). The agreement that applies depends on the sector and the role. It sets minimum pay levels, notice periods, leave and other terms. Do not write an offer from a template used in another country. It will not fit.

Ask your EOR partner which agreement applies to your roles. Then build the offer around it. Be clear on these points:

- Job title and level under the agreement
- Gross salary and any variable pay
- Working location and remote work terms
- Probation terms
- Benefits you want to add on top

Candidates in Italy read the offer closely. A clear, complete document builds trust.

## Middle weeks: make the first hire

Run a short, structured process. Keep the number of interview rounds low. Tell candidates up front that you hire through an EOR. Explain that the EOR is the legal employer and that your team manages their work. Most candidates accept this when it is explained plainly.

If the person you want lives outside Italy, start the relocation and visa questions immediately. These take time and you cannot rush them. Ask your EOR partner what documents are needed and who must file them. Plan the start date around the answers, not the other way round.

On the start date, make sure the basics are ready:

- Signed contract
- Registration with the social security bodies
- Payroll set up
- Equipment and software access
- A named manager and a clear first plan

## Middle to late weeks: build routines

Once the first person is in place, set the rhythm. Hold regular check-ins. Agree how you handle leave, expenses and public holidays. Italy has its own calendar, and August is often quiet. Plan sales and delivery around it.

Use this period to hire the next people if the first hire works. Reuse the same offer structure. Each new hire should be faster than the last.

Keep a simple log of questions that came up. It shows you what to fix before the team grows.

## Late weeks: review and choose the next step

Now look at the numbers and the facts. Ask yourself:

- Is the team hitting its goals?
- Are customers in Italy responding?
- Do you need more people in the same city?
- Does the team ask for a shared place to work?

If the answers are yes, you can think about an office. Start small. A coworking space or a serviced office gives you an address and meeting rooms without a long lease. You can often keep the EOR arrangement while you do this.

A permanent office and your own Italian entity come later. Move to them when you have steady revenue, a clear team plan and a reason to control employment directly. Your EOR partner can help you transfer staff to the new entity in an orderly way.

## What to avoid

Some mistakes repeat among foreign founders.

- Hiring before you know which collective agreement applies
- Treating the contract as a formality
- Leaving relocation and visa work to the last moment
- Opening an office before the team proves the market
- Having no owner for Italy inside your company

## The short version

Start with decisions, not candidates. Make the offer fit Italian rules. Hire one person well, then repeat. Review honestly. Add an office only when the team needs it.

The country site for your market has local details on hiring in Italy. You can also request a quote from us to plan your own timeline.

Italy has deep industrial know-how in vehicles, aircraft and the components that go into them. The talent is not in one place. It sits in clusters, each with its own history, schools and supplier networks. If you plan to hire here, knowing the map saves time.

This article walks through the main clusters from north to south. It then explains how a foreign company can hire in them without opening a local entity.

## Turin and Piedmont: automotive roots, growing aerospace

Turin is the historic home of Italian car making. Decades of design, powertrain and body engineering left a dense base of suppliers, test facilities and technical people. The polytechnic university feeds the region with engineers who know vehicle systems.

Today the same skills move into new areas. Electrification, software-defined vehicles, battery systems and advanced materials all draw on the Turin talent pool. The region also has a solid aerospace presence, which means engineers who understand certification, quality systems and long product cycles.

If you need vehicle engineers, homologation specialists or design professionals, start here.

## Lombardy and Emilia-Romagna: motors, machines and precision

Lombardy combines heavy manufacturing with strong engineering schools in Milan. Many tier-one and tier-two suppliers sit in this area. You will find mechanical, electronic and industrial engineers, plus a large base of skilled technicians.

Emilia-Romagna is known as Motor Valley. High-performance cars and motorcycles are built there. The area has people with rare skills in composites, engine development, aerodynamics and low-volume precision production. Packaging machinery and automation firms nearby add mechatronics and controls expertise.

These regions suit companies that need specialists in performance, lightweight structures or advanced manufacturing.

## Veneto, Friuli and the north-east: suppliers and mobility components

The north-east has many small and mid-size manufacturers. They supply parts, tooling and electronics to vehicle makers across Europe. The workforce is practical and production-minded. For firms that want to build a supplier team, a quality group or a manufacturing engineering function, this belt is worth a look.

## Lazio and Tuscany: space, defence and systems

Around Rome, the focus shifts to space systems, avionics, satellites and defence electronics. Research institutions and large aerospace groups shape the local market. Engineers here work on software, sensors, communications and systems integration.

Tuscany adds specialised mechanical and electronic firms, including makers of precision components for aircraft and rail.

## Campania and Naples: an aerospace base in the south

The south is often overlooked by foreign employers. That is a mistake in aerospace. Campania has a long tradition in aircraft structures, aero-engine parts and maintenance work. Naples has a university with strong aerospace engineering programmes. Industrial sites in the surrounding area handle composites, assembly and testing.

Puglia and neighbouring regions add to this, with aerospace production and growing research activity. Hiring in the south can give you access to skilled engineers in markets with less competition from other international employers.

## What this means for your hiring plan

Match the role to the cluster. Do not look for a motorsport composites engineer in a region known for aircraft maintenance. Do not expect to find a satellite software lead in a car-body hub.

A few practical points:

- Engineers in these sectors often prefer to stay near their family and their city. Remote or hybrid work from a cluster town is a strong offer.
- Technical Italian matters on the shop floor. Engineers in design and software roles usually work well in English.
- Supplier networks are tight. Reputation travels fast, so a clear and fair offer helps you in the next search.
- Salary expectations and contract terms follow national collective agreements. These vary by sector and must be applied correctly.

## Hiring without a local entity

Setting up a company in Italy takes time and local knowledge. For a small team, or a test of the market, it is often not worth it.

An Employer of Record (EOR) hires the person on your behalf under Italian rules. You choose the candidate, set the work and manage the day-to-day. The EOR handles the contract, payroll, social security and compliance. You can start a new engineer in Turin, Bologna or Naples without a branch or subsidiary.

If the hire comes from outside the EU, the EOR can also support the visa process and relocation. That is useful in aerospace and mobility, where specialists often move between countries.

When your team grows and the business case is clear, you can open your own entity later and transfer the staff.

## Getting started

Pick the cluster that fits the role. Define the contract type and the collective agreement that applies. Then decide whether you hire through your own entity or through an EOR.

An employee you hired in Italy tells you they want to move to another EU country. They want to keep the job. What changes for you?

The short answer: more than most employers expect, and less than they fear. The answer depends on one question. Will the person work from the new country, or will they only live there for a short time while still working in Italy?

## Start with the type of move

There are three common cases.

**A temporary posting.** The employee works abroad for a limited period and then returns. The Italian employment relationship stays in place.

**A permanent move with the same job.** The employee settles in the new country and works from there, often remotely. Your Italian base is no longer where the work happens.

**A transfer to a local role.** The employee leaves the Italian contract behind and signs a new one under local rules.

Each case triggers different rules. Treat them separately.

## Social security

Within the EU, one country's social security system normally applies to a worker at a time. EU coordination rules decide which one. In most cases it is the country where the person actually works.

For a temporary posting, the employee can usually stay in the Italian system. You need to obtain the proper certificate from the Italian authorities to prove it. Without it, the host country may ask for its own contributions.

For a permanent move, the host country's system usually takes over. That means registering the employer there, or using a local representative who can do it for you. Italian contributions stop. Local ones start. The rates, the bases and the benefits are different.

Do not assume the old setup carries over. Check before the first payslip is issued abroad.

## Income tax and withholding

Tax follows residence and place of work. A person who moves their home to another country usually becomes a tax resident there. The Italian withholding obligations may end. New withholding duties may begin in the host country.

If the employee works in the new country, you may have to run payroll there. Or you may need a local entity or provider to do it. Employers sometimes miss this step. They keep paying the person through Italian payroll and create a compliance gap.

There is also a risk of double taxation. Tax treaties between countries reduce it, but someone has to apply them correctly.

## The employment contract

The Italian contract does not vanish when the employee crosses a border. But the rules that govern it can change.

Two points matter most.

First, mandatory protections of the country where the person works can apply on top of the contract. These cover working time, rest periods, minimum notice and similar items. The contract may say Italian law applies. Local mandatory rules can still override it.

Second, the Italian national collective agreement tied to the role may no longer fit. The host country may have its own sector rules. Terms such as leave, notice and pay structure can differ. Review the contract and decide whether to amend it or replace it.

## Permanent establishment risk

A foreign company with an employee working in a country can create a taxable presence there. Authorities may argue the company has a permanent establishment. This can bring corporate tax and registration duties.

The risk is higher when the employee signs contracts, manages clients or acts as a senior decision maker. It is lower for support roles. But it exists in every case. Get advice before the move, not after.

## Practical steps for the employer

Use a short checklist.

- Confirm the type of move and its expected length.
- Identify which country's social security applies.
- Obtain the right certificate if the employee stays in the Italian system.
- Register in the host country if local payroll is needed.
- Review tax withholding in both countries.
- Check mandatory local employment rules.
- Update the contract or sign a new one.
- Assess permanent establishment exposure.
- Tell the employee in writing what changes and when.

## What does not change

The person is still your employee. Their right to live and work in another EU country is not in question. EU citizens do not need a work visa to take a job there. The paperwork is about your obligations as employer, not their right to move.

## Where an Employer of Record helps

A company with no entity in the host country faces a choice. It can set one up, or it can use an Employer of Record (EOR). An EOR becomes the legal employer locally. It runs payroll, registers with the social security system and applies local employment rules. You keep directing the work.

This is often faster than opening a branch for one or two people. It also lowers the permanent establishment risk, since the EOR carries the employment obligations.

Before any move, speak to someone who knows both countries. A small error in the first month can turn into a large correction later.

Opening an Italian entity is more than filing incorporation papers. The company must be able to pay people, invoice customers and report to the authorities. This list covers the practical setup, in the order it usually works best.

It is a general guide. Your accountant and your bank will confirm the details for your case.

## Before you start

- Decide who will sign. Italian banks and authorities want a named legal representative with a valid ID and a tax code.
- Choose the legal form with your advisers. It affects capital, governance and accounting duties.
- Appoint an Italian accountant (commercialista) early. Do not wait until after incorporation. They will often prepare the registrations for you.

## Tax registration

**Personal tax code for each director and shareholder.** Every individual involved needs an Italian tax code (codice fiscale). Foreign nationals can usually get one through the tax office or a consulate. A company shareholder abroad needs one too.

**Company tax code.** The company receives its own tax code when it is incorporated through the notary and the company register.

**VAT number.** The company opens its VAT position with the tax authority. In practice this is done with a declaration of start of activity, filed by the accountant. You must state the business activity code that matches what you will really do.

**Digital tools.** Get these as soon as the company exists:

- Certified email (PEC). It is mandatory for companies, and official notices arrive there.
- Digital signature for the legal representative.
- Access to the tax authority's online portal for the company.

Check the PEC inbox every day. Missed notices cause avoidable penalties.

## Company register and chamber of commerce

The company is entered in the business register. The chamber of commerce record is what banks and clients check first. Keep the registered office address, the legal representative and the activity description accurate and up to date.

## Banking

The bank account is often the slowest step. Plan for it.

- Open a business current account with an Italian bank. Some banks can start the process with the notary deed and the company documents, even before every registration is complete.
- Expect full identification checks on the legal representative and on the ultimate owners of the group. Prepare a clear ownership chart.
- Bring a short description of the business, the expected flows and the main counterparties. Banks ask for this to meet anti-money-laundering rules.
- If the parent company is funding the capital, make sure the transfer is traceable and labelled correctly.
- Ask for online banking, payment cards and the ability to pay payroll and taxes by electronic transfer.
- Ask whether the bank supports direct debits and the tax payment form used for monthly payments.

A foreign group with an existing bank relationship can ask its home bank for an introduction. It often helps.

## Payroll and social security registrations

If you will employ people in Italy, the company also registers as an employer.

- Social security registration with the national institute, to report and pay contributions.
- Workplace accident insurance registration with the national insurance body.
- Appointment of a payroll provider or labour consultant. Many companies outsource this to a labour consultant (consulente del lavoro).
- Choice of the collective agreement that applies to your sector. It sets minimum pay, leave and notice terms.
- Mandatory employment notifications before each new hire starts.
- Health and safety basics, including a responsible person and the required checks.

Payroll must be accurate from the first payslip. Fixing mistakes later is slow.

## Accounting setup

- Choose an accounting method and software your accountant can access directly.
- Set up electronic invoicing. Italy requires invoices to pass through a national exchange system. You need a channel code or a PEC registered for receiving invoices.
- Keep a chart of accounts that maps to your group reporting. Agree this with the parent finance team.
- Agree how and when the Italian books are closed, so group consolidation does not wait on Italy.
- Keep supplier and customer documents in a shared folder, organised by month.
- Agree who approves payments and who signs tax returns.
- Check whether an auditor or board of auditors is required for your legal form and size.

## Common mistakes

- Choosing a bank before checking it will onboard foreign-owned companies.
- Forgetting to register the PEC and missing official notices.
- Hiring before the employer registrations are complete.
- Using a generic activity code that does not match the real business.
- Leaving the accountant out of the first pay run.

## A faster route

An entity takes time and ongoing admin. If you only need to employ a few people, or want to test the market first, you can use an Employer of Record (EOR). The EOR is the legal employer in Italy. It runs payroll, social security, contracts and compliance, so you do not need your own bank account, tax registrations or local accounting team to start. You can open your own entity later, when headcount justifies it.

A job offer in Italy is judged on more than gross salary. Candidates look at the whole package. Benefits that cut real costs or save tax often matter more than a small raise.

If you are a foreign company hiring in Italy for the first time, this is where you can stand out. It is also where many employers get it wrong, because the benefits that work at home do not always translate.

This article covers three areas: meal vouchers, welfare and fringe benefits, and health cover.

## Why benefits matter more in Italy

Taxes and social contributions take a large share of gross pay. A benefit that is treated well for tax purposes puts more value in the employee's hands than the same amount paid as salary.

Italian employees know this. Many compare offers by what they keep, not by what is written on the contract. A clear benefits package signals that your company understands the local market.

Collective agreements also play a role. Many sectors set minimum benefits by contract. Your package should sit on top of these, not replace them.

## Meal vouchers

Meal vouchers are the benefit most Italian employees expect. They are common, easy to understand and widely used in supermarkets and restaurants.

According to the sources we use, the tax-favoured daily value for electronic meal vouchers is 10 EUR per day. The paper version has a lower limit, which is one reason many employers have moved to electronic cards.

The practical points:

- Electronic vouchers are simple to manage and are what most employees now prefer.
- The benefit is usually given for days actually worked.
- Check the current limit before you budget. Rules change with each budget law.

For a foreign employer, meal vouchers are a low-cost way to match local norms. Leaving them out can look like a gap, even if your salary is competitive.

## Welfare and fringe benefits

Corporate welfare is the second pillar. In Italy, employers can give goods and services to employees with favourable tax treatment, up to an annual threshold.

From the sources we use, the fringe benefit threshold is 1,000 EUR per year in the general case. For employees with dependent children, it is 2,000 EUR per year.

Below the threshold, the value reaches the employee without being taxed as ordinary pay. That makes it an efficient way to reward people.

Common uses include:

- Fuel or transport support
- Contributions to utility bills
- Gift cards and shopping vouchers
- Education and childcare services
- Supplementary services for family members

The higher threshold for employees with children is worth noting. It lets you tailor the package. A parent may value help with household costs more than a gift card.

Two cautions. First, the threshold is a ceiling, not a target. You do not have to use all of it. Second, the rules are updated often, so confirm the current limits and conditions before you commit to a plan.

## Health cover

Italy has a public health system, so health cover from an employer is an addition, not a necessity. Even so, it is one of the benefits employees value most.

Why it works:

- Private care can shorten waiting times for visits and tests.
- It covers the employee and, in many plans, the family.
- It is seen as a sign of a serious employer.

Many collective agreements already include a sector health fund. Before buying a separate policy, check what your agreement provides. You may only need to enrol employees and add a top-up for specific groups.

We do not quote figures for health plans here, because costs depend on the insurer, the level of cover and the age profile of your team. Ask for a written offer based on your actual headcount.

## How to build a package that works

Start simple. You do not need a long list.

1. Check what the applicable collective agreement already requires.
2. Add electronic meal vouchers. They are expected.
3. Use part of the fringe benefit threshold for services employees can actually use.
4. Offer health cover, or top up the sector fund.
5. Explain the package clearly in the offer letter, with the value of each item.

That last step is often skipped. Many employees do not see the value of welfare unless it is spelled out. A short summary in the offer helps with acceptance.

## Common mistakes

**Paying everything as salary.** This ignores the tax efficiency of welfare and can make your offer look weaker than it is.

**Copying a home-country package.** Stock options or a gym allowance may be welcome, but they do not replace meal vouchers or health cover.

**Ignoring the collective agreement.** Benefits defined by contract are not optional. Your own plan should be built around them.

**Not updating the plan.** Limits and conditions change. Review your package each year.

## What an Employer of Record can do

If you hire through an Employer of Record (EOR), the EOR runs payroll and applies the correct treatment to each benefit. It can set up meal vouchers, track welfare use against the threshold and enrol employees in health plans. You decide the package. The EOR handles the administration in Italy.

This matters most when you have a small team and no local HR. A wrong setup is hard to notice and costly to fix.

A bonus costs the employer the same amount whichever way it is paid. The difference is how much reaches the employee. In Italy, a bonus tied to productivity can be taxed at a flat rate instead of the ordinary progressive rates. This article compares the two routes from a cost and net pay point of view.

## The two routes

An **ordinary bonus** is paid as part of regular pay. It is added to the employee's taxable income and taxed at the normal progressive income tax rates. The higher the employee's total income, the more of the bonus goes to tax.

A **productivity bonus** is a payment linked to measurable results, such as output, quality, efficiency or profitability. If it meets the conditions, it can be taxed with a substitute tax at a flat rate of 1%. The rate applies up to a ceiling of 5,000 EUR of bonus. It is available only to employees whose income stays under a limit of 80,000 EUR.

## Check the limit for 2026

The 80,000 EUR income limit is the figure we found for 2025. We could not find a confirmation for 2026. The source for these numbers is a secondary one, not the tax authority itself. Before you build a bonus plan around the limit, confirm it for the current year. We do that check for clients as part of onboarding.

## What this means for the employer

The flat tax is an income tax measure for the employee. The gross amount you approve is the amount you budget. Moving a bonus from the ordinary route to the productivity route does not by itself lower your cost for the same gross sum.

What changes is the value of each euro you spend. The same gross bonus gives the employee a higher net amount. That is a stronger retention tool at no extra cost to you. You can also set a lower gross bonus and still deliver a net amount the employee finds attractive.

This note covers the income tax side only. Social contributions and any other charges on bonuses follow their own rules. Ask us to confirm them for your case before you commit to a plan.

## What this means for the employee

For an employee under the income limit, the flat rate is almost always better than the progressive rates. The effect is larger for employees with higher salaries, because their ordinary bonus would be taxed at the top of the progressive scale.

Employees above the income limit get no flat tax. Their bonus is taxed as ordinary income. If your senior staff are near the limit, the structure of their package matters. A bonus that looks generous in gross terms can be much smaller in net terms.

## Cost and net comparison in practice

Take the same gross bonus paid to the same employee in both ways.

- Employer cost: the same gross amount in both cases, before any contribution effects.
- Employee net, ordinary route: the gross bonus minus tax at the employee's marginal progressive rate.
- Employee net, productivity route: the gross bonus minus tax at 1%, as long as the bonus is within the 5,000 EUR ceiling and the employee is under the income limit.

Any part of the bonus above the ceiling goes back to ordinary taxation. So a very large bonus mixes both treatments. When you design pay for a senior role, you can split the reward. Pay the part linked to measurable results under the productivity route, up to the ceiling. Pay the rest as ordinary pay.

## What to put in place

The flat tax is not automatic. The bonus has to be linked to real, measurable targets, and the plan has to be documented. A discretionary bonus with no defined criteria is a poor fit for the favourable treatment.

For a foreign company hiring in Italy, a practical setup looks like this:

- Define clear targets for the role, such as sales, delivery or quality indicators.
- Write the criteria down before the performance period starts.
- Check each employee against the income limit for the year.
- Track the amount paid under the flat tax so you stay within the ceiling.
- Pay anything above the ceiling, or above the limit, as ordinary pay.

## Summary

The employer cost of a bonus is the same on both routes. The employee's net pay is not. A productivity bonus taxed at 1%, up to 5,000 EUR and for employees under 80,000 EUR, gives much more net value per euro spent than an ordinary bonus. Confirm the limit for the current year, since our source only gives it for 2025.

Ask ten foreign managers about Italian bureaucracy and you will hear the same stories. Endless queues. Stamps. Offices that close at noon. Some of it is true. Much of it is out of date or applies to a different kind of task than hiring.

This article separates what is slow from what is not, so you can plan a hire without fear or false hope.

## Myth: everything needs a paper form and a visit in person

Most employer registrations in Italy now run online. Social security registration, tax withholding set-up and the notification of a new hire to the authorities are handled through digital portals. A professional who does this every week files them in a routine way.

The real issue is not the portal. It is knowing which filings apply to your case, in which order, and what the system expects to see. A first-time foreign employer gets this wrong easily. An experienced local provider does not.

## What is usually fast

**Hiring an EU or Italian worker.** There is no work permit to wait for. The steps are mostly administrative: a written contract, a notification to the authorities before the start date, and registration with the social security and workplace insurance bodies.

**Payroll.** Once the employee is registered, payroll runs on a regular monthly cycle. Payslips, contributions and withholding follow fixed rules. This part is predictable.

**Contract drafting.** The applicable national collective agreement sets many of the terms. That removes a lot of negotiation. You choose the right agreement for the role, and the minimum conditions are already defined.

**Employee onboarding.** Once the legal entity or the Employer of Record (EOR) structure is in place, adding a further employee is far simpler than adding the first.

## What is genuinely slow

**Setting up your own Italian entity.** If you open a subsidiary, you need a company registration, a bank account, a tax number, and an authorized signatory. Banks in particular can be slow with foreign-owned companies. This is the step that most often delays a project.

**Work authorization for non-EU nationals.** This is the biggest source of delay. It involves immigration offices, consulates and document checks. Timing depends on the office, the country of origin and the quality of the file. A missing document can reset the clock.

**Document legalization and translation.** Foreign diplomas, birth certificates and criminal record certificates often need to be certified or translated. Each country has its own route. Plan for this early.

**Residence and local registration.** After arrival, the employee has to complete local registration steps. These depend on the municipality. Some are quick. Some are not.

**Anything that depends on a single official.** Italy is not one bureaucracy. It is many offices, each with its own habits. The same request can take very different time in different cities.

## What is slow because of the process, not the country

Some delays are self-inflicted. They come from incomplete files, late decisions, or unclear job descriptions. A visa application that describes the role vaguely will draw questions. A contract sent without the correct collective agreement will come back. These are not Italian problems. They are preparation problems.

## Myth: you need to speak Italian to handle it

The forms and official communication are in Italian. But you do not need to handle them yourself. A local partner reads the notices, answers the questions from the authorities and keeps deadlines. Your team only needs to supply the right documents on time.

## How to plan around the real delays

- Start the work authorization process as soon as the candidate accepts, not after the contract is final.
- Collect and certify foreign documents in parallel with everything else.
- Do not open an entity just to hire a small number of people. If speed matters, use an EOR and keep the entity question for later.
- Give the provider a precise job description and the real start date. Vague input creates slow output.
- Expect that non-EU hires take longer than EU hires, and tell the candidate so.

## The honest summary

Italian bureaucracy is not a wall. It is a set of separate steps, and most of them are routine. A few are slow, and those few are well known: entity set-up, bank accounts, work authorization and document certification.

If your hire is an EU citizen and you use an EOR, the process can be straightforward. If your hire is from outside the EU, or you want your own entity, build in time and start early.

Your company is hiring in Italy and your team will travel. Who pays for the hotel? Can you give a flat daily amount? Does it count as salary? This FAQ answers the common questions on per diems and reimbursements.

## What is the difference between a reimbursement and a per diem?

A reimbursement repays the real cost of a trip. The employee spends money, shows the receipt, and the company pays it back.

A per diem is a flat daily allowance. The employee gets a set amount for each day of travel and does not need to show every receipt.

Both exist in Italy. They are treated differently for tax and social contributions, so the choice matters.

## Do I have to reimburse travel costs at all?

If you ask an employee to travel for work, the cost of that travel is a business cost. The employee should not carry it. Transport, accommodation and meals during a work trip are normally covered by the employer.

Your contract, your internal policy and the applicable collective agreement set the details. Many collective agreements have their own rules on travel allowances. They can be more generous than your own policy. You need to check which agreement applies to the role before you write the policy.

## What counts as business travel?

Travel away from the usual place of work, for a work reason. The rules often depend on where the trip goes. A trip within the same municipality is treated differently from a trip outside it. A trip abroad is treated differently again.

The daily commute is not business travel. Do not reimburse it as if it were.

## Can I pay a flat per diem instead of collecting receipts?

Yes, in many cases. This is often called a trip allowance. It saves admin and gives the employee a clear, predictable amount.

There is a catch. Part of a flat allowance can be tax-free and part can be treated as taxable pay. The split depends on the type of trip and on how you structure the payment. If you treat it wrongly, the employee pays tax they should not pay, or you face a payroll correction later.

The cleaner the structure, the fewer problems. Decide in advance which model you use and write it down.

## Can I mix the two systems?

Yes, but be careful. A common approach is to reimburse transport and accommodation against receipts, and pay a flat amount for meals. This works well when the policy is written clearly. It fails when the rules change from trip to trip.

Do not pay a flat allowance and also reimburse the same cost. That is a double payment and it creates a payroll issue.

## What paperwork do I need?

For documented reimbursements, keep the invoices and receipts. Italian invoices and fiscal receipts have their own format. A card slip alone is often not enough.

For flat allowances, keep a record of the trip: the dates, the destination and the business reason. This is the proof that the allowance relates to real travel.

Ask the employee to submit an expense report in a fixed format and by a fixed deadline. Late claims are a common source of disputes.

## How are reimbursements shown on the payslip?

Amounts that are properly documented and fall under the tax-free rules appear separately from salary. Amounts that go beyond those rules are added to taxable pay. The payroll provider handles this. Your job is to give clean data on time.

## What about the employee's own car?

Some employees use a private vehicle for work trips. You can reimburse the use of the car, but the method must follow the rules for mileage reimbursement. Fuel receipts alone do not always cover it. Agree the method before the first trip.

## What about travel abroad?

Trips outside Italy often use a different allowance logic. Local costs differ by country, and the payroll treatment changes too. Set a rule for each destination type and check it with your payroll provider.

If an employee works abroad for long periods, other questions arise, such as social security and tax residence. Do not treat a long assignment like a short business trip.

## Does a travel policy help?

Yes. A written policy answers most questions before they start. It should say:

- which costs you cover
- whether you pay receipts, flat allowances, or both
- how the employee submits claims
- who approves them
- how fast you pay

Share it at hiring. Italian employees expect clear terms in writing, and a clear policy reduces disputes.

## Common mistakes

- Paying flat amounts with no written rule behind them.
- Ignoring the collective agreement that applies to the role.
- Reimbursing without proper receipts.
- Paying the same cost twice.
- Treating all trips the same, whether local, national or abroad.
- Sending expense data to payroll late.

## How an Employer of Record helps

If you hire through an Employer of Record (EOR), the EOR is the legal employer in Italy. It runs payroll and applies the right treatment to each payment. You set the travel rules for the business. The EOR checks that they fit the contract and the applicable agreement, then processes the claims correctly.

This removes a lot of guesswork. You keep control of the budget and the approvals. The EOR handles the Italian side.

## The short answer

Yes, but not in the way most people hope. A foreign company can employ someone who lives in Italy. What it cannot do is skip the local setup that comes with being an employer there.

If you hire someone in Italy, Italian rules apply to that person's job. It does not matter where your head office is. The employee works in Italy, so the contract, pay slips, taxes and social security follow Italian practice.

That leaves you with a few realistic ways to do it. Here they are in plain terms.

## Option 1: Hire directly, with no local company

This is what people usually mean by "direct employment". Your foreign company signs the contract and pays the person itself.

It is possible in principle. In practice it is hard. You still need to:

- register as an employer with the Italian authorities
- run payroll that follows Italian rules
- pay employer and employee social contributions
- withhold income tax from the salary
- follow the national collective agreement that applies to the role
- provide the benefits and leave that Italian employees expect

You need local knowledge for each of these. Most foreign companies do not have it in-house. Mistakes are common, and the employee, not only you, feels the effects.

There is also a tax question. Having an employee working for you in Italy can lead the Italian tax authorities to say your company has a taxable presence there. This depends on what the person does. Ask a local adviser before you assume it will not apply to you.

Direct hiring can work if you already have Italian advisers and a clear plan. For a first hire, it is rarely the easy path.

## Option 2: Open your own Italian company or branch

You can set up a local subsidiary or a branch. That gives you a proper home for Italian employees.

The upside is full control. The employees work for a company that exists in Italy. You build your own presence in the market.

The downside is effort. You need to set up the entity, open a bank account, appoint someone to run it, and keep accounts and filings in order. You also pay for accountants and payroll providers on an ongoing basis. If you only want to hire one or a few people, this can be a lot of overhead. It makes more sense when you plan a real, lasting business in Italy.

## Option 3: Treat the person as a contractor

Some companies ask the person to invoice them as a freelancer. It looks simple. It is often the riskiest choice.

Italian rules look at how the work is really done, not at what the contract is called. If the person works set hours, follows your instructions, and works only for you, the arrangement may be treated as employment anyway. That can mean back payments and penalties.

Contractors make sense for real independent work: a project, a specialist, someone with several clients. They are not a shortcut for a full-time team member.

## Option 4: Use an Employer of Record (EOR)

An Employer of Record is a local company that becomes the legal employer of your person in Italy. You choose the person and decide the work. The EOR handles the paperwork around it.

In practice, the EOR:

- issues a compliant Italian employment contract
- runs payroll and pays the person on time
- pays taxes and social contributions
- keeps up with the right collective agreement
- deals with the authorities
- can help with visas and relocation if the person is coming from abroad

You pay the EOR a service fee on top of the employment costs. In return, you do not need your own Italian entity.

This is the fastest route for a first hire or a small team. It also works well when you want to test the market before committing to a company of your own. If you later set up a subsidiary, the employees can usually move across to it.

The trade-off is that the EOR is the legal employer. You manage the day-to-day work, but contract changes and dismissals go through the EOR and must follow Italian rules.

## How to choose

A few questions help:

- **How many people will you hire?** One or a few points to an EOR. A large team points to your own entity.
- **How long do you plan to stay?** A short test points to an EOR. A long-term base points to a subsidiary.
- **Do you have Italian advisers already?** If yes, direct hiring or your own entity gets easier.
- **Does the person really work independently?** Only then is a contractor arrangement safe.

Whatever you pick, get the setup right from the start. Fixing a wrong arrangement later costs more than doing it properly now.

## Bottom line

You can employ someone in Italy without being Italian. But the employment has to run through an Italian-compliant setup. For most foreign companies hiring their first person, an Employer of Record is the simplest way to do that.

Yes. A company that set up an Italian entity can move its people back to an Employer of Record (EOR). It is less common than the other direction, but it happens, and it is workable if you plan it.

This article covers the reasons companies reverse course, what changes for employees, and what to settle before you start.

## Why companies go back to an EOR

The entity made sense when you expected steady growth. Then plans change. These are the usual triggers.

**Headcount falls.** A small team does not justify the fixed work of running a company. That work includes accounting, statutory filings, payroll and an administrator.

**The market is paused.** Leadership wants to keep a presence in Italy but cut fixed costs while it reassesses.

**A restructuring or acquisition.** The group is consolidating legal entities and wants fewer of them to maintain.

**The entity was premature.** You opened it before you had proof of demand. Now you want a lighter way to keep the team while you test.

**Management load.** Nobody in the group wants to own Italian compliance any more.

## What the move actually is

In plain terms, the employer changes. Today your entity is the employer. After the move, the EOR is. The employees do the same work for the same business, but their contract sits with a different legal employer.

This is a transfer of employment, not a layoff followed by a rehire. That distinction matters. It affects seniority, accrued rights and how employees see the change.

## What employees care about

Employees will ask the same questions in every case.

- Will my length of service be recognised?
- Will my pay and benefits stay the same?
- Will my accrued leave and end-of-service entitlements be protected?
- Who do I contact for payroll and HR questions?

You should have clear written answers before you announce anything. Italian employment rules give workers real protections. A poorly handled transfer can create disputes that cost far more than the entity ever did. Treat consent and communication as part of the project, not as paperwork at the end.

## Steps to plan

**1. Decide the scope.** Are you moving everyone or only some roles? Will the entity close, or stay as a dormant shell?

**2. Map every contract.** List each employee, their collective agreement, role level, pay, benefits and any individual agreements. The EOR needs this to replicate terms accurately.

**3. Settle accrued entitlements.** Decide with your advisors whether accrued items such as leave and end-of-service pay are paid out or carried over. Both can work. The choice must be documented and agreed.

**4. Agree the transfer in writing.** Each employee should understand and accept the new employer arrangement. Your Italian labour counsel should review the documents.

**5. Plan the payroll cutover.** Pick a clean switch point at a pay period boundary. Avoid overlap, where two employers pay the same person, and avoid gaps.

**6. Handle registrations.** Social security and tax registrations tied to the entity as employer need to be closed or updated. The EOR registers the employees under its own accounts.

**7. Deal with the entity itself.** Do not start winding it down until every employee has moved and the final payroll filings are done. Contracts, premises, bank accounts and data all need an owner during the transition.

## Risks to watch

**Continuity gaps.** If service is not clearly recognised, employees can claim they lost rights.

**Your role in the work.** The EOR is the legal employer. You still direct the daily work. Keep that line clear, and do not let your group set contract terms outside the EOR agreement.

**Timing with the entity's closure.** Closing too early leaves filings unfinished. Closing too late keeps costs running.

**Tax exposure.** If employees keep doing senior or deal-making work, your group may still carry tax questions about its presence in Italy. Get advice before you decide the entity can go.

## When it is not the right move

If you plan to hire many people over the long term, the entity may still be the better structure. Going back to an EOR fits best when your Italian team is small, uncertain or temporary. It also fits when you want to hand off compliance work and keep the people.

If you expect to grow again later, the path stays open. Many companies start with an EOR, open an entity, and some later return to an EOR. The structure should follow your business needs, not the other way round.

## Practical advice

Start with a full contract review, not a price comparison. Know your employees' terms before you speak to an EOR. A good provider will ask for those details first, because accurate terms are the base of a clean transfer.

Talk to employees early and plainly. Most worries come from silence.

Get the legal documents checked by someone qualified in Italian employment matters. This article is general information, not legal advice.

If you hire in Italy, you will hear the term CCNL very early. It stands for Contratto Collettivo Nazionale di Lavoro, or national collective labour agreement. It is not a side topic. It shapes almost every term of an Italian employment contract.

## What a CCNL is

A CCNL is an agreement between employer associations and trade unions for a given sector. It sets the rules that apply to everyone working in that sector, whether the employer is large, small, Italian or foreign.

The agreement covers the core terms of the job:

- Job classification and grade levels
- Minimum pay for each level
- Working hours and overtime rules
- Paid leave and sick pay
- Notice periods
- Extra pay elements and benefits
- Rules on probation and on fixed-term work

Many of these terms are not left to the employer's choice. The contract you sign with an employee refers to the CCNL, and the CCNL fills in the rest.

## Why every job ends up under one

Italy has no single national minimum wage set by statute. In practice, the CCNL fills that role. Courts use the pay levels in the relevant agreement as the benchmark for what counts as fair pay. If you pay below that benchmark, an employee can claim the difference.

So even when a CCNL is not formally binding on your company, it still applies in practice. Employers who try to avoid it usually end up with disputes, back pay claims and problems with the social security authorities.

The simple rule: every employee has a CCNL. The only real question is which one.

## Choosing the right CCNL

The CCNL is not chosen by the employee or by the foreign parent company. It follows the main activity of the employer in Italy. A software firm, a restaurant group and a manufacturing business each fall under a different agreement.

This matters for an international employer because your home-country logic may not map cleanly. A role you call "sales" or "engineering" at home may sit in a different sector in Italy, depending on what the Italian activity really is. The wrong choice can mean wrong pay levels, wrong leave rules and wrong contributions.

Several agreements can look similar on paper. They differ in pay tables, in the benefits they add and in how much flexibility they give you. Picking one is a business decision with a cost attached, and it should be made before the offer letter goes out.

## What it means for your budget

The salary you agree with a candidate is only one part of the cost. The CCNL adds to it in several ways.

**Minimum pay.** Each grade has a floor. You can pay above it, never below it.

**Extra pay elements.** Many agreements add pay components on top of the base salary. Your total annual cost can be higher than a simple monthly figure suggests.

**Benefits.** Some agreements require contributions to supplementary pension funds or health funds. These are part of the package, not optional extras.

**Leave and sickness.** The agreement defines how much paid leave staff receive and how sickness is paid. The employer often carries part of that cost.

**Termination terms.** Notice periods and the process for ending a contract depend on the grade and the agreement.

When you compare Italy to another country, compare the full cost under the right CCNL, not the headline salary.

## What it means for your HR practice

Italian employment is rules-based. The CCNL gives employees clear rights, and they know them. Payslips follow the agreement line by line. Job titles map to grades, and moving someone to a new grade has pay consequences.

This helps you in one way. The rules are known in advance, so you can plan. It limits you in another way. You cannot freely rewrite terms for one person without checking the agreement first.

A few habits help:

- Decide the grade before you decide the title.
- Keep job descriptions close to what the person really does. Grade disputes often start with a gap between the two.
- Check the agreement before promising any benefit in writing.
- Review the agreement when it is renewed, because pay tables and terms change.

## Where an Employer of Record helps

If you have no Italian entity, you still need a compliant employment relationship. An Employer of Record (EOR) hires the person in Italy on your behalf. It applies the right CCNL, issues the contract, runs payroll and handles the contributions.

You direct the daily work. The EOR carries the employer obligations under the agreement. That removes the need to learn each sector's rules yourself before you can make your first hire.

It also helps with the early decisions: which CCNL fits the role, which grade is correct, and what the real annual cost will be. Getting those right at the start is far cheaper than fixing them later.

## The short version

In Italy, the CCNL is the rulebook for the job. It sets pay floors, leave, notice and benefits. You do not opt out of it, and you should not guess which one applies. Pick the right agreement, budget for the full cost, and keep your contracts aligned with it.

You want to hire someone in Italy. You have not decided how. There are three common routes: engage a contractor, use an Employer of Record (EOR), or set up your own Italian entity. Each fits a different situation. This article compares them on speed, risk and cost, without a favourite.

## Contractor

A contractor is self-employed. They invoice you for a service. You do not put them on payroll.

**Speed.** This is the fastest route on paper. You sign a services agreement and start. There is no entity to register and no payroll to run.

**Risk.** This is where contractors get complicated. Italian authorities and courts look at how the work is really done, not at what the contract says. If the person works set hours, follows your instructions, uses your tools and works only for you, the arrangement can be treated as employment. The consequences can include back contributions, penalties and claims from the worker. The risk grows the longer the relationship lasts and the more the person is embedded in your team.

**Cost.** The visible cost is low. You pay the invoice and nothing else. The hidden cost is the exposure if the relationship is reclassified. Contractors also tend to expect a higher rate, because they carry their own taxes, contributions and downtime.

**Best for.** Short projects, specialists with several clients, and work you do not need to direct day to day.

## Employer of Record

An EOR becomes the legal employer in Italy. You choose the person and direct the work. The EOR issues the employment contract, runs payroll, pays contributions and handles the administration that comes with having an employee.

**Speed.** Usually fast, because the EOR already has an Italian setup. You do not wait for incorporation. The time it takes depends mostly on how quickly you agree the role and terms with the candidate, and on any work authorisation needed if the person is not already entitled to work in Italy.

**Risk.** Lower than with a contractor, because the worker is a real employee under the correct national collective agreement. You still carry business risk. You decide who to hire, how they perform and when the role ends, and dismissal in Italy follows its own rules. A good EOR helps you manage that, but it cannot remove it. You also depend on the provider, so check how they handle payroll errors, data and exit.

**Cost.** You pay the employee's full employment cost plus the EOR's fee. There are no incorporation or accounting costs of your own. For a small team, this is often cheaper than running an entity. As headcount grows, the fee adds up and the comparison can change.

**Best for.** Testing the market, hiring a few people, or hiring where you need compliance without building local infrastructure.

## Own Italian entity

You register a company in Italy and employ people directly.

**Speed.** The slowest route to the first hire. You must incorporate, open a bank account, register with the tax and social security bodies, set up payroll and find an accountant and a labour consultant. Each step has its own waiting time.

**Risk.** You become fully responsible for compliance. That includes payroll, contributions, health and safety, employment contracts, reporting and corporate filings. The legal protection of a local company is real, and so is the burden. Mistakes are yours.

**Cost.** Highest at the start, because of setup and ongoing professional fees. It becomes more efficient when you have enough people and enough long-term commitment to spread those fixed costs. You also gain full control over contracts, benefits and how the business is presented locally.

**Best for.** Companies with a long-term plan in Italy, a team that will grow, or customers and partners who expect a local company.

## How to choose

Ask these questions.

- **Will the person work like an employee?** If you set their hours and direct their tasks, a contractor is the wrong tool. Use an EOR or an entity.
- **How sure are you about Italy?** If you are still testing, avoid fixed costs. A contractor or an EOR keeps you flexible.
- **How many people will you hire?** A few people suit an EOR. A larger team usually justifies an entity.
- **How fast do you need to start?** Contractor and EOR are quicker. An entity takes planning.
- **Who do you want to carry the admin?** With an EOR, the provider does. With an entity, you do.

Many companies move through these routes in order. They start with a contractor for a defined project, move to an EOR when the person becomes a core team member, and open an entity once the Italian operation is large enough to stand on its own. The move from EOR to entity is common and can be planned, so starting with an EOR does not lock you in.

No route is the best in general. The right one depends on the role, the time horizon and how much risk and admin you want to hold yourself.

Your employee has accepted a role in Italy. The next question is always the same: what will life cost there? This FAQ covers housing and daily costs by city. It helps you plan relocation packages and set expectations early.

We give no price tables here. Rents and prices change fast and differ by street. Use this as a guide to what drives costs, then check current local listings before you fix any allowance.

## Is Italy expensive to live in?

It depends on the city. Italy has no single cost level. Large northern business cities tend to cost more, mostly because of rent. Smaller cities and much of the south tend to cost less. Daily costs such as food and local transport vary less than housing does.

## Which city is the most expensive for housing?

The big business centers in the north usually top the list. Demand from professionals and international companies pushes rents up, especially close to the center and near good transport links. Rome and Florence are also costly in their central areas. Tourism pressure affects the supply of long-term rentals in popular historic districts.

## Where can staff live for less?

Mid-sized cities often offer a better balance. Think of university towns and regional capitals with good rail links. Staff can also live outside a large city and commute. Suburbs and nearby towns cost less than the center, but check the train or metro connection before you recommend them.

## How does renting work for a newcomer?

Most rentals go through a real estate agent or a private landlord. Expect a security deposit and an agency fee in many cases. Landlords often ask for proof of income and a local contract. A foreign employee with no Italian history may find this slow. Employer support helps a lot here. A letter confirming the job and the salary makes landlords more comfortable.

Contracts also differ in length and terms. Some are standard long-term leases. Others are shorter and aimed at students or temporary workers. Your employee should read the type of contract carefully before signing.

## Is furnished or unfurnished better?

Unfurnished flats in Italy are sometimes truly empty, with no kitchen fittings. That is a cost many newcomers do not expect. Furnished flats cost more per month but save setup money and time. For a short assignment, furnished is usually the practical choice. For a long stay, unfurnished can be cheaper over time.

## What are the bills on top of rent?

Plan for electricity, gas, water, internet and mobile. There is also a local waste tax, and building service charges in apartment blocks. Heating costs depend on the region and the building. Colder northern areas use more heating. Older buildings with poor insulation cost more to run. Ask the landlord which charges are included in the rent and which are not.

## What about food and groceries?

Groceries are reasonable if staff shop at local markets and regular supermarkets. Eating out ranges widely. A simple lunch near an office is affordable. A dinner in a tourist area is not. Prices in the center of Rome, Florence or Venice are higher than in residential districts. Coffee at the bar counter is cheap by international standards. Sitting at a table costs more.

## How much do transport costs matter?

In most large cities, public transport is the cheapest way to get around. Monthly and yearly passes usually cost less than paying per trip. Many staff do not need a car in cities with good metro, tram and bus networks. A car adds fuel, insurance, parking and road tolls. In smaller towns and rural areas a car is often needed, which raises the monthly budget.

## What about healthcare and schooling?

The public health system covers residents who register for it. Some employees also choose private insurance for shorter waiting times. Families with children should look at schools early. Public schools are free to attend. International schools exist in the larger cities and are a major cost for families who choose them. Add this to the relocation budget if the employee has children.

## How should we set a relocation allowance?

Start from housing, since it is the largest and most variable item. Then add a margin for bills, transport and setup costs. Treat each city as its own case. A flat allowance for all of Italy will be too low for some staff and too high for others.

A few simple rules help:

- Set the allowance by destination city, not by country.
- Pay for temporary housing so staff can search in person.
- Help with the rental paperwork and the landlord letter.
- Review the allowance when the lease is renewed.

## Can we offer a lower package in the south?

You can adjust for local costs, but be careful. Salary levels in Italy are tied to national collective agreements, and the minimum does not change with the city. Cost differences are better handled through housing support than through pay below the contractual level.

## What is the best way to check real prices?

Look at current listings on the main Italian property sites for the exact neighborhood. Ask local contacts or your employer of record for a view on the market. Prices in the same city can differ a lot between districts. A local check before you commit saves money on both sides.

You hire someone in Italy. Their payroll file, contract and performance notes now exist in Italy. Soon your head office wants a copy. Your HR platform may sit on another continent. At that point GDPR applies, and so does Italian data protection law.

This article covers the basics. It is not legal advice. It will help you ask the right questions.

## Why GDPR applies to you

GDPR protects people in the European Union. It does not matter where your company is based. If you handle personal data of an employee working in Italy, you are in scope. The regulator in Italy is the Garante per la protezione dei dati personali. It is active on employment topics.

Italy also has its own rules on top of GDPR. They cover workplace monitoring, among other things. Local rules often matter more than foreign HR teams expect.

## Who is the controller?

Start with roles. The controller decides why and how personal data is used. The processor acts on the controller's instructions.

In an Employer of Record model, the EOR is the legal employer in Italy. It is usually a controller for the data it needs to run employment: payroll, tax, social security, contracts. Your company may also be a controller for data it uses to direct the work, such as objectives, reviews and access to its systems. In practice the two can be joint controllers for some data.

Do not leave this vague. Write down who decides what. Put it in your service agreement and in the privacy notice the employee receives.

## Pick a legal basis that works

Every use of personal data needs a legal basis. For HR data, the common ones are:

- The employment contract. Payroll, benefits and onboarding fit here.
- A legal obligation. Tax filings and social security reporting fit here.
- Legitimate interest. This can cover some internal reporting, but you must weigh it against the employee's rights.

Be careful with consent. An employee depends on the employer, so consent is rarely seen as freely given. Do not build your HR processes on it.

## Special categories need more care

Some data is more sensitive. Health information, union membership, religion and similar details get stronger protection. Sick leave records and medical certificates are the usual case in HR.

Share these only with people who need them. Your head office rarely needs a diagnosis. It may only need to know that someone is absent.

## Moving data within and outside the EU

Data can move freely inside the European Economic Area. Once it leaves, you need a transfer tool.

The main options are:

- **Adequacy decision.** The European Commission has decided that a country offers equivalent protection. Data can flow to it without extra steps.
- **Standard contractual clauses.** Approved contract terms between the sender and the receiver. This is the most common route for company groups and software vendors.
- **Binding corporate rules.** Internal group rules approved by regulators. They suit large groups and take time to set up.

With standard clauses, you also need to check whether the law in the receiving country undermines the protection. Document that assessment. Add technical safeguards such as encryption where they help.

Remember the vendors. Your payroll tool, cloud storage and support desk may each move data abroad. Each transfer needs its own basis.

## Share less by default

Data minimisation is a core GDPR principle. Ask what your head office really needs.

A finance team usually needs total employment cost, not bank details. A line manager needs working hours and performance data, not tax codes. Aggregated reports solve many requests without exposing individual files.

Set retention periods too. Keep data only as long as there is a reason. Italian law requires some records to be kept for set periods, so align your deletion rules with those duties.

## Monitoring employees

Italian law is strict about tools that can monitor workers at a distance. This includes cameras, location tracking, and software that logs activity. Some tools need a union agreement or authorisation from the labour authorities before you use them.

Foreign companies often roll out global monitoring or security software without checking this. Ask before you deploy anything that tracks behaviour. Employees must also be told clearly what is tracked and why.

## Employee rights

Italian employees can ask what data you hold, ask for corrections, and in some cases ask for deletion or restriction. You must answer without undue delay.

Plan for this before the first request arrives. Know where HR data lives. Know who handles requests. When data sits in several systems across several countries, requests become slow and risky.

## Breaches

If personal data is lost, leaked or accessed without permission, you may have to notify the Garante quickly. You may also have to tell the affected employees. Agree in advance who does what between your company, your EOR and your vendors. A breach is the wrong time to find out nobody owns the process.

## A short checklist

- Map what HR data you hold on Italian employees and where it goes.
- Define controller and processor roles in writing.
- Confirm the legal basis for each use.
- Put a transfer tool in place for every flow outside the EEA.
- Limit access to special category data.
- Check Italian rules before deploying any monitoring tool.
- Give employees a clear privacy notice in Italian.
- Set a process for access requests and breaches.

## How an EOR helps

A good EOR already runs Italian payroll and HR within local rules. It holds the employment records, applies retention rules and handles requests from employees. You still carry responsibility for data you receive and use. The easiest approach is to receive only what you need, through a clear agreement.

Italian candidates have never heard of your company. That is normal. It also means they will check you before they answer your message. They will look at your website, your LinkedIn page, your job post and how you write back. If these look thin, the candidate assumes risk and moves on.

This checklist covers the signals that make an unknown foreign employer look real. None of it costs much. Most of it is about being clear.

## Show who is behind the company

Candidates want to know that real people stand behind the offer. A logo and a careers page are not enough.

- Name the founders or leaders, with photos and honest bios.
- Link to their personal professional profiles.
- State where the company is registered and what it does, in plain words.
- Give a way to reach a human: a named contact, not only a form.

If the hiring manager is visible and answers questions, the company stops being an anonymous foreign name.

## Explain how the employment works in Italy

The biggest fear is practical. Who is my employer? Who pays me? Where do my contributions go? A foreign company without an Italian entity can feel risky to an Italian professional.

Say it early and clearly:

- Who the legal employer is in Italy.
- That the contract follows Italian rules and the applicable national collective agreement.
- That payroll and social contributions are handled locally.
- Who the candidate calls if something goes wrong with pay or paperwork.

An Employer of Record (EOR) model answers these points directly. The candidate gets an Italian contract and local administration. You keep day-to-day management. Say this on the job page, not only at offer stage.

## Write job posts like an Italian employer would

A post translated word by word from another market looks careless. Review it for these points.

- Write in good Italian, or good English if the role is truly international. Have a native speaker read it.
- Use the job titles Italian professionals actually search for.
- State the contract type, work location or remote arrangement, and the reporting line.
- Give a salary range. Italian candidates notice when it is missing.
- Describe the real tasks, not a list of buzzwords.

A clear post tells the candidate you understand the local market.

## Be transparent about pay and benefits

Compensation in Italy is read as gross annual pay, with benefits and any additional monthly payments described separately. Foreign companies often quote a single figure with no breakdown. That raises suspicion.

Show the structure. Say what is fixed and what is variable. Say what the company adds, such as equipment, training or flexible hours. If you do not know the local norms, ask your EOR partner to check your offer before you publish it.

## Make the company findable

Before replying, a candidate will search your name. Check what they find.

- A professional website with an About page and a clear product or service description.
- A complete company profile on the main professional network, with current staff listed.
- Reviews or employee comments, even if few. Silence is read as a warning.
- A press mention, customer list or case study that proves the business exists.

If you have no Italian presence, say why you are hiring there. A short, honest reason works better than vague ambition.

## Treat the process as part of the brand

How you run hiring tells candidates how you will run employment.

- Reply quickly and say what happens next.
- Keep interviews on time and use a named interviewer.
- Tell candidates the full process up front.
- Send the written offer in a format they can show a lawyer, a union contact or family.
- Never ask for sensitive documents before an offer is made.

Candidates talk to each other. A careless process travels faster than any careers page.

## Prepare for the questions you will get

Expect candidates to ask about stability. Will the company still be here next year? Is the Italian role a test? Prepare honest answers. If the role is new and the team is small, say so, and explain the plan. Candidates accept uncertainty more easily than evasion.

Also be ready for questions about notice, leave, sick pay and termination. You do not need to recite the law. You need a partner who can answer correctly and quickly.

## A short self-check

Before you publish your first Italian job post, ask yourself:

- Can a stranger tell who runs the company within a minute?
- Is the legal employer named?
- Does the post include pay, contract type and location?
- Is the language natural to a local reader?
- Would you accept the offer if you were the candidate?

If any answer is no, fix it first. Credibility is not built by claims. It is built by removing reasons to doubt you.
