Hiring in Italy starts well before the first contract. Companies that prepare the basics move faster and avoid rework. This checklist covers what to settle before you set up a local entity, or before you choose an Employer of Record (EOR) instead.

## Decide the route first

You have two main paths. You can open your own Italian entity. Or you can use an Employer of Record (EOR), which employs the person on your behalf while you direct the daily work.

Ask these questions before you pick:

- Do you plan to hire many people in Italy, or only a few?
- Do you need a local presence for customers, contracts or regulators?
- How soon does the first hire need to start?
- Are you testing the market, or committing to it?

A short test with a small team often fits an EOR. A long-term local operation often fits an entity. Write the answer down. It shapes everything below.

## Corporate documents

Whether you open an entity or not, your parent company needs clean records. Gather these early:

- Certificate of incorporation or equivalent registry extract
- Articles of association or bylaws
- Proof of the registered address
- A list of directors and authorised signatories
- Proof of who owns the company

Italian authorities and banks often ask for official translations and legalisation of foreign documents. Ask your advisor which documents need an apostille or a sworn translation. Start this early. It is slow and it blocks other steps.

## People and signatories

Someone must be able to sign for the company in Italy. Decide who:

- Who will be the legal representative of the Italian entity?
- Who approves hiring decisions?
- Who owns the relationship with the Italian payroll and tax providers?

If the person is not in Italy, check what identification and tax codes they need to act locally. Foreign directors usually need an Italian tax code before they can sign or open accounts.

## Banking and funding

An Italian entity needs a local bank account. Opening one can take time, and banks ask many questions about the parent group and its owners. Prepare:

- A clear description of what the entity will do
- Ownership and beneficial owner details
- A plan for how you will fund payroll and running costs

Decide how salaries will be funded each month. Late funding delays pay, and late pay creates problems with employees and with authorities.

## Registrations and compliance setup

An employer in Italy must be registered with the right bodies for tax, social security and workplace insurance. You also need a payroll process, a way to issue payslips, and a way to file the required reports on time.

Before you start, confirm:

- Who will run payroll and who will check it
- Who will handle social security and tax filings
- Who will keep employee records in the required form
- Who will handle workplace health and safety duties

With an EOR, these duties sit with the EOR. You still need to supply accurate data on time.

## Know your collective agreement

Italy uses national collective agreements by sector. They set minimum pay levels, working hours, leave, notice and other terms. The agreement that applies depends on your business activity and the role.

Before you write an offer, identify the agreement that fits. Do not copy the terms from another country. Check the job level and the pay against that agreement. This single step prevents many disputes later.

## Prepare the hiring package

Have these ready before you approach candidates:

- A clear job description and reporting line
- A salary range checked against the applicable agreement
- A start date that leaves time for registrations
- A draft of the employment terms, reviewed locally
- A plan for equipment, software access and data protection

The employment contract in Italy should be in line with local rules and often in Italian. Plan for that.

## If the hire is not an EU citizen

If the person needs permission to live and work in Italy, treat this as a separate project. It has its own documents, its own timeline and its own risks. Do not promise a start date until the route is confirmed. Check whether the person already has the right to work, and what type of permit would apply.

## Data protection and policies

You will process personal data of Italian employees. Prepare a privacy notice, a basic data processing record and a plan for how HR data is stored and shared with the parent company. Add internal policies that employees must receive, such as IT use and health and safety information.

## Quick checklist

- Route chosen: own entity or EOR
- Parent company documents gathered and translated
- Legal representative and signatories named
- Bank and funding plan ready
- Payroll and filing owners assigned
- Collective agreement identified
- Job description, pay and start date agreed
- Work permit route checked, if needed
- Data protection basics prepared

If most of these are done, you are ready to move. If several are missing, fix them before you commit to a start date.

You hired someone in Italy who will work from home. Now they need a working desk, a reliable laptop and a clear policy. This is a practical list of what to prepare, and what to decide before the first day.

## Start with who owns what

Decide early whether the company supplies the equipment or the employee uses their own. For most foreign employers, company-owned equipment is the cleaner choice. It keeps data on devices you control. It also avoids disputes about wear, repairs and returns.

Write the rule down. Put it in the remote work policy and the employment paperwork. Your employer of record (EOR) can help you align the policy with the employment contract and local practice.

## Core hardware

Give the employee what they need to do the job without workarounds.

- **Laptop.** Pick a model that fits the role. Developers and designers need more power than support staff.
- **External monitor.** A second screen reduces strain and speeds up daily work.
- **Keyboard and mouse.** Standard laptop keyboards are poor for full days of typing.
- **Headset with microphone.** Calls with a distributed team depend on clear audio.
- **Webcam.** Many laptop cameras are weak. A separate one helps in client meetings.
- **Laptop stand or monitor arm.** Screens should sit at eye level.

Buy an Italian-layout keyboard if the employee prefers it. Ask before you ship. Typing on the wrong layout is a small thing that annoys people every day.

## Furniture

The home workstation should be safe and comfortable. At minimum:

- A proper desk or table with enough depth for a monitor.
- An ergonomic chair with adjustable height and back support.
- Good lighting, ideally a desk lamp in addition to natural light.
- A footrest, if the employee asks for one.

Many employers offer a one-time setup budget instead of buying furniture directly. This is simpler to run. It also lets the employee choose items that fit their space. Set clear limits on what the budget covers and ask for receipts.

## Connectivity

A remote role is only as good as the connection behind it. Check these points before the start date.

- Confirm the employee has a stable home broadband line.
- Agree who pays for internet and phone use, and how. Some companies pay a fixed monthly contribution. Others reimburse a share of the bill.
- Consider a mobile hotspot as a backup for outages.
- Ask the employee to use a wired connection for important calls where possible.

Connection quality varies by area in Italy. Cities usually have good options. Smaller towns and rural areas can be slower. Ask early, not after the first dropped call.

## Security setup

Company devices need protection from day one.

- Enable full-disk encryption on every laptop.
- Use a device management tool so you can lock or wipe a lost machine.
- Require multi-factor authentication on all company accounts.
- Provide a password manager.
- Use a VPN or zero-trust access for internal systems.
- Tell employees not to share work devices with family members.

Personal data of Italian staff and customers falls under European data protection rules. Keep monitoring light and transparent. Do not install tools that track employees in ways they have not been told about. Check your plans with your EOR before rollout.

## Health and safety

The employer stays responsible for the safety of the work it asks people to do, including at home. In practice this means giving guidance on a safe workstation, and keeping a record that you did so. Ask your EOR what is expected for remote employees in Italy and how to document it.

## Delivery and customs

If you ship from outside the EU, plan for customs. Delays are common. Ship early and track the parcel. Use a courier that handles import paperwork. Another option is to buy the equipment locally in Italy and have it delivered directly to the employee. This avoids duties and speeds up the start.

Buying locally also makes warranty claims and repairs easier.

## Day-one checklist

Send this list to the manager before the employee starts.

1. Laptop is configured, encrypted and enrolled in device management.
2. Accounts and access are ready.
3. Peripherals have arrived and are tested.
4. Internet allowance is agreed in writing.
5. Safety guidance has been sent.
6. A contact person is named for equipment problems.

## Repairs, upgrades and returns

Equipment breaks. Plan for it. Name one person who handles replacements. Set a target time for fixing issues. Keep a spare loaner laptop if the team is large enough.

When employment ends, the employee must return company property. Arrange prepaid return shipping and give a clear deadline. Keep an inventory with serial numbers so you know what is out there.

## Keep it simple

A good setup is not expensive or complicated. Give people a decent laptop, a screen, a chair and a stable connection. Write the rules down. Keep records. Then let them work.

Foreign companies often want to give their Italian hires the same equity plan used everywhere else. It is a fair wish. It is also where many hiring plans hit trouble. Italy treats equity differently from many other countries. This article gives you the main ideas so you can plan before you grant anything.

This is general awareness, not tax advice. Rules change, and the details depend on the plan and on the person.

## Equity is usually treated as employment income

In Italy, shares or options given because of a job are generally seen as a form of pay. That has a simple consequence. The value an employee receives can be taxed as employment income, not as a capital gain. Employment income is normally taxed at higher rates than investment gains.

The label in your home country does not decide the outcome. A plan called a "share purchase scheme" or "incentive award" can still be treated as pay in Italy. What matters is the link between the benefit and the work.

## The timing question

For any equity award, ask when the tax event happens. There are several possible moments:

- When the award is granted.
- When it vests.
- When an option is exercised.
- When the shares are sold.

In Italy, the taxable moment often falls at exercise or at the point the employee gets the shares, not at grant. But the exact rule depends on how the plan is built. A plan with restrictions, a lock-up or a forfeiture clause may be treated differently from a plain grant.

The risk for you is a tax bill that arrives before the employee has any cash. If the shares are not listed and cannot be sold, the employee may owe tax on value they cannot touch. Good plan design looks at this early.

## Social contributions can apply too

Tax is only half of the picture. Equity treated as pay can also bring social security contributions, for both the employee and the employer. Foreign companies often forget this. They budget for the award and not for the employer cost that follows it.

This matters for your total cost of employment. When you compare the cost of an Italian hire with a hire elsewhere, include the contribution side of any equity you plan to grant.

## Who withholds and reports

Italian payroll works on withholding at source. The employer is expected to withhold tax on taxable pay and report it. When the employer is a foreign company with no Italian entity, this is a real problem. Who calculates the value? Who withholds? Who files?

If the equity comes from a foreign parent and the Italian side is not involved, the employee may be left to report it alone. That leads to errors, late filings and unhappy staff. A better setup has the Italian payroll side informed of every grant, vest and exercise, with data shared on time.

An Employer of Record (EOR) can take the Italian employer role, run payroll and handle reporting. It still needs accurate data from you. It must know the award terms, the dates and the value at each event.

## Valuation is not trivial

For listed shares, value is easy to find. For private company shares, it is not. You need a defensible valuation at the relevant date. Tax authorities can challenge a value that looks too low. Keep records of how you reached it. Use the same method each time.

## Cross-border employees need extra care

If the employee has lived or worked in other countries, more than one tax system may claim part of the benefit. Awards often vest over a long period. During that time the person may move, work remotely from abroad, or become resident elsewhere. Each change can alter who may tax what. Tax treaties help, but you need to apply them with care.

## Alternatives to think about

If a standard stock option plan looks too heavy for Italy, there are other routes:

- Cash-settled awards that track the value of your shares. They are taxed as pay, but they avoid share ownership and valuation issues for the employee.
- A local bonus plan tied to company results.
- Shares offered under a plan that fits Italian rules for employee share ownership.

Each option has its own tax and contribution profile. None is always best. The right choice depends on your company stage, your plan documents and what the employee values.

## A practical checklist

Before you offer equity to an Italian hire:

- Check how the plan will be treated for tax and contributions in Italy.
- Decide who will withhold and report.
- Plan for the case where tax is due and the employee cannot sell.
- Set a valuation method and keep records.
- Review the plan documents for local fit, including language and consent.
- Tell the candidate early what the tax result is likely to be.

The last point is often missed. Candidates compare offers. An award that looks generous on paper can feel poor once tax is clear. Honest talk at the offer stage avoids disputes later.

## Bottom line

Equity can work well in Italy. It needs planning. Treat it as pay, expect contributions, solve the withholding question, and be ready to value shares properly. Do this before the offer letter goes out, not after the first vesting date.

Posting a role in Italy is the easy part. The hard part is what happens after a candidate says yes. If you have not made a few decisions first, you will lose the candidate or delay the start date.

Use this checklist before you publish the job.

## 1. Decide how you will employ the person

This is the biggest decision. You have three realistic routes.

- Open an Italian entity and employ directly.
- Use an Employer of Record (EOR) that employs the person on your behalf.
- Engage the person as a contractor.

Contractor status is not a shortcut. If the person works under your direction, on your schedule, as part of your team, Italian rules may treat the relationship as employment anyway. Be honest about how the work will actually be done.

An entity gives you control but takes time and ongoing admin. An EOR lets you hire without an entity. You keep day-to-day management of the work. The EOR carries the legal employer role.

Pick the route first. Everything else depends on it.

## 2. Know which collective agreement applies

Italian employment is shaped by national collective agreements. They set minimum pay levels, working hours, notice periods, leave and other terms for each sector.

You do not choose a salary in a vacuum. The agreement for your sector sets the floor and the job classification. Find out which agreement fits the role before you write a salary range in the advert.

An advert that ignores the agreement will attract offers you cannot legally make.

## 3. Define the role clearly

Write down what the person will do, who they report to and where they will work. This feeds directly into the contract and the classification under the agreement.

Ask yourself:

- Is the role remote, office-based or hybrid?
- Will the person manage others?
- Will they sign contracts or represent your company?
- Do they need to travel?

Vague answers now become disputes later.

## 4. Set the salary with total cost in mind

The salary on the offer is not what the hire costs you. Employer social contributions, insurance and statutory payments sit on top. Italian pay also follows rules about additional monthly payments and accrued leave and severance that many foreign employers do not expect.

Build a full cost view before you commit to a budget. Ask for it in writing from whoever will run payroll. Then decide whether the role still makes sense at that cost.

## 5. Decide who runs payroll and compliance

Someone must register the employee, pay wages on time, file the required reports and handle social security. Italy is strict on all of this, and the paperwork is in Italian.

Choose now:

- Will you build this capability in-house?
- Will you outsource payroll to a local provider and manage the legal side yourself?
- Will an EOR cover both?

If nobody on your team reads Italian employment documents, do not plan to learn on the first hire.

## 6. Check right-to-work early

If your candidate is an EU citizen, the path is simple. If they are not, they may need a visa or permit before they can start. That process takes time and depends on the person and the role.

Do not make a start date promise until you know the candidate's status. Ask in the first conversation, in a neutral and lawful way, whether they have the right to work in Italy.

## 7. Plan the contract and the offer

The offer should match the agreement and the contract type you intend to use. Decide in advance:

- Permanent or fixed term.
- Probation period, if any.
- Notice period.
- Working hours and place of work.
- Benefits you want to add beyond the minimum.

Italian candidates often expect a clear written contract and a clear explanation of the pay structure. A loose offer letter in English will raise questions.

## 8. Prepare onboarding before day one

The new hire needs equipment, system access, a manager and a first-week plan. If you are using an EOR, also agree who handles the HR documents and who answers the employee's questions about pay slips and leave.

A good first week reduces early resignations. It also shows the candidate you are serious about the market.

## 9. Agree how you will exit if it does not work

This is the decision most teams skip. Dismissal in Italy is regulated. You cannot end the contract on short notice for any reason you like.

Understand the rules before you hire. Know the notice requirements and the grounds that are allowed. Decide who would manage a termination. It is much easier to plan this when everyone is happy.

## A quick readiness test

You are ready to post the role when you can answer yes to each of these:

- We have chosen our employment route.
- We know the collective agreement for the role.
- We have a full cost estimate.
- We know who runs payroll and compliance.
- We understand the candidate's right-to-work position.
- We have a contract outline and an onboarding plan.
- We know how termination works.

If you cannot say yes to most of these, pause the advert. A few days of preparation save weeks of delay later.

Founders often decide to move to Italy before they know how the move works. The questions below come up again and again. The answers are general. Your nationality, your role and your company structure change the details.

## Do I need a visa?

It depends on your passport. EU citizens can move freely. Citizens of other countries usually need a visa or a permit tied to a specific purpose, such as employment, self-employment or investment. The right route depends on what you will do in Italy and who will pay you.

Start this early. Visa steps involve documents from your home country, and those often take longer than expected.

## Can I work in Italy while my company is abroad?

This is the question that causes the most trouble. Working from Italy for a foreign company can create obligations for both you and the company. These may include payroll, social security and tax registration. Doing the work without a proper setup can lead to penalties later.

You have a few options. You can open a local entity. You can hire through an Employer of Record (EOR), which employs you in Italy on behalf of your company. Or you can use a different structure if your situation allows it. The EOR route is useful when you want to move now and do not want to set up a legal entity first.

## What does an Employer of Record do for a founder?

An EOR becomes your legal employer in Italy. It handles the employment contract, payroll, contributions and compliance. You keep working for your company, and your company directs your daily work.

It can also help with the practical side of the move. That includes visa support, relocation steps and registration with the Italian social security system.

An EOR is not a replacement for a long-term plan. Many founders use it to start, then open a local entity once the team grows.

## Will I pay tax in Italy?

If you live in Italy and make it your main home, you will likely become an Italian tax resident. That can affect how your income is taxed, including income from abroad. Special regimes may exist for new residents, and rules change over time.

Speak to a tax adviser before you move. Do not rely on a forum post. Your home country may also still claim a right to tax you, and a tax treaty may decide the outcome.

## What about social security and healthcare?

When you are employed in Italy, you and your employer normally pay social security contributions. These contributions connect you to the national system. Healthcare access usually follows registration as a resident.

If you come from a country with a social security agreement with Italy, you may be able to keep your contribution history. Check this before you choose your setup.

## Where should I live?

Italy is not one market. Milan, Rome, Turin and Bologna feel very different from smaller cities. Think about what you need:

- Airport and train links for travel
- A local startup or business community
- Cost of rent and daily life
- Schools, if you move with family
- Good internet

Visit before you commit. A short stay in each shortlisted city tells you more than a long article.

## How do I find housing?

Rental contracts in Italy often ask for documents you may not have yet. These can include a tax code and proof of income. Landlords may prefer tenants with a local employment contract. This is another reason an Italian employment setup helps early on.

Get your tax code as soon as you can. You need it for almost everything: contracts, utilities, a bank account and a phone plan.

## Can my family come with me?

In many cases, yes. Family members can often apply to join you through a family-related route. Requirements depend on your own permit and on your family relationships. Plan the paperwork for the whole household, not just for you.

## What documents should I prepare?

Expect to need some of these:

- A valid passport
- Your employment or service agreement
- Proof of qualifications
- Civil documents such as marriage or birth certificates, if family joins you
- Translations and legalisations where required

Check which documents need an official translation or a legal stamp. Doing this late is a common source of delay.

## What mistakes do founders make?

- They move first and sort out the employment setup later.
- They assume their home payroll still works once they live in Italy.
- They ignore tax residence until a bill arrives.
- They underestimate how long paperwork takes.
- They plan for themselves and forget their family.

## What is a sensible order of steps?

First, decide how you will be employed or engaged in Italy. Second, confirm the visa or permit route. Third, get tax and social security advice. Fourth, prepare documents. Fifth, plan housing and your arrival. Only then book the move.

Getting the order right saves time and avoids rework.

Hiring in Italy means thinking about total cost, not only salary. One tool that employers often overlook is the fringe benefit regime. It lets you give employees extra value with a lighter tax and contribution burden than the same amount paid as salary.

This article explains the annual cap, who gets the higher limit, and where the benefit works well in practice.

## The annual cap

The rule is simple. Benefits in kind and similar items given to an employee stay below a yearly threshold.

- The general threshold is EUR 1,000 per employee per year.
- For employees with dependent children, the threshold is EUR 2,000 per year.

The cap applies per employee, not per company. It is also an annual figure. You cannot carry unused room into the next period as a bank of credit.

We classify this figure as secondary. Thresholds and conditions in this area change with budget laws. Confirm the current limit with your payroll provider before you publish a benefits policy.

## Why the cap matters for cost

A euro paid as salary is taxed for the employee and carries employer contributions on top. A euro delivered inside the fringe benefit limit is treated more favourably. The employee keeps more of it, and you pay less on top of it.

This makes the cap a cost lever. It does not lower salary. It changes how part of the package is delivered.

There is a second effect. Employees see the benefit as a real addition. In a market where salary comparisons are tight, that helps with hiring and retention.

## Who gets the higher limit

The higher threshold depends on the employee's family situation. It applies to employees with dependent children. Your payroll provider will need documentation to confirm this status.

Build this into onboarding. Ask for the right documents at the start, and set a process to refresh them when family circumstances change.

## Common use cases

Companies use the cap in a few practical ways.

**Household costs.** Contributions toward utility bills are a common choice. They are easy to understand and easy to document.

**Welfare plans.** Some employers set up a welfare plan where employees choose from approved categories of spending. This gives people choice and keeps administration in one place.

**Family support.** For employees with children, the higher limit gives room for education or care related items. This is where the EUR 2,000 ceiling is most useful.

**Relocation top-ups.** For international hires, a portion of a package can sit inside the cap instead of in gross salary. Check with your advisor which items qualify.

The exact list of eligible items is set by law and practice. Do not promise an employee a benefit before payroll has confirmed it fits.

## What happens if you go over

The cap is a limit you must watch. If the total value for an employee goes above the threshold, the favourable treatment is at risk for that employee. Track the running total per person across the year.

This is easy to miss when several benefits come from different managers. Assign one owner for the data. Payroll should see every benefit before it is promised.

## How to plan a benefits policy

Start with the numbers. Decide what share of the package you want to deliver as benefits, and check it fits inside the cap for each group of employees.

Then keep it simple.

1. Define the benefits you will offer and the rule for each.
2. Collect family status documents at onboarding.
3. Record the value delivered to each employee through the year.
4. Review the policy whenever the law changes.

A short written policy avoids disputes. It also gives auditors a clear record.

## Fit with an Employer of Record

A foreign company with no Italian entity still needs to handle this. An Employer of Record (EOR) runs payroll in Italy, tracks the benefit totals, and applies the correct threshold for each employee. You decide the package. The EOR keeps the administration compliant.

This matters most for small teams. One or two hires do not justify building an internal benefits process. Using the cap well still saves money for both sides.

## Key points

- The general annual threshold is EUR 1,000 per employee.
- The threshold is EUR 2,000 for employees with dependent children.
- Benefits above the cap lose the favourable treatment.
- Confirm current limits with payroll before you commit.
- Track the running total per employee.

A Singapore SaaS company has customers in Italy. Deals come in through partners and inbound leads. Support runs at odd hours. The founders decide it is time to hire locally.

They do not want to set up an Italian company yet. They have no local accountant, no payroll provider and no one who reads Italian labour rules. They want a person on the ground, working this quarter.

This is how that path can look with an Employer of Record (EOR).

## Step 1: Pick the first role

Most SaaS companies start with a sales or customer success hire. This person speaks Italian, knows the buyers and can close deals in the local language.

The EOR becomes the legal employer in Italy. Your company directs the daily work. The EOR handles the contract, payroll, social security registration and compliance. The employee works for you in practice and is protected by Italian rules in law.

Before you write the offer, settle three things:

- The job title and the real tasks.
- The collective agreement (CCNL) that applies to your sector.
- The pay level, measured against that agreement and the local market.

Italian employment is built around national collective agreements. They set minimum pay, notice, leave and other terms. Your offer must fit inside them. A good EOR picks the right agreement and tells you what it means for the offer before you send it.

## Step 2: Onboard without a local entity

Once the candidate accepts, the EOR issues an Italian contract and registers the employee. The employee gets a payslip each month in Italy's format. Your finance team in Singapore receives one invoice and one set of reports.

You do not need a local bank account, a registered office or a tax representative. That is the point of the model. You test the market first.

## Step 3: Learn from the first hire

The first months show you what works. Is Italy a direct sales market for you, or does it run through partners? Do customers expect Italian-language support? Does the market respond to your price?

Keep the setup light while you learn. Review the role after a few months. Adjust targets to what you see.

## Step 4: Add the second and third hires

When the first hire proves the market, you add roles around them. Typical next hires for a SaaS company:

- A second sales person or account executive.
- A customer support or success specialist.
- A technical role, such as a solutions engineer.

Each new hire goes through the same process on the same contract base. The EOR already knows your company, so onboarding is faster. Pay bands stay consistent across the team, which avoids internal friction.

At this stage, set clear rules for remote work, equipment and expenses. Italian employees expect these to be written down. Put them in the contract or an internal policy that the EOR can review.

## Step 5: Grow into a team

With a small team in place, new questions come up.

**Management.** Someone needs to lead. Choose a team lead from within, or hire one. Their contract should reflect the added responsibility.

**Time zones.** Singapore and Italy are far apart. Agree on overlap hours. Run team rituals at a time that works for both sides.

**Culture.** Italian employees value clarity about role, pay and notice. Surprises damage trust fast. Keep promises and put changes in writing.

**Compliance as you grow.** More people mean more reporting. The EOR carries that load. You stay focused on the product and the customers.

## Step 6: Decide on the long term

At some point you face a choice. Keep the EOR, or open an Italian entity. The answer depends on your plans.

Stay with an EOR if you want flexibility, if headcount may change, or if you still test the market. Open an entity if you plan to grow far beyond a small team, need local contracts with customers, or want direct control of every function.

Moving from an EOR to your own entity is a known path. Employees can transfer. Plan it early so that contracts, benefits and seniority carry over cleanly.

## What to do first

Start small. Define the first role. Check the collective agreement that fits it. Agree the pay. Then let the EOR handle the legal work while you hire.

A founder in Singapore can have an Italian employee working within weeks. The rest of the team can follow when the market proves itself.

Founders often ask where the money comes from when they build a team in a new country. This FAQ covers the usual sources of capital and support, and how they relate to hiring in Italy. It is general guidance. Check the current terms of any programme before you plan around it.

## Where do founders usually look for capital first?

Most look at their existing investors. If you have raised a round, the first question is whether the budget already covers a team in Italy. Many boards approve a new market only when the hiring cost is clear and capped.

Other common sources are:

- Revenue from current customers.
- Venture capital and angel investors.
- Venture debt for companies that already have steady income.
- Corporate partners that want a local presence.

None of these are specific to Italy. They fund the company, and the company then decides where to hire.

## Are there grants for hiring in Italy?

Yes, support schemes exist. They come from national bodies, regional bodies and European programmes. They tend to target particular goals, such as research, innovation, hiring in specific regions, or hiring specific groups of workers.

Two points matter for a foreign founder.

First, many schemes require a local legal entity. If you have no Italian company, you may not qualify.

Second, schemes change. Rules, budgets and deadlines move. Treat any grant as a possible bonus, not as the base of your hiring plan.

## Do grants work if I hire through an Employer of Record?

It depends on the scheme. Some benefits attach to the legal employer. With an Employer of Record (EOR), the EOR is the legal employer in Italy. That can matter for eligibility.

Do not assume a scheme will apply. Ask the scheme's administrator, or an adviser, before you sign any hiring contract. Then ask your EOR provider how the employment is structured and what records they can give you.

## What about tax incentives?

Italy offers various tax and contribution incentives. Some relate to the type of worker, the location, or the kind of work. Others relate to research and development spending.

These incentives usually reduce cost after the fact. They do not fund the start of a project. So you still need cash to pay salaries and contributions up front.

Our advice is to build your first budget without incentives. Add them later if you qualify.

## Where do founders find support besides money?

Capital is only one need. Early teams in a new country also need advice, contacts and a place to test ideas. Common sources include:

- **Accelerators and incubators.** They offer mentoring, office space and introductions.
- **Regional development agencies.** They help foreign companies understand local programmes.
- **Chambers of commerce.** Many have desks for companies from your home country.
- **Universities and research centres.** They connect founders with skilled graduates and joint projects.
- **Founder networks.** Peers who have already hired in Italy can save you months.

These groups rarely pay for hiring. They help you find people, partners and customers.

## What is the biggest hidden cost when building a team in Italy?

Setting up a company before you know whether the market works. A local entity needs registration, an accountant, payroll, social security accounts and ongoing filings. That takes time and money before the first hire starts.

An EOR lets you hire without that setup. You choose the person. The EOR employs them under Italian rules, runs payroll and handles social security. You direct the daily work. This keeps your upfront cost low and your plan flexible.

If the team grows and you later open your own entity, you can move employees across. That is a good moment to look again at grants that need a local company.

## How should I plan the budget?

Keep it simple.

1. List the roles you need and the cost of each.
2. Add employer contributions and the provider fee.
3. Add recruiting and relocation costs if the person comes from abroad.
4. Set aside a reserve for surprises.
5. Treat grants and incentives as upside.

Share this plan with your investors. They usually prefer a clear monthly cost over an open-ended setup project.

## Should I wait for a grant before I hire?

Usually no. Application cycles can be slow. Waiting can cost you the person you wanted and the market window. If a scheme fits, apply in parallel. Do not make your first hire depend on it.

## What should I ask before I commit?

- Does the scheme need a local company, or can a foreign company apply?
- Does it recognise employees hired through an EOR?
- What reporting does it require, and who prepares it?
- What happens if the grant is refused? Can the hire still go ahead?

Clear answers to these questions save you from a funding gap later.

Most foreign companies start with a gross salary and add a rough percentage for contributions. That gets you a number. It is rarely the real number.

Italy has a layered employment cost. Some layers are visible. Others only show up after the first payroll run. This article lists the items that most often go missing from budgets.

## Start with the contract, not the salary

In Italy, the national collective agreement (CCNL) for your sector drives much of the cost. It sets minimum pay, extra monthly payments, leave rules, notice periods and allowances. Two employees with the same gross salary can cost very different amounts under different agreements.

Budget from the agreement that applies to the role. Do not budget from a salary figure alone. Ask which agreement applies before you make an offer.

## Workplace injury insurance

Every employer in Italy pays workplace injury insurance to INAIL. Many foreign teams do not know it exists until they see the line on a payroll report.

The cost is not flat. It depends on the risk class of the work. An office role and a field role sit in different classes and pay different premiums.

There is also a point that confuses even local advisers. The rate tables in force date from 2019. The rules on how they are applied changed in 2026, including how reductions for good safety records work. So a premium estimate based on an older article or an older quote may be wrong. Ask for a current calculation for the actual role.

## Severance accrual

Italian employees build up a severance entitlement, known as TFR, during employment. The employer sets this aside every year. It is paid when the contract ends, for any reason, including resignation.

This is a real liability from the first month. If your budget treats severance as a cost that only appears at dismissal, it is understated. Treat it as a monthly cost from day one.

## Extra pay and accrued leave

Many Italian contracts include additional monthly payments beyond the base salary. Foreign managers often read an annual salary and divide it evenly, then find the payroll is larger in certain months.

Accrued leave is another item. Unused days and paid hours do not disappear. They remain a liability on your books, and they are paid out if the employee leaves.

Check how your contract structures annual pay. Make sure the budget shows the cash profile by month, not only the annual total.

## Payroll and compliance work

Italian payroll is not a light task. Monthly processing, filings with social security and tax authorities, and year-end reporting all need local expertise. If you run payroll through a foreign provider, expect extra work to adapt it.

If you hire directly, you also need a local entity or a registration with the right authorities before the first employee starts. That means setup time, local advisers and fees before there is any revenue from the hire.

## Health and safety obligations

Italian employers carry legal duties on workplace safety. These include risk assessments, training, a designated safety role and medical checks for some roles. Remote workers are not exempt from every duty.

These are not large costs for a small team. They are easy to forget, and the penalties for missing them are real. Put them in the budget as a fixed annual item.

## Visas and relocation

If the person is not an EU citizen, work authorization adds time and cost. There are government fees, document preparation, translation and legal support. There may also be a delay between the offer and the start date, during which you pay for the process but get no work.

Relocation is similar. Housing search, registration with local offices and tax residency setup all take effort. Many companies cover some of it to win the candidate. Decide the policy before the offer, not after.

## Termination costs

Ending an employment relationship in Italy is regulated. Notice periods, procedures and possible disputes all matter. You should not assume that ending a contract is quick or free.

You do not need to budget for a dismissal in every case. You should know the likely cost range before you hire, so that the decision to hire is made with the full picture.

## Time and management cost

The last item is internal. Someone on your side will spend time on contracts, questions from the employee, local holidays, and coordination with advisers. In a small company, that someone is often a founder or a senior manager.

This cost does not appear on any invoice. It is still a cost.

## A simple way to budget

Build the budget in layers:

- Base salary under the applicable collective agreement.
- Employer social contributions.
- Workplace injury insurance for the role's risk class.
- Monthly severance accrual.
- Extra monthly pay and leave liability.
- Payroll, compliance and safety obligations.
- Visa and relocation, if needed.
- A reserve for termination.

Ask for each layer in writing, with the source and the date. Rules and rates change. A figure with no date is a risk.

## Why this matters

The goal is not to scare you away from hiring in Italy. Italy has strong talent and a stable legal framework. The goal is to avoid a budget that looks fine in the board deck and fails in the first quarter.

An employer of record handles most of these layers for you and gives you one monthly cost. You still need to understand what is inside it.

If you plan to hire a senior manager or executive in Italy, social contributions will not grow in a straight line with salary. Two rules change the picture for high earners: an extra 1% above a threshold, and a ceiling on the earnings that count. This FAQ explains both and what they mean for your package design.

## What is the extra 1% contribution?

Italian employees pay pension contributions to INPS. For pay above a set threshold, an additional 1% applies on top of the ordinary rate. It applies only to the portion above the threshold, not to the whole salary.

The threshold is EUR 56,224 per year. On a monthly basis, that is EUR 4,685.

An executive earning well above this level will therefore pay the extra 1% on every euro above the line. The effect on a single payslip is small. On a large package it adds up.

## What is the contribution ceiling?

The ceiling, called the *massimale contributivo*, is a cap on the annual earnings that count for pension contributions. For employees enrolled with INPS from 1996 with no earlier contribution history, the ceiling is EUR 122,295 per year.

Earnings above that amount do not generate further pension contributions. That matters most for senior hires, who often sit well above it.

## Does the ceiling apply to everyone?

No. The figure above is for workers who started contributing from 1996 with no earlier seniority. People with earlier contribution history can fall under different rules. Many international executives arrive with a mixed record, so check the specific case before you fix the budget.

## How do these rules affect an executive package?

Think of the package in bands.

**Below the threshold.** Ordinary contributions only. This band is simple to model.

**Between the threshold and the ceiling.** Ordinary contributions plus the extra 1% on the part above EUR 56,224. Each additional euro of gross pay costs slightly more in contributions than the one before it.

**Above the ceiling.** Pension contributions stop growing on the part above EUR 122,295 per year. Bonus and variable pay in this band do not add to the pension contribution base in the same way as pay in the lower bands.

For an employer, this means the cost of a raise or a bonus depends on where the executive's pay already sits. A bonus paid to someone already above the ceiling behaves differently from the same bonus paid to someone below it.

## What should I do when I split fixed and variable pay?

Split your package and test each part against the bands above. A few practical points:

- Model the full year, not only the monthly payslip. The ceiling is annual, so contributions can change late in the year as the cap is reached.
- Place bonuses in the calendar year where you want them to count. Timing can move a payment from one side of the ceiling to the other.
- Run the numbers for the net pay your executive expects. Gross-to-net in Italy depends on contributions and on income tax, and you need both.
- Keep the base salary realistic. Contract terms, notice and severance in Italy are tied to pay levels, so a low base with a large bonus has consequences beyond contributions.

## Does the ceiling make a senior hire cheaper?

It caps one cost line, but it is not a discount. Income tax still applies to the full pay. Other employer costs and contract obligations remain. The ceiling limits pension contributions on the top slice of earnings. It does not change the rest of the cost of employment.

## How reliable are these figures?

The figures here come from a secondary source that explains the INPS rules, not from an INPS circular read directly. Thresholds and ceilings are updated by INPS from time to time. Confirm the current values against INPS before you sign an offer or set a budget.

## What does this mean for foreign employers?

A company without an Italian entity cannot easily run Italian payroll and contributions on its own. An Employer of Record (EOR) hires the person in Italy, runs payroll, applies the thresholds and the ceiling correctly, and files with INPS. You keep day-to-day management of the executive. The EOR carries the compliance work and gives you a cost model you can check before the offer goes out.

Before you commit to a package, ask for a full cost breakdown with the extra 1% and the ceiling applied to the actual figures. It is the only way to see the true cost of a senior hire in Italy.

You have found a senior engineer who works at a large Italian corporate. They are good, they are interested, and they want to talk. This is the point where many foreign companies lose the candidate. Not because the offer is weak, but because they misread how the exit works in Italy.

This article covers three things: the counter-offer, the notice period, and what each side expects.

## Expect a counter-offer

Large Italian employers rarely let a senior engineer leave without a response. When the resignation lands, the manager will often ask for time. HR may come back with a raise, a new title, or a promise of a project the engineer has wanted for years.

Plan for this before you make your offer. Do not treat it as a possibility. Treat it as the default.

Three things help.

First, find out why the person is leaving. If it is money, a counter-offer can win. If it is scope, ownership, remote work, or a ceiling on growth, money rarely fixes it. Ask directly in the interview. Ask again before you send the offer.

Second, ask the candidate how they will respond. A candidate who has thought about it will tell you plainly. A candidate who says "they would never do that" has not thought about it.

Third, make your offer about the whole role, not only the salary. Say what they will own. Say who they will report to. Say what you will build in the first year. A counter-offer can match a number. It is much harder for it to match a clear future.

## Do not compete on salary alone

Corporate packages in Italy often include more than base pay. There may be variable pay, a company car, supplementary health cover, meal benefits, and a long record of seniority. The engineer will compare your offer with all of it.

Put your offer in the same terms. Show the full annual cost and the full value to them, line by line. If your package is lower on one item, say so and explain what is higher elsewhere. Candidates trust a clear comparison more than a vague claim of "competitive pay".

## Notice is real and it is long

In Italy, notice is set by the employment contract and the applicable national collective agreement. For senior staff it is usually longer than what many foreign hiring managers are used to. It often depends on seniority and job level.

This has practical effects.

- Your start date will be later than you want. Ask for the real notice terms before you set any project plan.
- The candidate may offer to negotiate an earlier exit. Some employers agree, many do not. Do not push the candidate to burn bridges for your timeline.
- Notice is also the window when the counter-offer happens. A long notice gives the current employer time to work on the person.

Stay in contact during this period. Keep it light and useful. Share the team plan, introduce a future colleague, send the onboarding outline. The goal is to keep the engineer connected to the new job while the old one is still pulling.

If you have no Italian entity, remember that the engineer cannot start working for you until the employment relationship is in place. An Employer of Record can issue the contract and handle payroll and social contributions from the first day, so the start date is limited only by the notice, not by your setup time.

## Check restrictive clauses early

Senior engineers sometimes have confidentiality terms, non-compete terms, or clauses on client contact. These vary by contract. Ask the candidate to read their own agreement and tell you what applies. Do not ask them to share confidential material. If a clause looks relevant, get local advice before you finalise the offer.

A clean exit protects the engineer and protects you.

## Set expectations on both sides

What the engineer expects from you:

- A written offer that is clear and complete.
- A proper Italian employment contract under the right collective agreement, not a vague contractor arrangement.
- Payslips, leave, and benefits that look normal for the role.
- A manager who understands that Italian working practices differ from your home market.
- A real answer on remote work, travel, and working hours.

What you can expect from the engineer:

- Professional behaviour towards the current employer during notice.
- Honest communication if the counter-offer is tempting.
- A strong sense of duty to finish handover well. In a corporate setting this is often a matter of personal pride.
- Questions about stability. A corporate employee leaving a large, known name is taking a visible risk. They will want to see that your company will still be there.

That last point matters. Be ready to explain your funding, your customers, and your plans in the market. Do not oversell. Senior people notice.

## A simple sequence that works

1. Agree the real reason for leaving.
2. Make a full, written offer that covers role, pay, benefits, and growth.
3. Ask how the candidate will handle a counter-offer.
4. Confirm notice terms and any restrictive clauses.
5. Prepare the contract so it can be signed as soon as the candidate is free to commit.
6. Keep steady, low-pressure contact through the notice period.
7. Plan onboarding for the first day, not the first month.

## The takeaway

Hiring a senior engineer from an Italian corporate is a slow, human process. The counter-offer is likely, the notice is long, and the engineer is weighing stability against opportunity. Be clear, be patient, and show a future that a raise cannot copy.

Many international companies want a support team in Europe. Italy is a practical choice. The country has a large pool of graduates in languages, a strong university system and a culture that values service. This article explains how to think about language skills and location before you open a role.

## Start with the language map, not the job title

A "multilingual support agent" can mean very different things. Before you post a role, write down what the agent must actually do in each language.

- Answer written tickets and chats.
- Speak with customers on the phone.
- Handle escalations and complaints.
- Translate or review help center content.

Writing is easier to find than fast, natural speech. A candidate may read and write German well but hesitate on a live call. Test the exact skill you need. Do not rely on a CV line that says "fluent".

## Which languages are easy to find

Italian and English are the baseline. Most candidates in customer-facing roles can work in English. Check the depth, because a person who can follow a meeting may still struggle with a billing dispute.

Spanish, French and German are the most common additional languages. Many Italians study at least one of them at school or university. Portuguese, Russian and the Nordic languages are rarer. Arabic, Chinese and Japanese are also rarer, though you can find them in larger cities with international universities.

There is another source: native speakers who live in Italy. Expats, students, partners of people working in Italy, and Italians who grew up abroad often have a true native level in a second language. They are a strong fit for rare languages. They may need visa or permit support, which a provider can handle for you.

## Where to base the team

Location shapes who you can hire. There is no single best city. Match the city to the language mix.

**Milan.** The most international market. It has the widest mix of native speakers, many multinational employers and good transport links. Competition for talent is also highest here. Expect candidates to compare offers.

**Rome.** A large pool of graduates and many international organisations. Good for English, French and Spanish. It also has a sizeable community of foreign residents.

**Turin.** A solid base for French, thanks to its location and history. It has a strong technical and industrial background, which helps if your support involves technical products.

**Bologna and other university cities.** Large student populations mean a steady flow of young graduates with language degrees. Padua, Florence, Trieste and Naples also fit this pattern. Trieste has historic links with Central European languages.

**Remote across Italy.** Support work moves well to remote or hybrid models. You can hire from a wide range of cities and towns and avoid the cost and competition of the largest centres. Make sure candidates have a stable connection and a quiet workspace. Agree on equipment and data security rules from the start.

## Match shifts to the time zone

Italy sits in Central European time. This works well for customers in Europe, the Middle East and Africa. For North American coverage, you will need late shifts. For Asia-Pacific, you will need early ones. Italian employment rules cover working time, rest periods and night work. Plan your rota with these rules in mind, and do not copy a schedule from another country. Ask your provider to check any shift pattern before you promise it to candidates.

## Write the job ad for the real skill

Good ads are short and specific. State the languages, the channel (phone, chat or email) and the level of speaking you need. Say whether the role is on site, hybrid or remote. Mention the product and the type of customer. Candidates respond better to a clear description than to a long list of buzzwords.

Offer a language test as part of the process. A short call in the target language and a written task will tell you more than any certificate.

## Retention matters as much as hiring

Support roles can have high turnover everywhere. A few practices help in Italy.

- Give a clear contract and a clear career path, for example toward team lead or specialist roles.
- Pay fairly for language skills. Rare languages have more bargaining power.
- Respect local labour rules on leave, notice and working hours.
- Keep onboarding in Italian where it helps, and provide training materials in the language the person will work in.

People stay when the job is stable and the rules are clear.

## How to hire without a local entity

Turin is Italy's best-known city for mechanical and automotive engineering. If your company needs engineers in vehicle design, powertrain, embedded software, testing or industrial automation, it belongs on your shortlist.

This article explains why the talent is there, how the local ecosystem works, and what to check before you hire.

## The Polytechnic is the anchor

The Politecnico di Torino is the main source of engineering graduates in the city. It is a technical university focused on engineering and architecture. Its programmes cover mechanical, aerospace, electrical, electronic, computer and industrial engineering. Many of its graduates stay in the Turin area.

For a foreign employer, this matters in three ways.

- **A steady pipeline.** Each year new graduates enter the market with solid technical training.
- **Research links with industry.** The university works with companies on applied projects. Engineers there are used to real industrial problems, not only theory.
- **International exposure.** Many programmes are taught in English, so graduates often work comfortably with foreign teams.

## An industry that never left

Turin built its identity on the car. Large manufacturers, design studios, component makers and testing firms are all part of the local fabric. Around them sits a wide supplier base: machining, tooling, plastics, electronics, software and engineering services.

This gives you something a university alone cannot. You can hire people who have already worked on production programmes. They know homologation, quality systems and supplier management. They have seen a product go from drawing to assembly line.

The sector is also changing. Electrification, connected vehicles, driver assistance and new materials are reshaping the work. Engineers in Turin are moving into battery systems, power electronics, simulation and software-defined vehicle platforms. The skill base is broadening beyond classic mechanics.

## Beyond cars

The same talent pool serves other fields. Aerospace, rail, robotics, industrial machinery and energy equipment all draw on the same engineers. If you are a company in one of these areas, you can recruit from a larger pool than the word "automotive" suggests.

Design is another strength. Turin has a long tradition of vehicle styling and industrial design. Engineers and designers often work close together here, which helps with product development.

## Who is a good fit for a Turin hire

Turin works well for:

- Foreign automotive suppliers that need a local engineering presence near Italian manufacturers.
- Startups building hardware, battery or mobility products that need prototyping skills.
- Software and simulation companies serving the vehicle industry.
- Industrial groups that want a European engineering team without opening a full entity.

It is less obvious for companies that need a large number of people in finance or sales. Other Italian cities have deeper pools for those roles.

## Practical costs to check

Salary is only part of the cost of an employee. In Turin you should also look at local taxes that affect take-home pay and how you present offers.

The city applies a municipal income tax surcharge. According to a secondary source, the rate is split into four brackets: 0.8%, 0.8%, 1.1% and 1.2%. There is also an exemption threshold of EUR 11,790. The surcharge is paid by the employee and withheld through payroll, so it does not add to your employer cost. It does change what a candidate receives net, so it is worth including in salary discussions. Confirm the current figures before you finalise any offer, since this source is not an official one.

Other items to plan for:

- The national collective agreement that applies to your sector. Engineering and metalworking roles usually fall under a specific agreement that sets minimum pay, notice and leave.
- Employer social contributions, which sit on top of gross salary.
- Payroll, benefits and reporting, all handled in Italian.

## Hiring without your own Italian company

Many foreign firms want to hire two or three engineers in Turin before deciding on a legal entity. Setting up a subsidiary takes time and requires local administration, accounting and payroll from day one.

An Employer of Record (EOR) is the faster route. The EOR becomes the legal employer in Italy. It issues the contract, runs payroll, pays contributions and handles compliance. You manage the daily work and the engineer's tasks. You keep control of the project, and the EOR handles the paperwork.

This suits teams that want to test the market, hire quickly, or keep headcount small. If you later open your own entity, the employees can be transferred.

An EOR can also help when the candidate is not from the European Union. Visa and relocation support matter in a city with a strong international student and graduate community.

## How to start

1. Define the role and the skills you need: CAD, simulation, embedded systems, testing or process engineering.
2. Check which collective agreement fits the job.
3. Decide where the person will work: your own space, a coworking site or from home.
4. Agree on the contract type and salary, including the net impact of local taxes.
5. Choose whether to hire through an EOR or through your own entity.

Turin gives you engineers with real industrial experience and a university that keeps producing new ones. For companies in automotive and related fields, that combination is hard to match elsewhere in Italy.

Milan is the main financial centre in Italy. Banks, insurers, asset managers, payment firms and fintech startups all sit in the same city. For a foreign company, this means a deep pool of skilled people. It also means you will not be the only employer looking for them.

This article covers which roles you are likely to hire, who you compete with, and what that means for how you approach the market.

## Roles foreign companies usually hire

Most international fintech and banking firms do not open a full branch on day one. They start with a small team that serves the local market or supports a regional hub. The roles tend to fall into a few groups.

**Engineering and data.** Backend engineers, mobile developers, data engineers and data scientists. These people build payment flows, lending products, fraud models and reporting tools. Candidates with experience in regulated environments are in demand.

**Risk, compliance and legal.** Compliance officers, anti-money-laundering analysts, credit risk analysts and regulatory reporting specialists. Anyone who knows how Italian and European rules apply in practice is valuable. This group is hard to hire because the knowledge is local.

**Sales and partnerships.** Relationship managers, enterprise sales leads and partnership managers. Italian banks and corporates prefer to deal with someone who speaks the language and knows how decisions are made inside Italian institutions.

**Product and operations.** Product managers, customer operations leads and onboarding specialists. These roles connect your product to Italian customers and to local partners.

**Finance and treasury.** Finance managers and controllers who handle local accounting, tax and reporting for the new entity.

## Who you compete with

Candidates in Milan have many options. You should plan for that from the start.

**Large banks and insurers.** They offer stability, structured careers and well-known names. Many senior people have spent years in these institutions and value that security.

**Local fintech scale-ups.** These offer faster growth, equity and a product culture. They compete directly with you for engineers and product people.

**Other international firms.** Global banks, payment companies and technology groups already run offices in Milan. They hire from the same people you do, and many offer English-speaking teams and international mobility.

**Consulting firms.** They attract analysts and risk specialists with training and a clear path up.

In practice, strong candidates often hold more than one offer. Speed matters. A slow process loses people to employers who move first.

## What candidates look for

Salary is only part of the decision. Italian professionals also look at the following.

- **A legal employer in Italy.** Many candidates want a proper Italian employment contract, with local benefits, social security and clear rights. An offer through a foreign contract, or a vague contractor arrangement, makes some people hesitate.
- **Clarity on the role.** They want to know who they report to, what the team looks like and whether the company will stay in Italy.
- **Flexibility.** Hybrid work is common in this sector. Fully remote arrangements are less standard for regulated roles.
- **Career path.** A small foreign team can feel risky. Show how the role will grow.

If you can answer these points early, you improve your position against larger and better-known employers.

## The hiring challenge for a foreign company

You may want to hire in Milan before you have an Italian entity. Setting one up takes time. You also need payroll, social security registration, a compliant contract based on the right national collective agreement, and local HR support. Banking and financial roles often fall under specific collective agreements, and getting the contract wrong creates problems later.

You also face a timing issue. The best candidates will not wait while you complete incorporation.

## How an Employer of Record helps

An Employer of Record (EOR) employs the person in Italy on your behalf. You decide who to hire, what they do and how they work. The EOR handles the legal employment side.

For fintech and banking hiring, this gives you several practical advantages.

- You can make an offer quickly, with a compliant Italian contract.
- The candidate has a real Italian employer, with payroll, contributions and benefits handled correctly.
- You test the market with a small team before you commit to an entity.
- You avoid mistakes in contract terms and collective agreement choice.
- If you need to hire someone from abroad, visa and relocation support can be part of the same service.

You can move to your own entity later if the team grows. The people you hired can transfer across.

## A simple approach

Start with a clear list of the first few roles. Decide which ones need to be in Milan and which can be remote. Prepare a contract and benefits package that matches what local employers offer. Move quickly once you find a good candidate. Use an EOR to employ them while you decide on a longer-term structure.

Milan rewards companies that are prepared. The talent is there. The competition is real. A fast, clear and compliant offer is your best tool.

Italy is a serious place to build a food, agritech or wine team. The country has deep craft knowledge, strong technical schools and a dense network of producers. For a foreign company, the hard part is not finding people. It is hiring them legally and quickly without setting up a local entity first.

This article covers the specialist roles that matter most, what makes them different from general hires, and how an Employer of Record (EOR) fits in.

## Roles international firms look for

**Enologists and winemakers.** Italian wine is built on regional knowledge. A winemaker who knows Piedmont is not automatically right for Sicily. Soils, grape varieties and local rules differ. When you hire, match the person to the region and the style you want to produce.

**Agronomists.** These specialists advise on crop health, soil, irrigation and yield. They are central to both traditional farms and agritech projects. Many work in the field and travel between sites, so your contract and expense terms should reflect that.

**Food technologists and quality managers.** They handle recipes, shelf life, safety systems and audits. Foreign buyers often need someone on the ground who can speak to Italian producers and keep standards consistent.

**Agritech engineers and data specialists.** Sensors, drones, precision farming software and automation all need people who understand both machines and farmland. This is a smaller talent pool. Expect competition, and expect candidates to value clear contracts and stable terms.

**Export and sales managers.** Italian food and wine brands depend on export. If you are a buyer, importer or distributor abroad, a local sales or sourcing manager can open doors that email never will.

**Sommeliers, brand ambassadors and tasting experts.** These roles support education, events and trade relationships. They are often part-time or seasonal in practice, which affects how the contract is written.

## What makes these hires different

Specialist food and wine roles share a few traits.

First, seasonality. Harvest, pressing and bottling create peaks. Your contract structure should match real work patterns, not just a generic template.

Second, the collective agreement. Italian employment is shaped by sector-level agreements that set minimum pay, hours, leave and notice. Agriculture, food industry and trade each have their own rules. Choosing the wrong one is a common and costly mistake. It affects salary floors, benefits and how your employee is classified.

Third, location. Many of these jobs are rural. Your employee may work from a vineyard, a lab or a farm, not a city office. That changes insurance, travel and equipment questions.

Fourth, certifications and technical qualifications. Some roles need specific training or professional registration. Check this before you make an offer, not after.

## Why not set up a company first

Setting up a legal entity in Italy takes time and ongoing admin. You need a registered office, payroll, tax filings, social security registration and local accounting. If you only need one or two specialists, or you want to test the market, that is a heavy start.

An Employer of Record hires the person on your behalf. You choose the candidate and direct the daily work. The EOR becomes the legal employer in Italy. It runs payroll, handles contributions, issues compliant contracts and manages the paperwork with the authorities.

For food, agritech and wine, this works well in several cases:

- You are a foreign producer opening a sourcing or quality office in Italy.
- You are an agritech company placing a field engineer near your pilot customers.
- You are an importer who wants a local export liaison.
- You are a wine brand that needs a regional specialist before committing to a full entity.

## How to hire well

Keep the process simple.

1. Define the role in practical terms. State where the person works, what they produce and who they report to.
2. Identify the right collective agreement early. It drives pay and conditions.
3. Decide whether the work is full-time, part-time or tied to a season.
4. Agree on how the employee will be equipped, including vehicles, devices and field gear.
5. Plan for language. Many Italian specialists speak English, but technical vocabulary and local suppliers are easier in Italian. A bilingual hire is a strong asset.
6. Write a clear job description and keep reporting lines short.

## What to expect

Italian employees tend to value stability and clarity. A well-structured contract, correct pay and visible benefits matter more than a flashy title. Treat the role as a long-term investment in local knowledge. Producers, growers and buyers in this sector trust people they have known for years.

If your specialist is moving to Italy from abroad, plan early for the right to work, housing and local registration. These steps take time and are easier when handled together with the employment setup.

The region also has a strong base in packaging machinery and automation. These fields share skills with the motor industry: mechatronics, control systems and quality engineering.

Bologna has become a European centre for high-performance computing. The Tecnopolo district hosts large research computing infrastructure. Universities, research bodies and weather and climate science groups work close together.

- Graduates in physics, mathematics, computer science and engineering come out of the local universities.
- Researchers and engineers with simulation and modelling skills are available.
- Companies in automotive, aerospace, life sciences or energy can build links with research teams.

The link between the two valleys is natural. Car and machine makers use simulation, digital twins and data analysis. The same people can work across both worlds.

## Who should consider hiring here

The region suits companies that need:

- Mechanical, electrical or software engineers close to a manufacturing base

It is less suited to companies that only need a mailing address. The value is in the skills and the industry around them.

A foreign company without an Italian entity can still hire in Bologna. An Employer of Record (EOR) becomes the legal employer in Italy. You direct the daily work. The EOR handles the contract, payroll, social contributions, local taxes and compliance.

2. Identify the right collective agreement for the sector.

4. Let the EOR issue the contract and register the employee.
