Florence and Tuscany have a long record in leather, fashion, textiles, jewelry, craft and design. If your company sells luxury goods or builds a creative team, this region is a natural place to hire. The skills are here. The supplier networks are here. The question is how to employ people there without opening a company in Italy.

This article explains where the region fits, which roles tend to work well, and how an Employer of Record (EOR) handles the employment side.

## Why the region fits

Tuscany is known for workshops and small manufacturers that serve major fashion houses. Many skills are passed on inside these workshops and are hard to find elsewhere. Florence adds design schools, a strong tradition in art and restoration, and a international visitor base that keeps retail and hospitality sharp.

For a foreign company, this means you can find people who understand materials, finishing and quality control at a high level. You can also find people who combine that craft knowledge with modern design and digital work.

## Roles that tend to work well

- **Product development and pattern making.** Technicians who turn a sketch into a producible item.
- **Leather goods and accessories specialists.** Sourcing, sampling and quality checks.
- **Textile and materials experts.** Fabric selection, supplier relations and testing.
- **Brand and visual designers.** Creative staff who can work with a remote head office.
- **Retail and client experience staff.** Multilingual people who serve international clients.
- **Production coordinators.** People who manage the link between your brand and local workshops.
- **Restoration and conservation specialists.** Useful for heritage brands and design-led companies.

Many of these roles can be remote or hybrid. Others need a person near the workshops, which is where a local employee makes the most sense.

## The practical problem for a foreign company

You may want one product developer near your suppliers. You may want a small design team. You do not want to set up a local company, open a bank account, register with the authorities and run payroll just to start.

An EOR solves this. The EOR is the legal employer in Italy. You choose the person and direct the daily work. The EOR handles the contract, payroll, social contributions, tax withholding and the required registrations.

## What the EOR does for you

**Contract and collective agreement.** Italian employment is shaped by national collective agreements for each sector. Fashion, leather, textiles and retail each have their own rules on pay grades, working time, leave and notice. The EOR picks the right agreement and builds the contract around it.

**Payroll and contributions.** Salaries are paid on time, with correct withholding and social contributions. You receive a clear monthly cost report.

**Compliance.** Registrations, mandatory communications and record keeping are done for you. You do not need to learn the rules or hire a local administrator.

**Visas and relocation.** If the person you want lives outside the EU, the EOR can support the work visa process and help with the move. This matters for senior designers, creative directors and specialists you want to bring to Florence.

**Social security representation.** If you employ people in Italy, someone must represent you before the social security bodies. The EOR takes that role.

## Planning a creative or luxury hire

Some points help you start well.

1. **Define the role in terms of the agreement.** A pattern maker, a designer and a shop assistant fall under different classifications. A clear job description speeds up the contract.
2. **Decide where the person works.** Close to the workshops, in Florence, or remote from elsewhere in Italy. Each choice affects the setup.
3. **Plan for language.** Craft staff often speak Italian first. Brand and retail staff usually add English and other languages. Say which you need.
4. **Think about intellectual property.** Designs, patterns and creative work should be assigned to your company in the contract. The EOR can include the right clauses.
5. **Allow time for onboarding.** Italian contracts have formal steps. Starting early avoids delays.

## Is an EOR the right tool?

An EOR suits you if you want to test the market, hire a small number of people, or move fast. It also suits companies that do not plan a permanent entity in Italy. If you later grow into a full local company, the team can be transferred.

For luxury and creative companies, the benefit is simple. You get access to a deep pool of skills without taking on the administration. Your people spend their time on product and brand. The EOR handles the paperwork.

Florence and Tuscany will not suit every role. Pure software or finance teams may find better matches in other Italian cities. But for craft, design, materials and client-facing work, the region is hard to beat.

Italy is a base for fashion and luxury. Foreign brands, suppliers and design studios come here for craft skills, materials know-how and a dense network of specialist workshops. Hiring locally is the best way to tap that. It also means you need to understand how the sector is organised and what candidates expect.

This article covers the roles you are likely to hire, where the talent is, and what to plan for as a foreign employer.

## Roles that matter

The sector splits into creative, technical, commercial and support functions. Each has its own market.

**Creative and product development.** Designers, pattern makers, technical designers and prototype specialists. A pattern maker turns a sketch into something that can be cut and sewn. Good ones are scarce and often known by name in their district.

**Production and quality.** Production planners, quality controllers, supply chain coordinators and sourcing managers. These people manage suppliers, check finishes and keep collections on schedule. Many have worked inside the same supplier network for years.

**Craft and manufacturing.** Leather workers, tailors, knitwear technicians, footwear makers, jewellery setters. If you plan to run or control production in Italy, this is where hiring is hardest. Skills are learned over years, and training takes time.

**Retail and client relations.** Boutique managers, sales advisers, clienteling specialists, visual merchandisers. Luxury retail depends on language skills, product knowledge and a calm, polished manner with clients.

**Commercial and brand.** Wholesale managers, merchandisers, marketing and communications staff, e-commerce managers. These roles often sit in the larger cities and work closely with head office abroad.

**Support functions.** Finance, legal, HR and logistics. Fashion companies need the same back office as any other business, but with seasonal rhythms.

## Clusters

Talent is not spread evenly. The sector grew in districts, each with its own specialty.

- **Milan and Lombardy** are the centre for design, communication, showrooms, buying and corporate roles. Most international brands place their commercial and creative teams here.
- **Veneto** has strong footwear and eyewear traditions, with many specialist manufacturers.
- **Tuscany** is known for leather goods, tanning, textiles and high-end tailoring.
- **Marche and Emilia-Romagna** have footwear, knitwear and clothing producers, many of them family-owned.
- **Piedmont** is linked to fine textiles and menswear.
- **Rome** has a long couture and jewellery tradition and a growing number of brand offices.

If you need creative or commercial staff, Milan is the natural choice. If you need makers, go to the district where the craft lives. Moving a skilled artisan to another city is rarely realistic. Plan to hire where the skill already is.

## What candidates expect

Italian professionals in this sector are proud of their work. They expect a foreign employer to respect it.

**A proper contract.** Candidates expect a written employment contract with clear terms, and a sector collective agreement that sets minimum pay, working hours, leave and notice. Employment in Italy is regulated closely, and good candidates know their rights. A vague or informal offer will lose them.

**Stability.** Many prefer a permanent role. Fixed-term offers work for projects or seasonal peaks, but senior and technical staff look for long-term commitment.

**Benefits beyond salary.** Supplementary pension, health cover, meal vouchers and similar extras are common. Candidates compare packages, so check what is normal for the role.

**Clear reporting lines.** If the manager is abroad, say so and explain how decisions are made. Local staff dislike waiting for answers across time zones with no one empowered to decide.

**Respect for craft and timing.** Production calendars follow collections. Asking for rushed changes late in the cycle damages trust with workshops and suppliers.

**Language.** Italian is expected for most local roles. English is common in corporate and creative teams, but not in workshops.

## Practical points for foreign employers

You do not need an Italian company to hire here. An Employer of Record (EOR) can employ staff on your behalf, handle payroll, contributions and compliance, and let you manage the daily work. This suits brands testing the market, opening a showroom, or adding a few specialists without building a local entity first.

Whatever route you choose, do these things early:

- Define the role and the applicable collective agreement before you advertise.
- Check the real market pay for the role and the district.
- Decide who manages the person day to day.
- Set up onboarding that explains your brand, your standards and your calendar.
- If you hire from outside the EU, plan for visas and relocation well before the start date.

Italian fashion and luxury rewards employers who take the time to understand it. Hire in the right cluster, offer a clear and fair contract, and respect the craft.

## Talent

Milan draws professionals from across Italy and abroad. Many people move there for their careers. The city has several large universities and business schools, so there is a steady flow of graduates. Many professionals work in international teams and are used to English as a working language.

This helps if you hire for sales, finance, engineering, marketing, legal or operations roles. It also means competition. Local employers know the market well, and good candidates compare offers. A clear job description, a fair salary and a fast process matter more than a famous name.

## Cost of living

Milan is one of the more expensive cities in Italy. Housing is the main cost for employees, and it shapes salary talks. Candidates from outside the city will ask about rent. Candidates already living there will compare your offer with what they pay now.

We have no verified figures on rents or prices for this article, so we do not quote any. Check current local data before you set a salary band. Ask candidates what they expect, and compare it with what similar roles pay in the city.

Most employment taxes in Italy are national. Income tax and social contributions follow national rules. On top of that, municipalities can apply a surcharge on personal income tax.

Milan applies a flat municipal surcharge of 0.8%. There is an exemption threshold of 23,000 EUR. Employees with lower income fall under the exemption. Employees above it pay the surcharge.

What this means for you:

- The surcharge is small compared with national income tax.
- It is paid by the employee. It is withheld through payroll.

The figures come from a secondary source, a specialist Italian tax site. Rates can change from year to year. Your payroll provider should confirm the current rate and the exact way the threshold applies before you finalise any offer.

Note that the surcharge depends on where the employee lives, not where the company is based. Staff who live outside Milan may pay a different municipal rate.

## What to do next

Start with the role, not the city. Decide what you need, which agreement applies and what the person will cost in total. Then test Milan against that plan.

Most foreign companies look at Milan or Rome first. That is a fair starting point. But it is not the only one. Many international employers now hire in smaller Italian cities and towns, and they often see better retention as a result.

This article explains why, and what you should plan for.

## Why people stay in smaller places

People rarely leave a job only because of pay. They leave when daily life gets hard. Long commutes, high rents and crowded transport wear people down.

In a smaller city, much of that pressure is lower. Many people live close to the office or work from home. They can walk to the market, the school and the doctor. Lunch is a real break, not a rushed sandwich.

This matters for remote and hybrid roles. A person who has a calm home life and a stable community has fewer reasons to look elsewhere.

## Roots are a retention tool

Many Italians want to live near family. They want to stay in the town where they grew up, or return to it. A job that lets them do this is rare in some regions. When you offer it, you stand out.

An employee who can stay near parents, friends and a familiar home tends to feel loyal to the employer that made it possible. You do not need to buy this loyalty with perks. You offer a real option that larger employers in big cities cannot match.

This applies to your own expatriate staff as well. A relocated professional with a family may find a smaller town easier to settle in. Schools, housing and local services can be simpler to deal with. Settling in faster helps people stay longer.

## A wider pool of talent

If you only recruit in a few big cities, you compete with every other international company there. Candidates in those places get many offers.

In smaller cities, fewer employers recruit for remote or international roles. Skilled people there may have fewer choices. A well-run offer from a foreign company can be very attractive to them.

Many regions also have strong local universities and technical schools. They produce graduates in engineering, languages, design and other fields. Some of those graduates leave for the big cities, and some would rather not.

## What to plan for

Smaller places have trade-offs. Be honest about them in your hiring plan.

- **Fewer local peers.** A specialist may be the only person in their field in town. Plan regular contact with the wider team, online and in person.
- **Travel.** Some towns are far from airports and fast rail. If the role needs travel, check the routes first.
- **Connectivity.** Test internet quality before you commit to a fully remote role.
- **Career growth.** Make the path clear. People stay when they can see what comes next.
- **Local rules.** Employment rules apply across Italy, but the working culture can differ by region. Local knowledge helps.

None of these are reasons to avoid smaller towns. They are things to solve before the first day.

## How to run it without a local company

You do not need to open a legal entity in Italy to hire in a small town. An Employer of Record (EOR) can employ the person on your behalf. The EOR handles the contract, payroll, social security and the other formalities. You direct the daily work.

This is useful when you want to test a location. You can hire one person in a town, see how it goes, and add more later. If the plan changes, you have not built a local structure that you must then close.

The EOR also applies the right national labour contract and local requirements, so you do not have to learn them yourself. The employee gets a compliant Italian contract with full rights. That clarity helps retention too, because people trust an employer that gets the basics right.

## Practical tips for retention

1. **Ask where people want to live.** Let the candidate tell you. Do not assume the capital is the best answer.
2. **Offer flexibility.** Remote or hybrid work is what makes a small-town hire possible.
3. **Plan team contact.** Schedule visits and shared events so nobody feels isolated.
4. **Respect local rhythms.** Holidays, family time and local festivals matter. Plan around them.
5. **Be consistent.** Pay on time, keep promises and communicate clearly.

## The bottom line

Hiring outside the big cities is not a compromise. For the right roles, it is a deliberate choice. It gives you a wider talent pool and employees who value the life they can build. That is a strong base for long tenure.

Start with one role. Pick a place that fits the work. Use an EOR so the legal side stays simple. Then review what you learn.

The North-East of Italy is one of the country's main industrial regions. Venice, Padua and the towns around them are home to a dense network of manufacturers. Many are small and mid-sized firms. Many sell most of what they make abroad.

If your company wants to build or expand a team here, the people you need already work in this system. This article explains what kind of talent you can find, and how to hire it without opening a local company.

## Why the North-East matters for manufacturing

The area is built around production. You find machinery, metalworking, furniture, fashion and footwear, food processing, packaging, and components for larger supply chains. Companies often cluster by sector. Suppliers, toolmakers and service firms sit close to each other. Knowledge moves between them.

This has a practical effect on hiring. A production engineer in Padua may have worked for several local firms. A technician near Venice may know how a whole supply chain runs, not just one plant. That depth is hard to find in a new market.

## Export skills are part of the culture

Many firms in the region have sold abroad for generations. Their staff are used to working with foreign clients. They know export paperwork, shipping terms, quality standards and customer audits. Many speak English. Some speak German, French or other languages that matter for their sectors.

If you want to sell into Europe, or source from it, these are useful people to have on your side. Typical profiles include:

- Export sales managers and area sales managers
- Customer service and order management staff
- Supply chain and logistics planners
- Quality managers and compliance specialists
- Production and process engineers
- Maintenance and automation technicians
- Procurement and supplier development staff

## What foreign companies usually want to do

There are a few common cases.

The first is a sales presence. You want someone near your customers or distributors in Italy and nearby markets. A local export sales person can open doors faster than a remote team.

The second is sourcing and quality. You buy from Italian suppliers and need someone on the ground. That person visits plants, checks samples, follows orders and solves problems early.

The third is engineering and technical support. You need people who understand Italian machinery or production methods, and who can support clients in the field.

The fourth is a small regional office. You do not need a large team. You need two or three people who can start quickly.

## The hiring problem

Hiring in Italy is not like hiring in many other countries. Employment contracts follow national collective agreements. These set pay levels, job grades, notice periods, leave and other terms. The right agreement depends on the sector and the role. Payroll, social contributions and reporting also follow local rules.

If you set up a local entity just to hire one or two people, you take on a lot of work. You need to register, find an accountant, set up payroll and handle compliance. That can take time and cost more than the hire is worth, especially if you are still testing the market.

## How an Employer of Record helps

An Employer of Record (EOR) hires the person on your behalf in Italy. The worker is a legal employee in Italy, with an Italian contract that follows the correct collective agreement. You direct their daily work. The EOR handles the employment side.

In practice, that means:

- A compliant Italian employment contract
- Payroll and social contributions
- Onboarding and employee paperwork
- Ongoing administration and support
- A clear way to end the arrangement if the plan changes

You do not need a local company. You can hire the person you found and start working with them.

This fits the North-East well. Many roles here are technical or tied to a specific sector. You often want to move fast to secure someone with the right profile. An EOR lets you do that without waiting for a local entity to be ready.

## Relocation and international staff

Sometimes the right person is not already in the North-East. You may want to bring in someone from your home country or from elsewhere. In that case, visas, work permits and relocation come into play. An EOR can support this too, so the employee arrives with the right status and the right paperwork in place.

## Tips for a good start

- Define the role clearly. Say whether it is sales, technical, quality or operations.
- Check which collective agreement applies before you set a salary.
- Decide how the person will work. On site, at a customer, or from home.
- Plan visits to local suppliers or customers early. Face-to-face contact matters in this region.
- Start small. One good hire can show you whether the market works for you.

## Summary

Venice, Padua and the wider North-East offer manufacturing know-how and export experience in one place. You can tap into it without building a local company first. An Employer of Record gives you a fast and compliant way to hire.

Foreign companies often enter Italy with a sales hire before anything else. It is a sensible move, but the questions come fast. Who should you hire? How do you pay them? Who covers the travel? This FAQ gives direct answers.

## Profiles

### Which profile fits a company entering Italy?

It depends on your product and your buyer.

- **Hunter.** Opens new accounts and builds a pipeline from nothing. Right for a market where you have no brand yet.
- **Account manager.** Grows existing customers. Right once you already have clients to look after.
- **Business developer.** Finds partners, distributors and channels. Right when you sell through others.
- **Technical sales or pre-sales.** Explains complex products to engineers and buyers. Right for industrial, software and life science offers.

Most market entries start with one senior generalist who can do a bit of each. Split the roles later, once volume justifies it.

### Does the person need to speak Italian?

In most cases, yes. Italy has a large base of small and mid-sized companies. Many decision makers prefer to negotiate in Italian, even when they read English well. Your hire should also speak the language of your head office. That person is the bridge.

### Local hire or relocated employee?

A local hire brings contacts, language and a feel for how buyers think. A relocated employee brings product knowledge and trust from head office. Each has costs. A relocation needs visa and housing planning. A local hire needs onboarding on your product. Many companies use both: a local lead with a short rotation from head office.

### Where should the person be based?

Italy is not one market. The north has dense industry and many exporters. Rome is strong for public bodies and institutions. The south has its own buyer base and its own pace. Pick the base city from where your customers are. Remote work is possible, but many buyers expect regular visits.

## Incentives

### How are sales people usually paid in Italy?

A fixed salary plus a variable part is the common model. The variable part is tied to targets such as revenue, new accounts or margin. Pure commission setups exist, but they are tied to different contract types and rules. For an employee, plan on a fixed base that gives real security.

### What does the contract have to follow?

Most Italian employment relationships fall under a national collective agreement for the sector. It sets minimum pay levels, working time, leave and other conditions. Your offer can go above it, never below. Check which agreement applies before you write the offer.

### Can we copy our home-country bonus plan?

Not as it stands. Some points need care:

- Variable pay should be written down clearly, with targets, measurement and payment dates.
- Targets that are vague or change often lead to disputes.
- Equity or share plans from abroad need local review for tax and social contribution effects.
- Once a bonus is paid regularly, people may start to see it as part of their pay.

Keep the plan simple. Three metrics at most. Review it on a fixed schedule.

### Should incentives be personal or team-based?

For a first hire, personal. One person, one set of targets, one clear link between effort and reward. Add team elements when you have a team.

## Travel

### Who pays for travel and client entertainment?

You do. The employee should not carry business costs. Agree a clear policy up front: what is covered, what needs approval, how receipts are submitted and how fast you reimburse.

### Is a company car normal?

It is common in field sales, especially where clients are spread over a wide area. A car given for personal use as well as work counts as a benefit and has tax and contribution effects. Compare it with a mileage reimbursement or a travel allowance before you decide.

### How should we treat travel time and days away?

Set expectations in the contract and in the policy. Say how often travel is expected, how overnight stays are handled and how rest time is respected. Italian rules on working time and rest apply, and sales roles are not exempt by default.

### What about travel abroad?

Sales hires often cover neighbouring markets. If the person works regularly in other countries, check the effects on social security and tax early. Sorting this out after the fact is costly and slow.

## Practical tips

- Define the territory, the target accounts and the first-year goals before you recruit.
- Write the job description in plain terms. Include language needs, travel and reporting lines.
- Give the hire a head office contact who can decide quickly. Slow answers lose Italian deals.
- Plan for onboarding. Your product knowledge will not transfer by itself.

## Do you need a legal entity to hire?

Not necessarily. An Employer of Record (EOR) can employ the person in Italy on your behalf. It handles the contract, payroll, contributions and compliance. You direct the daily work. This lets you test the market with a real hire before you set up a company.

You have found the person. The offer is ready. Now you need to know when they can start and when they will be paid. This article walks through the path from offer to first payslip when you hire in Italy through an Employer of Record (EOR).

We do not give a fixed number of days here. The real timeline depends on the role, the candidate's situation and how fast each side returns documents. What we can do is show you the stages, who owns each one, and where time is usually lost.

## Stage 1: Scope the role

Everything starts with a clear description of the job. The EOR needs the job title, duties, working location, working hours, reporting line and the pay you plan to offer.

Italy sets employment terms through national collective agreements. The right agreement depends on the sector and the type of work. Choosing it correctly sets the minimum pay, notice rules, leave and contribution base. A wrong choice causes rework later.

This stage is fast when you arrive with a complete brief. It is slow when the role is still vague.

## Stage 2: Agree the terms and the contract

The EOR prepares an employment contract in line with the applicable collective agreement and Italian law. You review the commercial terms. The candidate reviews the contract.

Most delays here come from negotiation, not from paperwork. If the candidate wants changes to pay, benefits or notice, each round adds time. Settle the main points in the offer conversation before the contract is drafted.

## Stage 3: Collect candidate documents

The EOR needs identity details, tax identification and bank details. It also needs information on family circumstances that affect tax treatment.

This part sits mostly with the candidate. Ask them early to gather everything. Missing documents are the most common reason a start date slips.

## Stage 4: Right to work

If the candidate is an EU citizen, this stage is simple. If the candidate lives outside the EU, you need a work authorisation and a visa before they can start. That is a separate track with its own timing, and it often decides the whole schedule.

If you plan to hire someone from abroad, begin the visa track as soon as the offer is accepted. Do not wait for the contract to be finished. Ask your EOR to run both in parallel where possible.

If the person already lives in Italy with a valid permit, check that the permit allows this type of work.

## Stage 5: Registration with authorities

Before the start date, the EOR registers the employment with the Italian social security and labour systems. It also sets up the worker for tax withholding and contributions.

This is where an EOR earns its fee. Your company has no Italian entity, so it cannot do this itself. The EOR is the legal employer and files in its own name. Registration must be in place on time, so the start date must be fixed with enough notice.

## Stage 6: Start date and onboarding

On the first day, the employee begins work for you. The EOR gives them the required notices and a clear contact for payroll questions. You give them tools, access and a manager.

Keep a record of the actual start date and hours worked. Payroll depends on it.

## Stage 7: First payroll run

Italian payroll runs on a monthly cycle. The EOR needs your approved data before the cut-off: hours, absences, any variable pay, expenses and bonuses.

The first payslip follows the first payroll cycle after the start date. If the start date falls just after a cut-off, the first payslip comes a full cycle later. This surprises many foreign employers. Pick the start date with the payroll calendar in mind and ask your EOR for the cut-off dates.

The first run is also the one most likely to need corrections. Check the payslip together with the employee and the EOR before the next cycle.

## What slows a hire down

- A vague job brief.
- Contract negotiation that continues after drafting.
- Missing candidate documents.
- A visa track that starts late.
- A start date chosen without looking at payroll cut-offs.
- Late approval of payroll data.

## What speeds it up

- Send the full brief on the first day.
- Settle pay and notice in the offer, not in the contract.
- Ask the candidate for documents as soon as they accept.
- Run the visa and contract in parallel.
- Fix the start date after you know the payroll calendar.
- Name one person on your side who approves payroll data on time.

## A practical way to plan

Work backwards. Decide the date you want the first payslip issued. Subtract the payroll cycle. That gives you the latest start date. Subtract registration, then the contract and documents, then the visa if there is one. The result is the date by which you must send the brief.

Ask your EOR to confirm each stage in writing, with an owner and a target date. Then you can see the schedule instead of guessing it.

A compliant hire is not slow by nature. It is slow when information arrives late. Give the EOR what it needs early and the process stays predictable.

A monthly payroll figure is not a budget. If you hire in Italy and multiply one month of cost by the months in a year, you will get the wrong number. The annual cost is higher, and it does not arrive evenly.

This article shows how to build a full-year budget for one Italian hire. It also shows where the peaks come from, so finance is not surprised.

## Start with the right unit

Most foreign finance teams budget per month. That works for contractors. It does not work for Italian employees.

An Italian employee has a gross pay level, employer social contributions on top, and several deferred or periodic items that build up during the year. Some are paid monthly. Some are paid once. Some are accrued and paid out later.

So budget on an annual basis first. Then spread the result across months in a way that shows the real cash profile.

## The employer contribution layer

Employer social security is the largest add-on to gross pay. One component is the pension, disability and survivors contribution, known as IVS. A secondary source puts the employer share of IVS at 23.81% of taxable pay.

That is one line of the employer contribution stack, not the total. Other contributions apply as well, and the rate depends on the sector, the company size and the contract type. Treat the IVS figure as a floor for your thinking, not as the full on-cost.

Two practical points:

- The percentage applies to taxable pay. If taxable pay rises in a month, the contribution rises with it.
- The figure comes from a secondary source. Confirm the current rate for your case before you lock the budget.

## Why the annual figure is higher than it looks

Monthly cost looks smaller than the annual cost for three reasons.

**Extra payments.** Italian contracts commonly provide additional monthly payments beyond the regular ones. Your national collective agreement sets how many and when. These increase total pay for the year. Contributions follow them.

**Deferred pay.** Italian employees build up a severance entitlement during employment. The employer sets it aside every year and pays it out when the employment ends. It is a real liability from the first month. It does not show up in a simple monthly payroll view.

**Untaken leave.** Paid leave builds up all year. If it is not used, the balance is a cost on the books. Budget for the leave to be taken, and for the cover that may be needed.

## Where the peaks fall

Cash cost is not flat. Expect peaks in the months when extra payments are made. In those months, gross pay is higher than usual, and the employer contributions on that pay are higher too.

The usual pattern is:

1. A regular run rate in most months.
2. A visible jump in the months with an extra payment.
3. A further effect when bonuses or variable pay are paid out.
4. A one-off outflow at the end of employment for the accrued severance amount.

Your collective agreement decides the exact months. Ask for the payment calendar before you build the monthly view.

## A simple way to build the budget

Use a short table with one row per cost item and one column per month.

**Step 1. Gross pay.** Enter the annual gross, including the extra payments, then place each payment in its month.

**Step 2. Employer contributions.** Apply the contribution rates to the taxable pay of each month. Use the IVS share as one line, then add the other lines that apply to your sector and contract.

**Step 3. Severance accrual.** Add a monthly accrual line. This is a non-cash charge in the month, and a cash payment later. Show both views if your board wants both.

**Step 4. Variable pay.** Add bonuses, commissions and allowances in the month they are paid, not the month they are earned.

**Step 5. Other employment costs.** Include insurance, benefits, training, equipment and any mandatory health checks that apply to the role.

**Step 6. Contingency.** Add a buffer for rate changes and for contract changes during the year.

## Two views for two audiences

Finance needs both views, and they answer different questions.

- **Annual cost view.** Total cost of the hire for the year, with accruals. Use it for approvals and for comparing markets.
- **Cash view by month.** Actual outflows. Use it for treasury and for explaining peaks to the CFO.

If you only show the monthly run rate, you will under-report the annual cost. If you only show the annual total, you will miss the months where cash spikes.

## Common mistakes

- Dividing annual cost by the number of months and calling it a run rate.
- Forgetting that contributions are charged on the extra payments as well.
- Leaving out the severance accrual because it is not paid now.
- Using a rate from one sector for a role under a different collective agreement.
- Ignoring that a mid-year start changes which peaks fall in your first year.

## A note on mid-year starts

A hire who starts part-way through the year does not carry the full set of annual items in year one. Extra payments and accruals are usually pro-rated. The first-year cost is lower than the full-year cost, and the second year steps up. Show that step in the plan so the second-year budget is not a surprise.

## What to check before you sign off

Before you approve the headcount budget, confirm four things.

1. Which collective agreement applies to the role, and what it says on extra payments.
2. The current employer contribution rates for the sector and company size.
3. The expected pay calendar, so peak months are placed correctly.
4. Who carries the severance liability in your structure, and how it is shown in your books.

With those four answers, the budget becomes a plan you can defend. Without them, it is a guess.

Choosing a city is one of the first decisions when you hire in Italy. It shapes who you can recruit, what they cost and how fast you can grow. Many companies pick the best-known name and move on. A short scoring exercise gives a better answer.

This article gives you a framework. You set weights, score each candidate city and compare the totals. The method matters more than any single result.

## Step 1: Decide what the hub is for

The right city depends on the role of the team. Write down the answer before you look at any map.

- A sales team needs to be near clients or well connected to them.
- An engineering team needs a deep pool of technical graduates and experienced developers.
- A support or operations team needs language skills and stable, affordable staffing.
- A single senior hire may not need a hub at all. They may work from home, and the city only matters for occasional meetings.

If you cannot say what the hub is for, you are not ready to choose a city.

## Step 2: Set the weights

Use a simple scale. Mark each criterion as high, medium or low importance for your case. Then give high criteria a larger share of the final score. Keep the scale coarse. Fine-grained weights create false precision.

Here are the criteria that matter most, with a typical weight for a first hub.

**Talent pool (high).** Can you find the profiles you need, and can you find more than one? A city with a single suitable candidate is a risk. Look at local universities, existing employers in your field and how many professionals already work in your sector there.

**Total employment cost (high).** Salaries differ between regions. So do rents and the cost of living, which push salary expectations. Check market pay for your exact role in each city. Do not use national averages.

**Transport and access (medium).** How easy is it to reach the city from your head office and from your clients? Consider direct flights, fast trains and travel time for visiting staff. A hub that your own managers struggle to reach will be neglected.

**Client and partner proximity (medium to high).** For commercial roles, being close to customers can matter more than any cost saving. For back-office roles, it matters little.

**Language and international exposure (medium).** Larger business centers tend to have more people with strong English and other languages. Smaller cities may offer loyal staff but a thinner international pool.

**Retention and competition (medium).** A city full of employers in your field gives you choice, but it also means competitors can hire your people. A smaller market may give lower turnover. Decide which risk worries you more.

**Quality of life and relocation appeal (medium).** If you plan to move people from abroad, the city must be attractive to them. Think about housing, schools, safety and daily life. This also affects how easily family members settle.

**Office and space needs (low to medium).** Many teams start in shared space or fully remote. If you do not need an office yet, give this criterion a low weight.

## Step 3: Pick a short list

Choose a small number of candidate cities. Include a large business center, a mid-sized city and, if it fits your sector, a specialized hub known for your industry. Comparing different types of city shows you what you are trading off.

## Step 4: Score and compare

Give each city a score for each criterion. Multiply by the weight. Add up the totals. Then read the result with care.

- If two cities are close, choose the one with the better talent pool.
- If one city wins on cost but loses badly on talent, do not choose it.
- If your top choice depends on one assumption, test that assumption with real conversations before you commit.

Speak to local recruiters, to peers in your industry and to a few candidates. Ask what salaries they expect and what they would need to join a foreign company. This costs little and corrects many wrong assumptions.

## Step 5: Keep the decision reversible

Your first hub does not have to be your last. Hiring through an Employer of Record (EOR) lets you place people in different cities without opening a local entity in each one. You can start with one city, learn from it and add another as the team grows. You can also change your mind if the first choice does not work out.

This lowers the cost of a wrong guess. The decision still deserves care, but it is not permanent.

## Common mistakes

- Choosing the city with the most famous name without checking talent in your field.
- Using national salary data for a local hiring decision.
- Ignoring how your own managers will travel there.
- Weighting everything equally, which hides what really matters.
- Waiting for a perfect answer instead of testing the market.

## A simple rule

Put talent first, cost second and access third. Adjust only if your business has a clear reason to do so. Most first hubs succeed or fail on whether the right people can be found and kept.

You found a strong candidate in Italy. Then they tell you they have another offer from an Italian company. Your first instinct may be to raise the salary. Often that is the wrong move, and sometimes it is not even possible.

This article covers what else you can offer, and how to present it.

## Understand what the candidate fears

A candidate with a local offer compares you to a known quantity. The local company has an office, a legal entity and a name they can look up. You are a foreign company they may never have heard of.

So the real question is rarely money. It is risk. Ask directly:

- What worries you about joining a foreign company?
- What does the other offer give you that you value most?
- What would make you say yes today?

Listen for words like stability, contract, growth, team, flexibility. Those are your levers.

## Remove the employer risk

Many Italian candidates worry that a foreign company will not treat them like a normal local employee. They fear payment delays, missing contributions, or a contract that is hard to enforce.

An Employer of Record (EOR) answers this fear. The candidate signs an Italian employment contract with a local employer. They get Italian payslips, the right social security registration and a collective agreement that applies to their role. Their rights are the same as if they worked for an Italian company.

Say this plainly. Do not wait for the candidate to ask. Explain who the legal employer is, who pays them, and who they call if something goes wrong in payroll.

## Show the contract early

Uncertainty kills offers. A competing company may have already sent a full contract draft. If you only send an email with a salary figure, you look less serious.

Share a clear summary of the terms as soon as you can:

- Type of contract and role title
- Applicable collective agreement
- Working hours and remote work rules
- Paid leave and other benefits
- Probation terms and notice terms

Let the candidate read it, ask questions and take it to a trusted advisor. Openness builds trust faster than any pitch.

## Sell the work, not only the package

A salary is a number. A job is what the person does every day. Candidates in Italy often join a small local company where the scope is narrow and the path upward is slow. You may offer something different.

Think about what is true for your company and say it:

- Exposure to international customers and teams
- Real ownership of a product, market or project
- A clear path to a larger role as the Italian presence grows
- Working in English with colleagues in several countries
- Direct access to leaders who make decisions

Be specific. Name the project they would start with. Name the person they would report to. Offer a call with that manager so the candidate meets the real team, not just a recruiter.

## Offer flexibility that costs you little

Many local employers still expect people in the office on most days. If your team is built for remote or hybrid work, that is a real advantage. State it in the contract, not just in conversation.

Other low cost items can matter more than a small salary increase:

- Flexible hours that fit family life
- A budget for training and conferences
- Equipment of the candidate's choice
- Support for a home office

These show respect for how the person wants to work.

## Handle the notice period with care

If the candidate is currently employed, they will have to give notice. A local competitor may offer a faster start. Do not push the candidate to leave badly. Italian professional circles are small, and a candidate who burns a bridge may carry that stress into your company.

Instead, agree a realistic start date. Stay in contact during the notice period. A short message from the future manager, an invitation to a team call or an early welcome pack keeps you present while the other company waits.

## Move fast, but stay calm

Speed matters. If the other company decides in days and you take weeks, you lose. Prepare your internal approvals before you make the offer. Know who signs, what the limits are and how quickly the EOR can issue the contract.

But do not use pressure tactics. Short fake deadlines make a candidate suspicious. Give a fair time to decide and be available for questions.

## If you must discuss money

Sometimes the salary gap is real. You can still stay flexible without simply raising the base pay.

- Look at the structure of the package, not only the total
- Consider a bonus linked to clear goals
- Consider a review of the role level after a set period
- Explain total employment cost and what the candidate receives, so the comparison is honest

An honest comparison often helps you. Candidates see the whole picture and judge on facts.

## Know when to let go

Some candidates will take the local offer. That is fine. Thank them, keep the relationship warm and ask for feedback. The reason they give tells you what to fix in your next process. Often the answer is not salary at all.

## Summary

When a candidate holds a competing Italian offer, work on trust first. Explain the local employer, show the contract, describe the real job and offer flexibility. Move quickly and treat the candidate with respect. Salary matters, but it is rarely the only reason someone says yes.

You are about to hire in Italy. You need local advisors who know how Italian rules work in practice. The wrong choice costs you time, and sometimes penalties. This guide covers how to choose.

## Know which advisors you actually need

Most founders say "accountant" and mean three different roles.

- **Commercialista.** Handles tax, bookkeeping, VAT and company filings.
- **Consulente del lavoro.** Handles payroll, contracts, social security and labor rules. This is the person who matters most when you hire.
- **Avvocato.** A lawyer for corporate matters, disputes, dismissals and complex contracts.

Some firms offer all three. Many do not. Ask early who covers what, and who is accountable for each task.

## Check credentials first

Italian professionals belong to regulated bodies. Ask for the registration of each person who will work on your file. You can verify membership on the public register of the relevant professional body.

A commercialista should be registered with the order of accountants. A consulente del lavoro should be registered with the labor consultants' order. A lawyer should be registered with the local bar.

If someone cannot show registration, move on.

## Look for experience with foreign companies

Italian practice differs from your home country. A good advisor for a local family business may not be right for you.

Ask these questions:

- How many clients do you have that are owned or run from abroad?
- Have you handled a company with no Italian entity, or with a newly formed one?
- Do you have experience with employees reporting to a manager in another country?

Listen for specific examples. Vague answers are a warning sign.

## Test their English

You will read advice, sign documents and make decisions. Poor communication creates risk.

Ask for a short call before you commit. Check three things. Do they explain Italian terms clearly? Do they answer the question you asked? Do they put key points in writing afterward?

Note that official filings and many contracts will be in Italian. Ask who will translate and explain them. Ask whether translations come with the service or cost extra.

## Understand how they price

Fees vary widely. Do not pick on price alone, but do not accept unclear pricing either.

Ask for a written scope that states:

- What is included each month.
- What is billed separately, such as payroll runs, new hires, terminations or tax notices.
- Who pays for government fees and stamps.
- How fee changes are announced.

Fixed fees for recurring work are easier to plan. Hourly rates suit one-off questions. Be careful with very low quotes. They often hide extras.

## Ask about deadlines and process

Italy has strict filing and payment deadlines. Missing one can trigger penalties.

Ask how they track deadlines. Ask what they need from you, and by when. A good advisor gives you a simple calendar and a list of inputs. A weak one chases you at the last minute.

Also ask how they handle a notice from the tax or social security authorities. You want a clear process and a named contact.

## Check systems and access

You should be able to see your own data. Ask whether you get access to a client portal or shared folder. Ask how documents are stored and who can see them.

Ask about data protection. Your employee data falls under EU rules, so the firm must handle it correctly. A serious firm will answer without hesitation.

## Match size to your stage

A solo professional is often responsive and affordable. The risk is dependency on one person. If they are ill or leave, who covers?

A larger firm has depth and backup. The risk is that your small account gets junior attention.

For a first hire, a small or mid-sized firm with a named senior contact often works well. Ask who will actually do the work day to day.

## Ask for references

Request two or three clients similar to you. Speak to them. Ask about response time, accuracy and how problems were handled.

Do not rely only on online reviews. Many professionals get clients by referral, so reviews are thin.

## Plan for coordination

Your accountant, payroll provider and lawyer must share information. Ask whether they already work with the other advisors you plan to use. Decide who is the main point of contact. Without this, tasks fall between roles.

## Consider whether you need to build this network at all

Setting up advisors takes time. You must vet them, manage them and pay several parties. If you only want to hire a few people, an Employer of Record can cover payroll, contracts and compliance under one agreement. You still may need a tax advisor for your wider business, but the employment side is handled for you.

## A short checklist

1. Define which roles you need.
2. Verify registration for each professional.
3. Confirm experience with foreign-owned companies.
4. Test communication in a trial call.
5. Get a written scope and fee list.
6. Review their deadline and notice process.
7. Check data access and protection.
8. Speak to references.
9. Agree on one main contact.

Take your time on this choice. A good advisor saves you more than they cost.

A global benefits policy sounds simple. Every employee gets the same package, wherever they live. In practice it does not work. Benefits are tied to local tax, social security and market habits. The same package can be generous in one country and strange in another.

The better goal is not identical benefits. It is equal value, set by one policy, delivered in a local way. Think global policy with local fit.

## Start with principles, not products

Do not begin with a list of perks. Begin with what you want the benefits to do. Write down a few clear principles. For example:

- Everyone gets health cover that works in their country.
- Everyone gets a way to save for retirement.
- Everyone gets meaningful time off and family support.
- Total reward stays in a defined range for the same level of role.

These principles travel. A specific perk does not. A gym allowance means little where the real need is private health top-up. A company car is a status item in some markets and a tax problem in others.

## Separate what is fixed from what is local

Split your policy into two parts.

**The global core.** This is what you control from the centre. It covers your principles, your budget logic, your eligibility rules, and your approval process. It also covers how you compare total cost across countries.

**The local layer.** This is what each country decides. It covers the legal minimums, the collective agreements, the tax treatment and the common market practice. In Italy, a lot sits here.

If you try to push the core into the local layer, you create exceptions on every hire. If you push local rules into the core, you create a policy nobody can apply.

## What Italy changes

Italy has strong statutory and collective rules. Many benefits are not optional extras. They come from the national collective agreement that applies to the role and sector. Leave, notice, sick pay and extra payments often depend on it. Your global policy has to sit on top of these rules, not replace them.

This matters in one practical way. Some of your global benefits will already be covered by the local floor. Others will overlap. If you add a global benefit without checking, you may pay twice for the same thing.

Italy also has a developed welfare culture. Employers often give part of the package as welfare instead of cash, because the tax and contribution treatment can be better for both sides. Meal vouchers are the best known example.

## Meal vouchers: a small example of local fit

Meal vouchers are common in Italy. Many employees expect them. Electronic vouchers have a reference figure of 10 EUR per day, a point that came up in recent budget law news. Confirm the current threshold with your local adviser before you set budgets, because thresholds change.

Now look at it from the head office. A US or UK team may see this as a small food perk. For an Italian employee, it is part of normal pay structure. If you remove it or ignore it, the offer looks weaker than the number on paper suggests.

The lesson is general. Do not copy a benefit from your home country into Italy. Ask what the local market uses to deliver the same value, and match that.

## Compare on total cost and total value

To harmonise, you need one way to compare. Use total employer cost on one side and net value to the employee on the other.

For each country, build a simple table:

- Base pay
- Mandatory employer contributions
- Statutory and collective extras
- Voluntary benefits
- Total employer cost

Then look at the employee side. What does the person actually receive, after tax and in useful terms? A benefit that costs you little but is taxed heavily may be worth less than a smaller benefit with better treatment.

This view stops two common mistakes. One is overpaying in countries with high mandatory costs. The other is underpaying in countries where the market expects more through benefits.

## Set guardrails, not rules for every case

Give local managers a range, not a script. For example, define a target band for total reward by role level. Inside the band, let each country choose the mix. Outside the band, require approval.

Also decide in advance:

- Who owns the benefits budget in each country.
- How often you review local practice.
- What happens when a country rule changes.
- How you handle employees who relocate.

The last point is easy to forget. When someone moves to Italy, their benefits do not move with them. The local rules apply from the start. Plan the transition before the move, so the person knows what changes.

## Keep communication simple

Employees do not need to see your whole framework. They need to see what they get, in their own country, in clear words. A short local benefits summary, in the local language, does more than a long global handbook.

Inside the company, explain the logic once. Tell managers that fair does not mean identical. It means the same intent, delivered in the way that works locally.

## Use local support where rules are heavy

If you do not have an entity in Italy, you still have to meet local rules from the first day. An Employer of Record can apply the collective agreement, run payroll and manage welfare benefits on your behalf, while you keep control of the policy. That lets you hire without building local expertise first. You set the principles. The local partner handles the detail.

Your first Italian team lead sets the tone for everything that follows. They will hire the next people. They will explain your company to the local team. They will tell you what works in Italy and what does not.

So the profile and the scope matter more than the salary discussion. Get these right and the rest is easier.

## Start with the job, not the title

In Italy, titles carry weight. A "team lead", a "manager" and a "head of" mean different things to candidates, and they can affect contract classification and the collective agreement that applies. Do not borrow a title from your home market and hope it fits.

Write down what the person will actually do in the first months:

- Which work do they own?
- Which decisions can they make alone?
- Who do they report to, and in which time zone?
- Will they manage people on day one, or build the team first?

If you cannot answer these in a few lines, the role is not ready to be advertised.

## Two common profiles

Most companies need one of two people. Be honest about which one you are hiring.

**The player-coach.** This person does the work and guides a small group. They suit a team that is still being built. They are hands-on, they write the processes as they go, and they are comfortable with a loose structure. The risk is overload. If you give them too much delivery work, the leadership part never happens.

**The people manager.** This person spends most of their time on hiring, feedback, planning and coordination. They suit a team that already has some delivery capacity. The risk is distance. If they have no technical or commercial credibility, the team will not follow them.

Mixing the two without saying so is the most common mistake. The candidate hears one job in the interview and finds another after they start.

## What to look for

A good first team lead in Italy usually shows these traits:

- **Experience with foreign headquarters.** They have worked with managers abroad, in English, across time zones. They know how to translate between your culture and the local one.
- **A local network.** They know where to find good people and who to avoid. This matters because your first hires will mostly come through them.
- **Comfort with ambiguity.** You have no local entity, no established routines and maybe no office. They need to act without a manual.
- **Credibility with the team.** They have done the work themselves. Italian teams tend to respect competence shown, not authority claimed.
- **Clear written English.** Your reporting lines, goals and feedback will pass through them. Weak English creates silent misunderstandings.

A long list of past titles is less useful than a short list of teams they built and results they can describe.

## Define the scope in writing

Before the first interview, prepare a short scope document. Keep it to a page. It should cover:

1. **Mission.** What the team must achieve in plain terms.
2. **Authority.** Hiring, budget, tools, customer contact. Say what is allowed and what needs approval from headquarters.
3. **Reporting line.** Name the person abroad who manages them, and how often they will talk.
4. **Growth path.** Whether the team is expected to grow, and what happens to the lead's role if it does.
5. **Success measures.** Two or three outcomes you will review together, agreed in advance.

Share this document with finalists. Good candidates will ask sharp questions about it. Weak ones will not read it.

## Decide how much authority to give

Foreign companies often hire a local lead and then keep every decision at headquarters. The lead becomes a messenger. Strong people leave quickly in that situation.

The opposite error also happens. A company gives full freedom, then reacts badly when the first decision differs from the home market approach.

A workable middle path: give clear authority over daily work and hiring within an agreed plan. Keep strategy, pricing and brand with headquarters. Review the split together after the early months and widen it as trust grows.

## Plan the legal side before the offer

You do not need a local company to hire in Italy. An Employer of Record can employ the person on your behalf while you direct their daily work. This lets you test the market and the person before committing to a subsidiary.

Still, settle the contract basics before you make an offer: the role level, the applicable collective agreement, working hours, remote arrangements and the notice terms. Candidates in Italy expect these details to be clear early. Vagueness reads as risk.

## A short checklist

- The role is described as player-coach or people manager, not both.
- The scope fits on one page.
- The reporting line and meeting rhythm are named.
- Authority limits are written down.
- The contract framework is clear before the offer.

Hire slowly for this role. One strong team lead makes every later hire cheaper, faster and better.

You are hiring in Italy and your interview process was built somewhere else. That is normal. The risk is not that your process is wrong. The risk is that candidates read it differently than you intend.

This guide covers the format that works well in Italy and what candidates tend to expect from you.

## Start with the relationship

Italian interviews are usually less transactional than in many other markets. Candidates want to understand who you are, not only what the job is. Expect a short warm-up before the structured part. Do not rush it.

A friendly but professional opening works best. Introduce yourself, your role and your company. Say clearly why you are hiring in Italy. Candidates often have never heard of a foreign company before, so context matters.

Use formal address in your first emails unless the candidate moves to a casual tone. In English this is less visible, but polite phrasing still helps.

## Choose the interview language on purpose

English skills vary a lot between candidates, even among strong professionals. Decide which language you need for the role and say so in the job post.

If English is required for the work, test it in the interview. If it is not, offer to run part of the conversation in Italian with a local colleague or advisor. A candidate who is nervous in a second language can look weaker than they are.

Send questions in advance if you want deeper answers. Many candidates prepare better this way.

## Expect a walk through the CV

Italian candidates often explain their career as a story. They will talk about their studies, their path and the reasons behind each move. This is not rambling. It is how many people present credibility.

Let them do it, then steer. Ask for specific examples from recent roles. Behavioral questions work, but some candidates are less used to the exact structured format that is common in US or UK interviews. Rephrase if needed. Ask "Tell me about a project you led and what happened" instead of using a rigid formula.

## Multiple rounds are common

Candidates will not be surprised by several stages. They may be surprised by a process with no human contact until an offer. Plan at least a screening call, a conversation with the hiring manager and a technical or practical step where relevant.

Keep the stages short and tell candidates the full process upfront. Silence between rounds is read as lack of interest. Send a quick update even when there is no news.

## Be direct about pay and contract

Salary is a normal topic and candidates want to know early. Give the range for the role and say whether it is gross. Many people think in gross annual terms, but confirm so there is no confusion.

Candidates also care about the full package. Be ready to explain:

- The type of employment contract.
- Working hours and how flexible they are.
- Remote or hybrid options.
- Benefits and any bonus structure.
- Leave and notice terms.

Italian employment is shaped by national collective agreements, and candidates know this. If you can say which one applies to the role, you look prepared. If you are working with an Employer of Record (EOR), explain that the EOR is the legal employer and that day-to-day work happens with your team. Candidates worry about this point more than foreign employers expect.

## Address stability

An unknown foreign company without an Italian entity raises a fair question: is this job safe? Do not wait for the candidate to ask. Explain how the employment is set up, who pays salary and contributions, and how long the company has operated.

Candidates trust clear answers. They distrust vague ones.

## Know the style of the conversation

Italian candidates often speak with energy and will interrupt politely to add a point. This is engagement, not rudeness. Do not read it as lack of discipline.

They may also be modest in a different way. Some will avoid bragging and describe results as team outcomes. Ask "What was your personal part?" to get a clear answer.

On video calls, be punctual, keep your camera on and check the time zone twice. Small signals of respect matter.

## Let candidates interview you

Leave real time for their questions. Good candidates will ask about the team, management style, growth and how decisions are made. They also want to know how a remote manager will support them. Prepare honest answers.

If your company is distributed, say how Italian employees connect with colleagues. Isolation is a common concern.

## Close with clarity

End each interview by stating the next step and when they will hear back. After the final round, move quickly. Strong candidates often have other options, and a slow offer can lose them.

When you make the offer, put it in writing and explain each part. Be ready for a negotiation on salary, start date or flexibility. This is common and not a sign of bad faith.

## Summary

Keep the process human, structured and transparent. Offer the right language. Explain the employer setup and the package. Give feedback fast. Do this and Italian candidates will see a serious employer, even if you have no local office.

You hired in Italy through an Employer of Record. Now you have set up your own Italian entity and want your people on your payroll. The risk is simple. If you handle the move badly, employees lose their seniority and their TFR is paid out early. That costs them money and costs you trust.

The fix is a balance transfer. This article explains what it is and how to run it.

## What is at stake

Seniority drives several rights in Italy. It affects notice periods, some contract benefits, and protection on dismissal. It also affects how the national collective agreement (CCNL) treats the employee over time.

TFR is the severance amount that builds up during employment. The employer sets it aside. It is paid when the employment ends, or it goes to a pension fund if the employee chose that route.

If the EOR relationship ends and your entity hires the person fresh, both can reset. Seniority starts again. The EOR must settle TFR. The employee sees a break that was never needed.

## Two ways to move

**Resign and rehire.** The EOR contract ends. Your entity signs a new contract. This is simple on paper. It is also the option that breaks continuity. Seniority is lost unless you agree otherwise, and TFR is paid out at the end of the EOR contract.

**Transfer of the contract.** The employment continues without a break. The employee moves from the EOR to your entity as the same employment relationship. Seniority stays. The TFR already accrued moves with the employee. This is the balance transfer.

For most teams, the transfer is the better path.

## How the balance transfer works

The idea is that the accrued TFR does not get paid out and then rebuilt. Instead, the liability moves from the EOR to your entity. Your entity then continues to accrue TFR on top of the existing balance.

In practice you need these pieces:

- **A written agreement between all parties.** The EOR, your entity and the employee all sign. The employee must consent to the change of employer.
- **A clear statement of continuity.** The agreement says the employment continues and that seniority is recognised in full from the original start date.
- **A TFR statement from the EOR.** It shows the accrued balance at the transfer date, so both sides agree on the number.
- **A settlement of the money.** The EOR either transfers the funds to your entity or credits the amount against fees you owe. Your entity then carries the liability on its books. Agree this in writing before the move.

## What to check before the transfer

Several items sit outside TFR and seniority. Check them so nothing is lost or paid twice.

- **Accrued leave and permits.** Agree whether unused leave is carried over or paid out.
- **Probation.** The employee already served it. Do not apply a new probation period.
- **CCNL and job level.** Keep the same agreement and level, or one that is not worse. A downgrade invites disputes.
- **Pension fund choices.** If the employee directs TFR to a pension fund, the fund contributions must continue without a gap.
- **Benefits and allowances.** Match the package, or explain any change clearly.
- **Loans or advances.** If the employee drew an advance on TFR, record it and carry it across.

## Common mistakes

**Treating the move as a new hire.** Even a well-meant offer letter can reset seniority if it says nothing about continuity.

**Skipping the employee's consent.** A change of employer needs agreement. Do not assume it.

**Leaving the TFR number vague.** If the EOR and your entity disagree on the balance later, the employee is caught in the middle. Fix the figure in the signed documents.

**Starting too late.** The EOR contract has terms. Read the exit clauses early. Notice and handover steps take time, and your entity must be ready to run payroll from day one.

## A simple order of work

1. Confirm your entity can run payroll and is registered with the relevant authorities.
2. Ask the EOR for a TFR statement and a list of accrued entitlements for each employee.
3. Draft a single transfer agreement that all parties sign.
4. Agree how the TFR money moves, and when.
5. Brief each employee in plain language on what stays the same.
6. Start payroll in your entity on the transfer date, with no gap.

Have a local employment adviser review the documents. Rules and the exact treatment of each item depend on the CCNL and the facts of the case.

## The takeaway

A balance transfer keeps the employment continuous. Seniority stays. TFR stays with the person. You avoid a payout and a rebuild, and your team sees the move as a step forward, not a reset.

Italy has a deep pool of software engineers. Many work for local firms, consultancies or foreign companies already. Hiring them from abroad is very possible. It just works differently from hiring in the US or the UK.

This guide covers where to look, what to expect on timing, and how to write a pitch that gets answers.

## Where developers are found

### Professional networks

LinkedIn is the main channel for mid and senior engineers. Most Italian developers keep a profile and many reply to a clear, personal message. Generic outreach gets ignored. A short note that names their stack and says why you picked them performs far better.

### Developer communities

Italy has active local communities around languages and frameworks. Meetups, Slack and Telegram groups, and conference audiences are full of people who care about their craft. Sponsoring a talk or answering questions in a group builds trust over time. Posting a job link cold does not.

### Open source and code platforms

GitHub shows real work. If you hire for a specific language, search for contributors based in Italy. Read their code before you write to them. Mention a project by name. That one detail sets you apart from every other message in their inbox.

### Universities and technical schools

Italian universities produce strong engineering graduates, especially in the big northern cities and in Rome, Naples and Turin. Contact career offices and research groups if you want junior talent. Many graduates are open to remote roles with foreign firms, because local pay for juniors can feel low to them.

### Referrals

The Italian tech scene is small. A good hire often knows other good people. Ask every developer you hire, and every candidate you reject politely, whether they know someone suitable. Referrals tend to close faster and stay longer.

## Timelines to expect

Hiring in Italy is rarely instant. Plan for these stages.

- **Sourcing and first contact.** Allow time for replies. Many candidates answer after a few days, not hours.
- **Interviews.** Keep the process short. A long chain of technical rounds loses people to faster offers. A single technical conversation plus a talk with the team lead is often enough.
- **Notice period.** This is the part foreign teams miss most. Italian employees usually have contractual notice periods with their current employer. For senior roles these can be long. Ask about notice early so your start date is realistic.
- **Contract and onboarding.** The employment contract must follow Italian rules. Payroll, social security registration and benefits must be ready before day one. If you have no Italian entity, this is where an Employer of Record (EOR) removes the delay. You do not need to set up a company first.

The practical rule: tell candidates the full timeline at the start. Surprises later cost you the hire.

## What to put in your pitch

Italian developers read a lot of vague job posts. A strong pitch is specific.

**State the role and stack in the first lines.** Name the language, the framework, the product and the team size. Skip filler about being a fast-growing family.

**Be clear about remote work.** Say if the role is fully remote, hybrid or tied to a city. Many candidates want remote work and will filter on it first.

**Show the salary range.** Pay transparency builds trust. If you hide it, you lose people who suspect it is low. Quote the gross annual figure and say if it is paid in the standard Italian structure.

**Explain the employment setup.** Candidates worry about foreign employers. Tell them they will have a proper Italian employment contract, with Italian social security, paid leave and the usual protections. Say who the legal employer is. When an EOR holds the contract, say so plainly and explain that you manage the daily work.

**Describe the work and the people.** Who will they report to? What will they build in the first months? Engineers care about technical quality, code review habits and how decisions get made.

**Respect language and time zones.** Most Italian developers work well in English. Say which language the team uses. Name the overlap hours you expect.

## Common mistakes

- Treating Italy as a low-cost market. Strong developers know their value and compare offers from across Europe.
- Asking for a long unpaid take-home test.
- Ignoring notice periods when you set a start date.
- Offering a freelance arrangement when the candidate wants a stable employment contract.
- Replying slowly. Good candidates often hold several conversations at once.

## A simple approach

Pick two or three channels and work them well. Write a pitch with the stack, pay, remote terms and employer details. Keep interviews short. Be honest about timing. Then use an EOR so the contract, payroll and compliance are in place when the candidate says yes.
