You hired well in Italy. Now you want people to stay. In a remote-first company, that depends on two things: whether they feel they belong, and whether they can see a future.

Pay matters. But pay alone rarely keeps a good person. Belonging and growth do more work than most managers expect.

## Why remote makes belonging harder

An Italian employee working from home often sits far from your head office. They may be the only person from their country on the team. They miss the hallway talk. They miss the small signals that tell you whether you are valued.

In many Italian workplaces, relationships carry weight. People like to know who they work with. They want to be seen as a person, not a task list. A remote setup that treats them as a resource will feel cold fast.

The risk is quiet. People rarely complain. They update their profile and take a call from a recruiter.

## Build belonging on purpose

Do not leave it to chance. Small, steady habits work better than a big yearly event.

- **Hold regular video calls with cameras on.** Keep them short. Make room for a few words about life before the agenda.
- **Meet in person when you can.** Bring the Italian team to your main office, or send leaders to Italy. Face time builds trust that lasts for months.
- **Pair new hires with a buddy.** Pick someone who is not their manager. Give them time to answer simple questions.
- **Share context, not only tasks.** Explain why the company makes its choices. People stay where they understand the direction.
- **Respect local rhythm.** Know the national holidays. Do not schedule key calls at hours that ignore local habits. Small signs of respect add up.

## Make the employment feel solid

Italian employees care about security. A clear contract, correct payslips and on-time payments tell them you are serious. If something goes wrong with payroll or paperwork, trust drops quickly and is hard to rebuild.

This is where an Employer of Record (EOR) helps. The EOR is the legal employer in Italy. It handles contracts, payroll, contributions and compliance. Your team in Italy gets a proper local employment relationship. You keep day-to-day control of the work. Fewer administrative errors means fewer reasons for doubt.

## Growth: show a path

Remote workers worry about being forgotten. Out of sight can mean out of mind when promotions are discussed. Fight this directly.

**Write down career steps.** Define what the next level looks like. Say what skills and results it takes. Do it for roles held in Italy, not only at headquarters.

**Hold real career talks.** Not just performance reviews. Ask what the person wants to learn and where they want to be in a few years. Then act on the answer.

**Fund learning.** Give a budget and time for courses, books and conferences. Let people choose. Italian professionals often value training in their field and in languages.

**Offer stretch work.** Let people lead a project, mentor a newcomer or present to leadership. Visibility counts when you are remote.

**Promote from within.** When a role opens, look at your Italian team first. Each internal move shows the others that growth is real.

## Recognition without theatre

Praise should be specific and timely. Say what the person did and why it mattered. Do it in public when that fits, and in private when it does not.

Avoid empty perks. A gift card does less than a manager who understands the work. Avoid slogans about being a family. Italian employees tend to prefer honest, respectful treatment over corporate warmth.

## Listen and act

Ask for feedback often. Short surveys help, but a direct conversation is better. When you hear a problem, fix it and report back. People stop talking when nothing changes.

Watch for warning signs:

- Cameras that stay off and silence in meetings.
- Fewer questions and less initiative.
- Declining requests to join optional sessions.
- A manager who has not spoken to the person one to one in a long time.

Act early. A frank conversation costs little. Replacing a trained employee costs far more.

## Managers make the difference

People leave managers more than companies. Train your leaders to run remote teams well. They should give clear goals, check in without hovering, and trust people to deliver. Make sure managers outside Italy understand local expectations on working time, leave and communication.

## A short plan

- Set a rhythm of team calls and one to one talks.
- Plan in-person time for the Italian team.
- Write career paths and share them.
- Fund learning and let people pick.
- Keep payroll and contracts accurate through a reliable local employer.
- Ask for feedback and show what you changed.

Retention is not a perk program. It is a habit of showing people they matter and that they can grow with you. Do that consistently, and your Italian team will have good reasons to stay.

Performance reviews are normal in Italy. But a review that works in New York or London can cause problems in Milan or Rome. The reasons are legal, cultural and practical. This guide covers the format that works and the fairness points that matter most.

## Why fairness matters more in Italy

Italian employment law protects employees strongly. A review is not only a talk about goals. It can become evidence if a dispute starts later. A poor rating that is vague, undocumented or inconsistent with past feedback is hard to defend.

So treat every review as a record. Write down what was said, on what basis, and what was agreed.

## Check the collective agreement first

Most Italian employees are covered by a national collective agreement (CCNL). It sets job levels, pay components and sometimes rules on bonuses and career progression. Before you design your review process, read the agreement that applies to your employee. Your review must not conflict with it.

In particular, check:

- how job levels and promotions are defined
- whether bonuses or pay steps are tied to set criteria
- any rules on notice, warnings or disciplinary steps

A rating system that ignores these rules can create expectations you cannot meet, or trigger claims you did not plan for.

## Keep ratings separate from discipline

A performance review is a development tool. A disciplinary process is a formal legal procedure with its own steps and rights for the employee. Do not mix them.

If a review shows a serious problem, do not announce a sanction in the meeting. Record the issue, set clear expectations and take advice before any formal step. Skipping this separation is one of the most common mistakes foreign employers make.

## A format that works

Keep the structure simple and repeat it every time.

**1. Agree objectives in writing.** Set them at the start of the period. Make them specific and tied to the role. Both sides should sign off.

**2. Collect input from more than one person.** Ask the direct manager and, where relevant, colleagues the employee works with. This reduces the risk that one person's bias drives the result.

**3. Use a self-assessment.** Let the employee write their own view before the meeting. It makes the talk a conversation, not a verdict.

**4. Use a short, clear rating scale.** Define each level in plain words. Avoid scales where most people end up in the middle with no explanation.

**5. Hold the meeting in private.** Allow enough time. Start with what went well. Then cover gaps with examples.

**6. Send a written summary afterward.** Include ratings, examples, agreed actions and support offered. Invite the employee to add comments.

## Be concrete, not personal

Italian employees often respond badly to vague criticism. They respond well to specific facts. Say "the report was late on these occasions and this is the effect" instead of "you lack commitment."

Keep comments about work and results. Do not comment on personal traits, family situation, health, age, gender, origin or beliefs. Anything that looks like discrimination can create serious risk.

## Treat people consistently

Fairness means similar cases get similar outcomes. Use the same form, the same criteria and the same timing for comparable roles. If you rate two people differently, be able to explain why with facts.

Train managers before they run reviews. Remote managers abroad need the most guidance. They may apply home-country habits, such as blunt feedback or forced ranking, that do not fit local expectations.

## Be careful with data and monitoring

Performance data is personal data. Collect only what you need. Tell employees what you track and why. Be especially careful with tools that monitor activity, such as software that tracks keystrokes, location or screen time. Italian rules on remote monitoring of workers are strict. Do not use such data in a review unless you have confirmed it was collected lawfully.

## Link pay and promotion carefully

If bonuses depend on the review, define the formula in advance. Put it in writing. Do not change the rules after the period ends. If the collective agreement or the contract already gives a pay element, a review cannot simply remove it.

## Language and culture

Offer the review in a language the employee understands well. If the employee works in Italian, give the written summary in Italian too. This avoids misunderstandings and helps if the document is ever needed later.

Expect more discussion than you may be used to. Employees may want to explain context and push back on ratings. That is not defiance. Allow it, note it, and respond calmly.

## After the review

Follow up on what you agreed. Check in regularly, not only at review time. Employees should never be surprised by a rating. If you give feedback throughout the period, the formal review is just a summary.

## Where an Employer of Record helps

If you employ people in Italy through an Employer of Record (EOR), the EOR is the legal employer. You direct the daily work. Your EOR partner can advise on how to run reviews within local rules, check the applicable collective agreement and review documents before a sensitive conversation. That keeps your process fair and your records sound.

A salary band in Italy starts from a legal and contractual floor, not from a market survey. If you begin with market data alone, you may land below the minimum for the role. If you begin with the floor alone, you may not attract anyone.

This guide shows how to combine both.

## Start with the CCNL

Most employees in Italy are covered by a national collective labour agreement, known as a CCNL. It sets minimum pay by job level and sector. Employers must respect it, even when the employment contract says something different.

The CCNL does more than set a base figure. It also defines how pay is structured, what extra payments apply, how overtime is treated, and how much paid leave and notice the employee gets. These terms change the real cost and the real value of an offer.

So the first step is simple. Identify which CCNL applies to the role, then find the level that matches the duties. The floor is the minimum for that level. Your band cannot start below it.

## Choose the right agreement and level

The agreement follows the activity of the employer, not the nationality of the parent company. A software firm, a logistics business and a consulting company can each fall under a different CCNL. Pick the one that fits the real activity in Italy.

Level matters as much as sector. Each level describes a set of tasks and a degree of autonomy. A job title from your home market may not map cleanly. A "senior manager" in your org chart could sit at a different level here. Map by duties, not by title.

Getting this wrong has two costs. If you classify too low, you risk disputes and back payments. If you classify too high, you pay more than you need to for the whole term of the contract.

## Add market data above the floor

The CCNL floor tells you the minimum. Market data tells you what it takes to hire.

For most skilled roles, the market pays above the contractual minimum. This is common in technology, finance and other competitive fields. In lower-demand roles, the market may sit close to the floor.

Use several sources for market data:

- Salary surveys from recognised providers in Italy.
- Job postings for similar roles in the same city.
- Feedback from recruiters who place candidates locally.
- Your own offers and rejections from earlier searches.

No single source is enough. Compare them, and note the date of each. Pay levels shift, and old data misleads.

Location also matters. Pay in a large northern city often differs from pay in a smaller town or in the south. If the role can be done remotely, decide whether you will pay by location or at one rate for the country.

## Build the band

Once you have the floor and the market range, set three points.

**Minimum.** Never below the CCNL floor for the level. For a competitive offer, set it a little above.

**Midpoint.** The market rate for a fully competent person in the role. This is where most hires should land.

**Maximum.** The ceiling for top performers or people with rare skills. Keep room for growth so you do not have to promote someone just to give a raise.

Keep the band narrow enough to be meaningful. A very wide band makes offers hard to defend and invites unequal pay for similar work.

## Look at the whole package

Candidates in Italy compare more than the base figure. They look at the full package. That includes the extra monthly payments set by the CCNL, the leave allowance, supplementary health cover, meal vouchers, and any variable pay.

Some of these items are required by the CCNL. Others are optional, and they can help you compete without raising the base. Meal vouchers and health plans are common tools. Variable pay can reward results while keeping fixed cost under control.

Be clear about which items are gross and which are net. Candidates often think in net terms, while employers budget in gross terms. A good offer explains both.

## Remember total employer cost

The salary is not the cost. Employer social contributions, severance accrual, insurance and other charges sit on top. Budget the total cost for each point in your band, not just the pay figure.

This step prevents surprises. A band that looks affordable in gross pay can exceed budget once contributions are added. Run the numbers at the minimum, midpoint and maximum before you publish the band.

## Check internal fairness

Compare the band with your pay structure in other countries. You do not need identical pay. You do need a reason for each difference, and the reason should be based on role, level and local market, not on guesswork.

Document how you set the band. If a question comes up later, you can show the CCNL level, the data you used and the date you reviewed it.

## Review on a schedule

A band is not permanent. CCNLs are renewed, and minimums change when they are. Market pay moves too. Set a regular review, and check the band again whenever a new agreement comes into force.

## A short checklist

- Identify the CCNL that applies to the activity.
- Match each role to a level by duties.
- Record the contractual floor for each level.
- Collect market data from several sources and note the dates.
- Set a minimum, midpoint and maximum.
- Add the package items that help you compete.
- Calculate total employer cost at each point.
- Review the band on a fixed schedule.

This approach keeps you compliant and competitive. The floor protects you from underpaying. The market data protects you from losing candidates.

Entering a new country is a bet. You can make it smaller. One sales hire, set up with a clear test design, tells you most of what you need to know about Italy before you commit to an entity, an office or a team.

This article explains how to design that test so the downside stays small.

## Start with the question, not the hire

A market test answers a question. Write it down before you recruit anyone.

Good questions are specific:

- Do Italian buyers respond to our offer in Italian?
- Can we win deals with our current price and contract terms?
- Which type of customer converts fastest?
- Does our product need local proof, such as references or certifications?

Bad questions are vague: "Can we succeed in Italy?" You cannot answer that with one person in a short time. You can answer the four above.

Pick one or two questions. Everything else in the design follows from them.

## Choose the right profile

A test hire is not a country manager. Do not hire someone who needs a team to be effective.

Look for a salesperson who:

- has sold similar products to similar buyers in Italy
- can open doors with their own network
- is comfortable working without a local office
- can write and speak well in Italian and in your company language
- likes building process, not only closing deals

Seniority matters less than fit. A strong individual contributor with a relevant network will often produce more signal than an executive who expects support staff.

## Keep fixed costs low

The purpose of the test is to limit what you lose if the answer is no. So limit commitments that are hard to reverse.

Avoid, for now:

- renting an office
- setting up a local company before you know you need one
- hiring support roles
- buying local tools and licences you may not use

A remote salesperson with a laptop, a phone and access to your CRM is enough. If you need a legal and payroll structure to employ them, use a model that lets you hire without building your own entity first. An Employer of Record (EOR) does this. It employs the person on your behalf in Italy, handles payroll, contributions and compliance, and you direct their daily work.

This keeps your setup time short and your exit simple.

## Define success before you start

Write the targets and the stop rules at the beginning. Do it together with the hire, so both sides understand the test.

Use leading indicators as well as revenue. Sales cycles are often longer than a short test period, so revenue alone can mislead you.

Track:

- number of qualified conversations
- number of demos or meetings held
- number of proposals sent
- reasons for lost deals
- feedback on price, language and product fit

Then set three decisions in advance:

1. **Scale:** what results make you add people or open an entity.
2. **Adjust:** what results mean you change the offer, price or target segment.
3. **Stop:** what results mean you end the test.

If you decide these after the fact, you will argue yourself into whatever you hoped to see.

## Give the hire what they need to sell

Many tests fail because the company sends a person to Italy with nothing local to sell with.

Prepare before day one:

- Italian-language website pages, a deck and a one-page offer
- pricing in euros and terms that Italian buyers can sign
- a clear process for contracts, invoicing and support
- a named person at headquarters who answers within a day
- a lead list or ideal customer profile to start from

If these are missing, you are testing your own preparation, not the market.

## Plan the employment side early

The employment contract is part of the test design. Italian employment is governed by national collective agreements that set parts of pay, benefits and notice rules. Your hire's package should follow the agreement that fits the role. An EOR will tell you which one applies and what the full cost looks like, so you can build the test budget on real numbers and not guesses.

Also decide early how you will handle:

- the structure of pay, including any variable part tied to results
- expenses and travel
- what happens at the end of the test, whether you continue, convert to your own entity, or part ways

Ask about the exit terms before you sign. A low-risk test needs a low-friction exit.

## Review on a fixed rhythm

Hold a short review at regular intervals. Look at the indicators, the lost-deal reasons and the customer feedback. Keep a written log.

At the end of the test, answer the questions you started with. Be honest about what the data shows and what it does not.

If the result is positive, you now have a person, a pipeline and real knowledge of the market. If it is negative, you have lost little and you know why.

## What you get from this approach

One hire will not tell you everything. It will tell you whether Italian buyers want what you sell, at your price, in your way. That is the information you need before a larger investment.

Small scope, clear questions, written stop rules and an easy exit. That is the whole design.

You hired in Italy through an Employer of Record (EOR). Now your own Italian entity is ready. The next step is moving your people across. The legal work matters, but the people side decides whether the move goes well.

This guide focuses on two things: continuity and communication.

## Start with what must not change

Your employees did not ask for this change. For them, it should feel like a change of payroll sender, not a change of job. Decide early what stays the same:

- Role, title and reporting line.
- Pay and benefits, at least at the same level.
- Working location and working pattern.
- Recognition of their time already served.
- The collective agreement that applies to their work.

Write this list down. It becomes the backbone of your plan and of your message to staff.

## Map what the EOR does today

An EOR does many small jobs that people never see. Before you switch it off, list them all. Typical items include:

- Monthly payroll and payslips.
- Social security and tax filings.
- Holiday and leave tracking.
- Benefit schemes and insurance.
- Expense reimbursement.
- Employee contracts and personnel files.
- Health and safety duties.

Your new entity must be able to do each of these on the day it takes over. If it cannot, the gap lands on your employees first. A late payslip or a missing benefit will damage trust faster than any legal detail.

## Get the entity ready before you announce

Do not tell staff about the transfer until the entity can actually employ them. Check that it is registered with the right authorities, has a payroll process, and has the insurance and registrations an Italian employer needs. Check that you have a labor adviser or payroll provider in place.

Announcing too early creates questions you cannot answer. Staff will fill the silence with worries.

## Review the EOR contract

Your agreement with the EOR sets the terms for ending the service. Look for notice periods, handover duties, fees on exit and any restrictions on moving staff. Talk to the EOR early. A good provider expects this day and will help with a clean handover of records.

Ask for a full export of employee data, leave balances, payroll history and contract documents. You will need them to keep continuity.

## Plan the legal route with an adviser

How the employment moves from one employer to another depends on the facts. Your adviser will tell you which route fits your case and which formal steps and signatures are needed. Make sure the route preserves the employee's service history and does not leave any gap in coverage.

This article does not replace that advice. Use it to prepare the questions you bring to your adviser.

## Communicate in the right order

The order of messages matters.

**Managers first.** Brief them before anyone else. They will get the questions, so they need the answers.

**Then each employee, personally.** Do not rely on a company-wide email alone. A short call or meeting with the direct manager works best. Follow it with a written summary.

**Then the formal documents.** Send the new contract or transfer paperwork with a clear explanation of what changes and what does not.

Keep the message simple. Say why you are doing it, what stays the same, what changes on paper, and who to ask. Offer to answer questions in Italian if that is the employee's first language.

## Questions staff will ask

Prepare clear answers to these:

- Will my salary change?
- Will my benefits change?
- Is my service history recognised?
- Who is my employer from now on?
- Who do I contact for payroll or HR questions?
- Will my holiday balance carry over?
- Do I need to sign anything?

If you do not know an answer, say so and give a date for the reply. Then keep that promise.

## Run the payroll cutover carefully

Payroll is the most visible part of the transfer. Pick a cutover point that matches a pay period boundary. Run a parallel check if you can: compare what the EOR would have paid with what your new process calculates. Fix any differences before the first real payslip.

Tell employees what the first payslip will look like and who issued it. Surprises here cause the most anxiety.

## Keep records clean

Store the handover documents in one place. Keep a record of what was communicated and when. If an employee later asks about their history, you should be able to show it.

## After the move

Check in with each employee a few weeks later. Ask if payroll, benefits and tools work as expected. Fix small problems fast. Thank the EOR for the handover and close the loop on any open items.

A good transfer is quiet. People keep working, get paid correctly, and know who their employer is. That is the goal.

A job ad written for your home market often falls flat in Italy. The words may be right. The signals are not. Italian candidates read ads with a few clear questions in mind: What is the role? What is the contract? What is the pay? Who will I work for?

This guide covers tone, structure and the details you should always include.

## Write in Italian

If the role is based in Italy, publish the ad in Italian. An English-only ad narrows your pool and signals that the job is not really rooted in the country. Candidates may read English well, but they notice when a company has not made the effort.

If the role needs English, say so in the Italian text and state the level you expect. You can add a short English version below it. Keep the Italian as the main text.

Do not machine-translate and post. Have a native speaker read it. Stiff or odd phrasing reads as careless.

## Get the tone right

Italian professional writing leans more formal than many English-speaking markets. Aim for clear and respectful, not stiff.

- Use plain, direct sentences.
- Address the reader in a polite, professional way.
- Avoid slang, jokes and internal jargon.
- Skip hype. Words like "rockstar" or "ninja" put people off.
- Do not promise a "family" culture. Describe the work instead.

Be warm, but be specific. Candidates trust concrete detail more than enthusiasm.

## Use a simple structure

A good ad is easy to scan. Use this order.

1. **Job title.** Use a standard title that people search for. Avoid invented titles. If you use an English title, add the Italian equivalent.
2. **Who you are.** Two or three sentences on the company, what it does and where it operates. Say clearly that you are a foreign company hiring in Italy, and explain how the hire will be employed.
3. **The role.** Describe the main tasks and what success looks like. Keep it to a short list.
4. **Requirements.** Split into must-have and nice-to-have. Long wish lists discourage strong candidates.
5. **What you offer.** Contract type, pay, working model, benefits.
6. **How to apply.** One clear step, with a named contact or a simple form.

Keep the whole ad short enough to read in a couple of minutes.

## Include the must-haves

These are the details Italian candidates look for. If they are missing, many will move on.

**Contract type.** Say whether the role is permanent or fixed-term, and whether it is full-time or part-time. Italian candidates care a great deal about contract stability. Vague wording raises suspicion.

**Pay.** State a salary range. Ads without pay information get less trust and fewer applications. Say whether the figure is gross annual pay. Be consistent with how the market quotes salary.

**Collective agreement.** Italian employment is shaped by national collective agreements. Naming the agreement that applies tells candidates you understand local rules. It also shows what they can expect on leave, notice and working time.

**Employer identity.** Candidates want to know who their legal employer is. If you use an Employer of Record (EOR), say so in plain words. Explain that the EOR is the formal employer in Italy and that day-to-day work is directed by your company. This avoids confusion at the offer stage.

**Work location and model.** State the city or region. Say if the role is on-site, hybrid or remote. If remote, say which areas of Italy are fine.

**Benefits.** List what is real. Training, equipment, flexible hours and health cover all matter. Only list what you will actually provide.

**Language requirements.** Name the languages needed for the job and the level.

## Be fair and inclusive

Write the ad so that it does not exclude anyone without a job-related reason. Do not ask for a photo, age, marital status or family plans. Use neutral wording for the job title and the text. Where the Italian title has gendered forms, show both or use a neutral form.

## Avoid common mistakes

- Posting a translated copy of a US or UK ad without adapting it.
- Hiding pay until the third interview.
- Listing ten requirements when two are essential.
- Using a title that no one in Italy searches for.
- Leaving out the employer's legal identity.
- Asking for a long application form up front.

## Where to post

Post where Italian candidates actually look. Use the major professional networks and the main Italian job boards. Add niche boards for specialist roles. Share the ad with your own network too, since personal referrals carry weight in Italy.

## Reply fast

Speed shows respect. Confirm receipt of each application. Give a clear timeline. Tell unsuccessful candidates. A reputation for good manners spreads quickly in a professional community.

## Final check

Before you publish, ask four questions.

- Could a candidate tell the contract, pay and location in under a minute?
- Is the Italian natural to a native reader?
- Is the employer's legal identity clear?
- Is every claim true?

If the answer to all four is yes, the ad is ready.

Italy's reputation in design and manufacturing is not built in a few big cities. It is built in industrial districts: clusters of small and mid-sized firms, workshops, suppliers and technical schools that sit close together and share a trade.

If you plan to hire in Italy, these districts are where many of your best candidates already work.

## What an industrial district is

A district is a local ecosystem around a product or process. Furniture, fashion, ceramics, packaging machinery, food equipment, eyewear, automotive parts, precision mechanics. Each has its own towns, its own suppliers and its own way of training people.

The key point is density. A designer, a toolmaker, a materials specialist and a production planner may all live within a short drive of each other. They have worked with the same partners for years. Knowledge moves between firms through people, not through manuals.

## Why this matters for hiring

Most foreign companies look for Italian talent in the same few places: Milan, Rome, maybe Turin. That works for sales, finance and software. It works less well for design engineering, product development and production roles.

Those people are often in smaller towns, close to the district where they trained. They know the materials, the machines and the quality standards of their sector at a level that is hard to find elsewhere.

A few examples of what you can find:

- Product designers who have worked directly with factories, so their designs can actually be made.
- Process engineers who understand small-batch and custom production.
- Technicians with hands-on skill in finishing, tooling and assembly.
- Quality and testing specialists trained inside demanding supply chains.
- Export and supplier managers who know how district firms sell abroad.

## What makes these workers different

Two traits stand out.

First, they combine craft and engineering. Many started on the shop floor or in a family business, then moved into technical roles. They think about how a thing is made while they design it.

Second, they are used to working with suppliers as partners. In a district, your supplier may be a neighbour you have known for decades. That habit carries over to international projects. These professionals tend to solve problems by talking to the right person early.

## The practical problem for foreign companies

The talent is real, but reaching it is hard if you have no Italian entity.

The usual path is to open a local company, register with the authorities, set up payroll, learn the national collective agreements and manage social contributions. For a company that only wants to hire a few specialists in a district town, that is a heavy project. It also takes time before the first person can start.

There is a second problem. Candidates in district towns often prefer a stable, local-style contract with clear terms. They want to know who their employer is, how they will be paid and what rules apply. An unclear setup makes good people hesitate.

## How an Employer of Record helps

An Employer of Record (EOR) hires the person on your behalf in Italy. The EOR is the legal employer. You direct the daily work. The EOR handles the contract, payroll, contributions and compliance with Italian rules.

For district hiring, this has clear advantages:

- You can hire a specialist in a small town without opening a company.
- The contract follows the right national agreement for the sector, so the candidate sees a familiar, correct setup.
- Payroll and contributions are handled locally, on time.
- You can start with a small team and grow, or test the market before committing.
- If you need to bring a non-EU specialist to Italy, the EOR can support visas and relocation.

## Where to look first

Start from your product, not from a city. Ask which Italian district is known for that product or process. Then look at the schools, the larger firms and the supplier networks in that area. Experienced people often move between firms, so the pool is wider than the job market suggests.

Talk to candidates about the work itself. District professionals value being shown a real problem and a real product. They respond well to clear technical briefs and to teams that respect craft.

## What to plan for

Expect hiring to be relationship-driven. Referrals matter. Local reputation matters. Be clear about role, reporting line and tools from the first conversation.

Plan for language. Many technical staff work well in English, but day-to-day shop-floor talk is in Italian. Pair your new hire with someone who can bridge both, or give them time to build that link with your team.

And plan the employment setup before you make the offer. A candidate who sees a proper contract, a named employer and a clear start date is far more likely to say yes.

## In short

Italy's design and manufacturing strength lives in its districts. The people there are skilled, practical and well connected to their trade. You do not need a local company to reach them. You need the right employment structure and a clear idea of what you want to build.

Most cost comparisons between an Italian entity and an Employer of Record (EOR) list prices side by side. That misses the real difference. The two options split costs differently. An entity is mostly fixed cost. An EOR is mostly variable cost. Which one is cheaper depends on how many people you hire, and how sure you are about keeping them.

## What an Italian entity costs

An entity has costs that start before anyone is hired. They do not stop if the hire does not work out.

- **Setup.** You need a deed of incorporation, a notary, a registered office, a tax code, and a bank account. Each step takes time from your legal and finance staff.
- **Local administration.** You need an accountant for statutory books and tax filings. You need a payroll provider or an in-house payroll function. You need a labour consultant who knows the national contract that applies to your sector.
- **Governance.** Someone must act as legal representative. Someone must sign filings. Often a local director or a trusted manager has to be found, paid, and supervised.
- **Compliance upkeep.** Annual accounts, tax returns, social security registrations, workplace safety duties, and insurance all recur whether you employ one person or many.
- **Management time.** Your head office spends hours on approvals, signatures, and questions from local advisers. This cost is rarely written down, but it is real.

These are fixed costs. You pay them at the start and keep paying them. The cost per employee is low only when the headcount is large enough to spread them.

## What an EOR costs

With an EOR, the provider is the legal employer in Italy. You direct the daily work. The provider handles contracts, payroll, social security, and local compliance.

The cost structure is different:

- **No setup.** You do not incorporate, open a bank account, or appoint a legal representative.
- **A fee that grows with headcount.** You pay a service fee per employee, on top of the employment cost itself. If you have no employees, you pay nothing.
- **No separate payroll or accounting build.** The provider already has the systems and the advisers.
- **Less management time.** You approve the hire and the pay. The provider handles the rest.

This is a variable cost. It rises as you hire and falls as you reduce. You can start with one person and add more as the market proves itself.

## The employment cost is the same in both cases

One point is often confused. Salary, employer social security contributions, and statutory pay items come from Italian rules. They apply to the employer no matter who that is. An entity does not make them cheaper, and an EOR does not make them higher in themselves.

So the comparison is not about the employment cost. It is about everything around it: the structure you must build and run, against the fee you pay for someone else to run it.

## How to think about the break-even

There is no universal headcount where an entity wins. The answer depends on a few things you can estimate yourself.

1. **Total fixed cost of the entity per year.** Add up the accountant, the payroll function, the legal representative, the registered office, and the management time.
2. **Total EOR fee per year.** Multiply the per-employee fee by the planned headcount.
3. **Certainty of the plan.** If you are testing the market, the fixed cost is a bet. If the project fails, you still carry the entity and the cost of closing it.
4. **Other business in Italy.** If you plan to sell, sign local contracts, or hold assets, you may need an entity anyway. Then the EOR is a bridge, not a replacement.

A small team, a first hire, or an uncertain pilot favours the variable model. A large, stable team with a long-term local presence favours the fixed one.

## Costs people forget

A few items hide in the fixed side:

- **Closing costs.** Winding up an entity takes time and professional fees. An EOR contract ends with notice and a handover.
- **Delay.** Setting up an entity takes time before the first hire can start. A delayed hire is a cost in lost sales or lost delivery.
- **Errors.** A mistake in contract type, payroll, or registration can lead to penalties. An entity carries that risk directly. With an EOR, the provider carries part of it under the service agreement. Check the contract to see exactly which part.

## A practical way to decide

Write two columns. In the first, list every cost that exists even with zero employees. In the second, list every cost that appears only when you hire. For the entity, most items land in the first column. For the EOR, almost all land in the second.

Then ask a simple question. If your Italian plan changes in six months, which column hurts more? If the answer is the first, start with an EOR. You can move to an entity later, once headcount and revenue justify the fixed cost.

If your company runs on a US, UK or Asian calendar, your Italian team will not be off when you expect. Some of their days off will surprise you. Some of your busiest weeks will be quiet in Italy.

This article shows where the calendars differ and how to plan around it.

## Italy does not follow your calendar

Italy has its own set of national public holidays. Many are tied to the Catholic calendar. Others mark civic events, such as Liberation Day and Republic Day. Some will feel familiar if you come from a Western market. Others will not.

A few differences matter for planning:

- **No Thanksgiving.** US teams often assume a shared late-year lull. In Italy, there is no such pause at that point.
- **Easter Monday is a day off.** Many calendars treat Easter as a Friday and Sunday event. Italy also closes on the Monday after.
- **Ferragosto.** This is a mid-summer public holiday. It sits inside the longest quiet period of the Italian year.
- **Saints' days.** Each city also has a local patron saint day. In some cities, offices close or run light on that day.
- **Bridge days.** When a holiday falls near a weekend, many people take the day between as leave. The office is technically open, but half the team is away.

Your global calendar will not show most of this. You need to add it yourself.

## The summer slowdown

The biggest planning risk is not a single public holiday. It is the summer. Many Italian businesses slow down for weeks in the warmest months. Some close completely. Clients and suppliers go quiet too.

If your Italian employee depends on Italian partners, expect delays in that period. Approvals take longer. Replies are slow. Meetings are hard to book.

This is normal. Italian workers are entitled to rest, and many take their leave in a block. Plan for it the way you plan for year-end in the US.

## The year-end period

The winter break is long in Italy. Many people stay off from before Christmas until after Epiphany, which is a public holiday. If you need your Italian team for a year-end close or a January launch, raise it early. Do not assume they will be at their desks.

## How to plan team availability

Do this once a year and keep it simple.

1. **Build a shared calendar.** Add Italian public holidays next to your home-country holidays. Use a single view for the whole company.
2. **Mark the quiet seasons.** Block the summer and year-end periods as low availability for Italy. Treat them as soft limits for deadlines.
3. **Ask for leave plans early.** Ask your Italian staff to share planned leave well ahead. Many will already know when they want to go.
4. **Set cover rules.** Decide who covers support, payroll approvals and customer calls when someone is away. Write it down.
5. **Avoid launches at the edges.** Do not schedule a release, audit or board deliverable right before a long break. Give the team time to finish and hand over.
6. **Respect local days.** If your employee works in a city with a patron saint day, add it to the calendar. Do not ask for work that day.

## Do not ask people to work through holidays

Some managers from other markets treat holidays as flexible. In Italy, that goes badly. Holidays and rest are part of the employment relationship, and staff expect them to be honoured. Asking for work on a public holiday creates friction and can create legal exposure.

If you need coverage, plan it in advance. Agree it with the employee. Make sure it follows the rules that apply to their contract.

## Time zones are the smaller problem

Teams often worry about time zones first. In practice, holidays cause more missed deadlines. A two-hour gap is easy to manage. A week when half the country is away is harder.

Make holiday awareness part of your onboarding. Show new managers the Italian calendar. Explain why summer and year-end are slow. Teams that know this in advance plan better and push less.

## What an Employer of Record can do

An Employer of Record (EOR) in Italy handles the employment side for you. That includes keeping the payroll calendar in line with local holidays and leave. Your team lead still decides who covers what, but the local rules are handled for you. You do not need to track each regional day by hand.

The result is a team that works in sync with the rest of your company, with fewer surprises.

If you already employ people in Germany, France or Spain, Italy will feel familiar in many ways. The basic model is the same. Employment is regulated, written terms matter, and employees have strong protections. But some details differ, and those details cause most of the surprises for foreign companies.

This article gives a practical comparison. It does not replace advice on a specific hire.

## Where Italy is similar to its EU peers

**Employment is a regulated relationship.** As in most EU countries, you cannot simply agree anything you like. There are legal minimums on pay, working time, rest and leave. Contracts must respect them.

**Written terms are expected.** Employees must be told the key conditions of their job. This covers role, pay, working hours, place of work and the applicable rules. This follows common EU standards, so a company used to Western Europe will not find the idea new.

**Social contributions are shared.** Employer and employee both pay into the social security system. The employer withholds the employee share and pays it over with its own. This is the same logic as in France, Germany, Spain and the Netherlands.

**Termination needs a reason.** In most EU countries, an employer cannot dismiss someone without a justified ground. Italy is in the same group. If you come from an at-will system, this is the biggest shift, and it applies across the whole region.

**Employees have a voice.** Worker representation and union presence exist in Italy as they do elsewhere in Europe. You may never meet them in a small team. In a larger one, you should expect them.

## Where Italy is different

**Collective agreements carry a lot of weight.** In Italy, sector-level collective agreements shape many terms. They affect pay levels, job grades, working hours, extra payments, leave and notice. The agreement for your sector is often more important than the individual contract. Other countries also use collective agreements, but the Italian system is something you must pick correctly from the start. Choosing the wrong one, or ignoring it, creates risk.

**Pay is often more than the base salary.** Many Italian employees receive extra payments on top of the monthly figure. Some are set by the collective agreement. Some build up over time and are paid on exit. A foreign company that budgets only for base pay will underestimate the real cost. Check the full package before you make an offer.

**The cost of employment is high relative to take-home pay.** Employer contributions add a meaningful layer on top of gross salary. This is true in several EU countries, but you should model it for Italy specifically and not copy a figure from another market.

**Payroll and reporting are detailed.** Italian payroll involves several institutions, with their own filings and deadlines. Teams used to a single payroll portal may be surprised by how many parties are involved.

**Process matters as much as substance.** In Italy, a correct outcome reached by the wrong procedure can still be a problem. This is especially true for dismissals and disciplinary steps. Notice, form and timing need care.

**Language and documents.** Many documents, forms and communications with authorities are in Italian. Contracts for local employees are normally in Italian too. Plan for translation and for someone who can read the originals.

## What this means for a foreign company

The common EU pattern helps you. If you have hired in another member state, your instincts about written terms, protected employees and shared contributions will carry over.

What will not carry over is the detail. Three areas need local input before you hire:

- **The right collective agreement** for the role and sector.
- **The full cost** of the package, including extras and exit-related amounts.
- **The correct process** for onboarding, changes to terms and, if needed, ending the relationship.

Getting these right at the start is far cheaper than fixing them later.

## Hiring without a local entity

Setting up a company in Italy takes time and ongoing admin. If you want to hire one person or a small team, an Employer of Record (EOR) is a common route. The EOR is the legal employer in Italy. It runs payroll, applies the right collective agreement, handles contributions and keeps the paperwork in order. You direct the daily work. The EOR carries the local compliance.

This suits companies that want to test the market, hire quickly or avoid building a local back office. It also helps when the person you want needs support with a visa or relocation.

## A short checklist

- Define the role and sector first. The collective agreement follows from that.
- Ask for the total employment cost, not just gross salary.
- Do not assume your home-country contract template will work.
- Plan for Italian-language documents.
- Treat termination as a process with steps, not a single decision.

Italy is not an outlier in Europe. It follows the same principles as its peers. It simply asks for more attention to local detail.

You have decided to build an engineering hub in Europe. The shortlist is Berlin, Paris and Italy. Most founders pick the first two by habit. Italy deserves a real look.

This is not a ranking. It is a way to think about the choice as the person who has to live with it.

## Start with what the hub is for

Before comparing cities, answer one question. What will this team do in the first year?

If you need a large group of senior engineers fast, you are buying access to a deep, competitive market. If you need a small, stable core that stays for years, you are buying retention and fit. These are different problems. They point to different places.

## Berlin: the crowded market

Berlin is where many international founders go first. English works at the office. Engineers expect to work for foreign companies. The startup scene is mature.

That is also the downside. Every well-funded company in Europe recruits there. Strong candidates have options and know it. Offers move quickly. Counter-offers are common. Turnover can hurt a young hub.

Berlin suits you if you need brand visibility, want to hire many people, and can pay to compete. It is harder if you are a small foreign company nobody has heard of.

## Paris: strong talent, strong structure

Paris has deep engineering talent, especially in mathematics, machine learning and hardware-adjacent fields. Large tech employers and a well-funded ecosystem sit there. Engineers are well trained and ambitious.

France is also known for a heavily structured employment framework. Contracts, notice rules and employee protections are detailed. For a founder, this means you need local knowledge before the first hire, not after. A mistake in the first contract is expensive to fix.

Paris suits you if you want top-tier technical depth and are ready to respect a rigid system.

## Italy: the less contested option

Italy is the market founders overlook. That is the opportunity.

The country has a large pool of trained engineers. Many of them work in cities where few international companies hire directly. Engineers there often get fewer offers from foreign firms. A serious offer from a real product company stands out. People tend to stay when the work is good and the team is solid.

The trade-offs are real. Fewer candidates know English-first startups. Local employment rules, collective agreements and social contributions are specific. Hiring needs patience at the start, and you cannot copy a Berlin playbook.

Italy suits you if you want a stable team, lower competition for each role, and a place where your company can be a top employer from day one.

## The real founder question: who is the employer?

Talent is only half the decision. The other half is how you employ people.

To hire in any of these countries, you normally need a local entity. That means incorporation, payroll, tax registration, accounting and a legal representative. It takes time. It adds fixed cost before you know if the hub will work.

An Employer of Record (EOR) removes that step. The EOR becomes the legal employer. You manage the work. They handle contracts, payroll, social contributions and compliance. You can start hiring in weeks and decide on your own entity later, once the team is proven.

For a founder testing a market, this matters more than the city. It lets you run a real pilot instead of a bet.

## How to decide

Use this short test.

- **You need volume and speed, and have budget:** Berlin.
- **You need deep technical specialists and accept structure:** Paris.
- **You want a stable core team and less bidding pressure:** Italy.

Then add a second filter. Where do your first hires already live? Where does your head of engineering want to build? A hub led by someone who believes in the location will outperform a hub chosen on a spreadsheet.

Also consider a staged plan. Start with a small team in one country through an EOR. Learn how hiring, payroll and management feel. Add a second location only when the first works. Many hubs fail because the founder opened too many fronts at once.

## What to check before you commit

- Which collective agreement applies to your engineers, and what does it require?
- What are the total employment costs beyond salary?
- How long does a normal notice period last, and who bears it?
- Can you sponsor a visa if your best candidate lives outside the EU?
- Who handles relocation if you want to bring in talent?

Ask these before you write a single offer. The answers differ by country, and they change your real cost and risk.

## Bottom line

Berlin is the obvious choice and the most contested. Paris offers depth and rigidity. Italy offers quieter competition and loyal teams, if you accept a learning curve on local rules.

A founder does not need the perfect city. You need a place where you can hire well, keep people, and move without building a legal structure first.

If you plan a hub in Southern Europe, Italy, Spain and Portugal are the obvious candidates. They share a Mediterranean business culture and good access to European markets. They differ in talent pools, cost profile and working hours. This article compares them on those points so you can match the country to the role.

No single country wins on every measure. The right answer depends on what you hire for, where your customers are and how fast you need to start.

## Talent

**Italy** has a deep and varied labour market. It is strong in engineering, manufacturing, design, fashion, food, automotive, industrial automation and life sciences. Many Italian professionals have specialist skills built inside long-standing industrial companies. If your product touches hardware, machinery, pharma or luxury goods, Italy gives you a pool that is hard to match in the region. Finance, legal and technical sales talent is also available in the large cities, especially in the north.

Italy is less uniform than the other two. Talent clusters around Milan, Turin, Bologna, Rome and a few other centres. Outside these, the pool for niche roles can be thin. Remote hiring helps, but you should plan your location around the roles.

**Spain** offers a large and young workforce with a strong base in sales, customer support, marketing and software. Madrid and Barcelona are established tech and startup hubs. Spanish is also a major global language, which makes Spain a natural base for Latin American coverage. If you need multilingual support or a commercial team that sells into Spanish-speaking markets, Spain is often the easiest choice.

**Portugal** has a smaller population and therefore a smaller pool, but it has built a reputation for software, shared services and customer operations. English levels are generally high, and Lisbon and Porto attract many international teams. The trade-off is competition. Many foreign companies already hire there, so strong candidates have options, and the market can feel crowded for popular profiles.

## Cost

Cost is more than salary. Employer contributions, mandatory benefits, notice rules and local collective agreements all shape what a hire really costs.

Portugal has traditionally been seen as the lower-cost option for salaries, though that gap has narrowed in the big cities where international demand has pushed pay up. Spain sits in a similar middle range for many roles. Italy often shows a higher overall cost of employment for the employer because of contribution levels and the weight of collective agreements, but pay for specialist and industrial roles reflects the skills involved.

Do not compare headline salaries alone. In Italy, the national collective agreement for your sector sets minimum pay, extra monthly payments, leave and notice terms. These rules apply to your hire whether you plan for them or not. The same logic holds in Spain and Portugal, where sector agreements and statutory benefits add to the base pay. The useful number is the total annual cost per employee, built from verified rates for your sector and role.

For a small team in a first market entry, the cost difference between the three is often smaller than the cost of hiring the wrong profile or waiting months to start. Speed and fit usually matter more than a small saving on salary.

## Time zone

Italy and Spain run on central European time. Their working days line up closely with Germany, France, Switzerland and the rest of continental Europe. Meetings with headquarters in those countries need no special planning.

Portugal keeps the same clock as the United Kingdom and Ireland. That puts it slightly behind Italy and Spain. For a UK-facing team, this is a real advantage. For a team that must overlap with the rest of continental Europe, the gap is small but visible, especially at the end of the day.

For North America, all three countries are on the earlier side of the transatlantic window, and Portugal gives a slightly better overlap with the American morning. For Asia and the Middle East, the later end of the European day is what you can share, and Italy and Spain are marginally better placed.

Spain has one more habit worth noting. Lunch and the working day often run later than in Italy or Portugal. If your customers expect early calls, check this against your sales rhythm.

## How to choose

Use a simple rule of thumb.

- Choose **Italy** when you need industrial, engineering, design or specialist technical skills, or when the Italian market is itself your target.
- Choose **Spain** when you need scale in sales, support or marketing, or when you want a base for Spanish-speaking markets.
- Choose **Portugal** when you build a software or operations team that works closely with the UK, and you accept a smaller pool and stronger competition for candidates.

Many companies end up with more than one country over time. A common path is to start where the first critical hire lives, then add a second location when the team grows.

## Starting without a local entity

Whatever you choose, setting up a legal entity takes time and ongoing admin. An Employer of Record (EOR) lets you hire locally under local law without that setup. The EOR is the legal employer, handles payroll, contributions and contracts, and you direct the daily work. This is useful when you want to test a market, hire a single key person or move fast. In Italy, an EOR can also support visas, relocation and social security representation for foreign staff.

The practical step is to define the roles first, then compare the total employment cost and the time to start in each country for those roles.

Italy has a deep engineering talent pool. It is spread across the country, not concentrated in one city. For a foreign company, this matters. The right hire may live in Turin, Bologna or Naples, and the right city depends on your sector.

This guide covers where Italian engineers train, what they specialise in, and where the main hubs are.

## How engineers are trained

Engineering education in Italy is mostly public and technical. Students pick a discipline early and stay in it. A bachelor's degree is followed by a master's degree. Many graduates continue to a doctorate, often with industry partners.

The result is strong theoretical grounding. Italian engineers tend to be good at mathematics, physics and first-principles problem solving. Many also have hands-on experience from thesis projects run inside local companies.

Language is usually not a barrier. Many engineers work in English every day, especially in multinational teams and research groups. Master's programmes taught in English are common at the larger technical universities.

## The main universities

A few institutions are known well beyond Italy.

- **Politecnico di Milano** is the largest technical university in the country. It is strong in mechanical, electronic, telecommunications, computer and civil engineering, as well as design and architecture.
- **Politecnico di Torino** has deep ties to the automotive and aerospace sectors. It is a natural source of mechanical, aerospace, electrical and software engineers.
- **University of Bologna** covers a broad range of engineering fields. It feeds the machinery, automation and motor industries of its region.
- **University of Padua** supplies industrial, information and bioengineering talent to the north-east.
- **Sapienza University of Rome** is among the largest universities in Europe. It produces engineers in aerospace, electronics, energy and computing.
- **University of Naples Federico II** is the main engineering school of the south. It is known for mechanical, aerospace, electronic and computer engineering.
- **University of Pisa and Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna** are strong in computer science, robotics and biomedical engineering.
- **University of Genoa** is linked to shipbuilding, ports, robotics and maritime technology.

There are many other solid universities. Smaller regional engineering faculties often feed local industry very well.

## Specialisations where Italy is strong

**Mechanical and industrial engineering.** Italy is a major manufacturing country. Engineers here know machinery, tooling, precision production and process design. This is the deepest pool.

**Automotive and motorsport.** Italian engineers work on high-performance vehicles, powertrains, chassis and, increasingly, electrification. Turin and Emilia are the centres.

**Aerospace and defence.** Engineers in Piedmont, Lombardy, Lazio, Campania and Puglia work on aircraft, helicopters, space systems and propulsion.

**Automation and robotics.** Packaging, food machinery and factory automation are strong niches. Many companies need controls and mechatronics engineers. Italy has them.

**Electronics, telecoms and embedded systems.** Semiconductor design, power electronics and communications engineering have solid academic roots and a growing industrial base.

**Software and data.** Italy has capable software engineers, data scientists and AI researchers. Milan is the main market. Rome, Turin, Pisa and Naples also have active communities.

**Energy and civil engineering.** Renewable energy, grids, infrastructure and building engineering are all well supported by the university system.

**Biomedical engineering.** Medical devices are a real strength, especially in Emilia-Romagna, Lombardy and Tuscany.

## Regional hubs

**Milan and Lombardy.** The business capital. Best for software, data, telecoms, industrial design and corporate engineering roles. Competition for talent is highest here, and so is the number of international employers.

**Turin and Piedmont.** Automotive, aerospace and advanced manufacturing. Good for mechanical, electrical and embedded engineers.

**Bologna and Emilia-Romagna.** Often called the Motor Valley. It also leads in packaging machinery, automation and biomedical devices.

**Veneto and the north-east.** Manufacturing clusters with strong mechanical, electrical and industrial engineers. Padua is the academic anchor.

**Genoa and Liguria.** Maritime engineering, robotics and port technology.

**Tuscany.** Pisa and Florence offer robotics, photonics, electronics and software talent.

**Rome and Lazio.** Aerospace, space, defence, telecoms and public-sector technology.

**Naples, Campania and the south.** A large university output and lower competition for engineers. Aerospace and software are growing. Remote and hybrid roles work well here.

## What this means for your hiring plan

Match the city to the skill, not the other way round. If you need automotive engineers, look at Turin and Emilia. If you need software developers, start in Milan but also look at Naples, Pisa and Rome, where you face less competition.

Remote work widens the pool. Many Italian engineers will work from their home city for a foreign employer. You do not need an office in Italy to hire them. You do need to employ them correctly under Italian rules, with the right contract, payroll and social security setup.

That is where an Employer of Record helps. It becomes the legal employer in Italy. You direct the daily work. The EOR handles contracts, payroll, contributions and compliance. You can hire an engineer in Turin or Naples without setting up a local company first.

Italy is not Silicon Valley. It does not try to be. But it has a startup scene that is real, spread across several cities, and open to founders from abroad. If you plan to build a team in Italy, it helps to know where the activity is and who funds it.

This guide covers the main hubs, the types of accelerators, and the investor landscape. It also explains how to hire people there before you set up a company.

## Hubs

Italian startup activity is spread out. There is no single center. Each city has its own strengths.

Milan is the business and finance capital. Many venture funds, corporate innovation teams and professional services firms are based there. Founders who want investor access often start in Milan.

Turin has an industrial past and a strong engineering base. Its technical universities feed talent into software, mobility and manufacturing technology.

Rome has a large public sector and a growing technology community. It suits founders who sell to government bodies or large institutions.

Bologna combines strong universities with a dense network of manufacturers. It works well for deep tech, robotics and industrial software.

Naples, Padua, Trento and other cities also host university spin-offs and research groups. Smaller hubs can offer lower costs and less competition for talent.

The practical point is simple. Pick the city that matches your sector and your hires, not the one with the biggest name.

## Accelerators and incubators

Italy has several kinds of programs for early-stage companies.

- **University incubators.** Many technical universities run programs for spin-offs and student teams. They offer space, mentors and access to research labs.
- **Corporate accelerators.** Large Italian companies in energy, banking, fashion, food and manufacturing run programs that pair startups with business units. The upside is a pilot customer. The downside is a slow decision process.
- **Independent accelerators.** Private programs offer small investments in exchange for equity, plus mentoring and demo days.
- **Public and regional programs.** National and regional bodies support innovative companies with services, grants and incentives. Terms change often, so check current calls before you plan around them.

For an international founder, the most useful programs are those that accept teams from outside Italy and run in English. Ask each program about language, residency requirements and equity terms before you apply.

## Investors

The Italian investor base includes angel networks, early-stage venture funds, corporate venture arms and public-backed investment vehicles. Foreign funds also invest in Italian companies, often alongside local partners.

A few observations help set expectations.

- Early-stage rounds are common. Later-stage capital is thinner, so many companies look abroad for larger rounds.
- Angel groups matter. They often lead first rounds and open doors to funds.
- Corporate investors bring customers as well as capital. That can be worth more than the cheque.
- Public-backed funds can co-invest with private partners and add credibility.

If you already have investors abroad, an Italian co-investor can help with local introductions and trust. If you are raising locally, expect investors to ask about your plan for hiring and your plan for retaining talent.

## Talent

Italy produces strong engineers, designers and scientists. Many are open to working for foreign companies, especially remotely or in hybrid roles. Competition for senior people exists, but it is lower than in the largest tech markets.

Salaries, notice periods and employment terms follow Italian rules and national collective agreements. These are different from what many foreign founders expect. Getting them wrong early creates cost and risk later.

## Hiring before you have a company

Many international founders want to test the market first. They want to hire a few people in Italy without registering a local subsidiary.

An Employer of Record (EOR) handles this. The EOR becomes the legal employer in Italy. It runs payroll, social contributions and compliance. You manage the daily work. Your team gets a compliant Italian contract and you avoid the setup time of a new entity.

This fits startups well. You can start with one hire, add more as you grow, and convert to your own entity when the numbers justify it. An EOR can also support visas and relocation for people who move to Italy from abroad.

## How to start

1. Choose the hub that matches your sector and the talent you need.
2. Shortlist programs and investors that work in English and accept foreign teams.
3. Confirm current incentives and rules directly with the program or authority.
4. Hire your first people through an EOR while you validate the market.

Italy rewards founders who arrive with a clear plan and local help.

Many foreign employers build an Italian offer the same way they build one at home. They take a gross salary, apply a rough tax rate, and guess the net. Then the candidate's own calculation comes out higher. The gap is usually the tax wedge relief.

This article explains what the relief does and how it changes the way you should make offers.

## What the tax wedge relief is

The tax wedge is the difference between what an employer pays and what an employee takes home. Italy has added several measures that cut the wedge for employees on lower and middle incomes. They work on the employee's side of the payslip. They reduce income tax, so net pay rises without a change in the gross figure.

There are three parts to know.

### 1. A share of employment income is not taxed

For lower incomes, a fixed share of employment income is simply excluded from tax. The share depends on the income band:

- Up to 8,500 EUR: 7.1% of employment income.
- From 8,500 to 15,000 EUR: 5.3%.
- From 15,000 to 20,000 EUR: 4.8%.

The share falls as income rises. The relief is largest, in relative terms, for the lowest paid roles.

### 2. An extra tax deduction in the middle range

For incomes between 20,000 and 32,000 EUR, there is an additional deduction of 1,000 EUR per year. Above 32,000 EUR it shrinks. It reaches zero at 40,000 EUR.

This matters because many first hires for a foreign company sit in this range. Junior and mid-level staff, support roles, and sales or operations people often fall here.

### 3. A supplementary payment for the lowest incomes

There is also an integrative treatment of up to 1,200 EUR per year. It applies to incomes up to 15,000 EUR and only under certain conditions. It is less likely to affect a typical offer, but it shows the direction of the system.

## Why net pay looks higher than expected

Most online salary tools and old rules of thumb do not model these measures well. A candidate who runs a current payroll calculation sees a net figure that is higher than the one your estimate gave.

This helps you in two ways.

First, you may not need to raise the gross salary to hit a net target. If a candidate says they need a certain take-home amount, check it against a current calculation before you add to the gross.

Second, your offer may look more attractive than you expected. A gross figure that looks modest on paper can produce a competitive net figure.

## What this means for how you build an offer

**Start from the net the candidate cares about.** Italian candidates often think in monthly net pay. Work out the gross that gives that net, using the current rules. Do not copy a gross from another country.

**Check where the salary sits relative to the bands.** The relief changes shape as income rises. A small raise in gross can move a candidate out of a band where a larger share of income is untaxed. The net gain from the raise can be smaller than it looks. Look at the net result of each option before you decide.

**Be careful near the upper edge of the range.** The 1,000 EUR deduction phases out between 32,000 and 40,000 EUR. In that stretch, each extra euro of gross brings less extra net than it does elsewhere. If you are choosing between two salary levels in that zone, compare them on net.

**Do not promise a net figure from a rough estimate.** The rules depend on the income band and on personal conditions. A calculation based on the actual contract and the employee's situation is the only reliable base.

**Keep the employer cost separate.** The relief changes the employee's tax. It does not change what you pay in employer contributions. So a better net for the employee does not mean a lower cost for you. Budget the full employer cost on its own line.

## A note on the figures

The figures above come from secondary sources and describe how the measures work. Rules and thresholds can change, and the final result depends on the individual's situation. Always confirm with a payroll calculation on the actual contract before you send an offer.

## The practical takeaway

Italian net pay is often higher than foreign employers expect. That is a result of deliberate tax relief for employees, not an error in your numbers. Use it. Build offers from the net backwards, test each salary level against the bands, and avoid raising gross pay when the net is already competitive.

A clear and accurate net figure also builds trust early. Candidates see that you understand local pay, and that helps you close the hire.

If you hire in Italy, you will meet the word *inquadramento*. It means the level an employee is placed in under the national collective agreement (CCNL) that applies to your sector. This level matters more than most foreign employers expect.

## What a level is

Each CCNL contains a classification system. It groups jobs into broad categories, such as blue-collar workers, white-collar employees, middle managers and executives. Inside the categories, the agreement lists levels. Each level has a written description of the tasks, the autonomy and the skills it covers.

The agreement also lists example roles for each level. These examples are a guide. They are not a closed list.

## Levels set the salary floor

Every level in the CCNL has a minimum monthly pay. Italians call it the *minimo tabellare*. You cannot pay below it. The minimum rises as the level rises.

The agreement may add other fixed items on top of the base pay. These can include seniority steps, allowances and extra monthly payments. The mix differs between sectors. So the same job can have a different cost floor in retail, in metalworking and in IT services.

You can pay above the floor. Many employers do, especially for scarce skills. The floor is a legal minimum. It is not a market rate.

## Duties decide the level, not the title

This is the point that surprises most international teams. In Italy, the level follows the work the person actually does. It does not follow the title on the contract.

A company may call someone "Head of Growth" or "Senior Associate". Italian law and the CCNL look at the real tasks. If the person does work that fits a higher level, they can claim that level. They can also claim the pay difference for the period they worked at that higher level. Courts have ruled on this many times.

The reverse also holds. A grand title does not force you to pay a higher level if the duties do not match.

## How titles and levels fit together

You can use any job title you like. A title is a label for your org chart, your clients and LinkedIn. The level is a legal and payroll fact.

A clean approach is to keep both in the contract. The title says what the role is called. The level says how it is classified under the CCNL. Payroll, social contributions and some rights follow the level.

Keep your global grading system if you have one. Just map each of your grades to a CCNL level before you make an offer. Do this per role, not per country.

## How to choose the right level

Start from the job, not from the salary you want to offer.

1. Choose the correct CCNL for the sector and the activity of the employer.
2. Write a short list of the real daily tasks.
3. Compare those tasks with the level descriptions in the agreement.
4. Check the example roles for the closest match.
5. Set the pay at or above the minimum for that level.

If a role sits between two levels, look at autonomy and responsibility. Does the person decide alone, or do they follow set procedures? Do they manage others? Do they sign off on budgets? These factors often tip the choice.

## Common mistakes

- **Using the wrong CCNL.** The level table and the pay floors change with the agreement. A wrong choice breaks everything that follows.
- **Copying a foreign grade.** A "Senior" in your home country may not match a senior level in Italy.
- **Setting the title first.** A title promised in a job offer can create expectations about level and pay.
- **Ignoring role growth.** People take on more tasks over time. If the real work moves up, the level should follow.
- **Fixing the level only once.** Review it when duties change. Do it before a dispute starts.

## Why it matters for budgeting

The level drives your base cost. It also affects notice periods, sick pay rules and other terms that the CCNL links to classification. A one-level error on a team of several people adds up fast.

For a company planning its first Italian hire, a level check should come before the offer letter. It is cheap to do. It is expensive to correct later.

## What an Employer of Record does here

An Employer of Record (EOR) becomes the legal employer in Italy. As part of that, it picks the CCNL, maps the role to a level and checks that the pay meets the floor. It keeps the classification in the contract and in payroll. You keep day-to-day control of the work.

This removes a common risk for foreign companies. You get a classification that matches the duties, and a title you can still use freely.
