Your first employee in Italy sets the tone for everything that follows. They become your local face, your source of market knowledge and your test of how well your company works across borders. The choice between a junior and a senior hire is not about talent. It is about what your company can support from abroad.

This article compares the two options on three points: risk, autonomy and cost.

## Risk

A first hire carries risk on both sides. You are new to Italian employment practice. The employee is joining a company with no local track record.

**A senior hire** usually has a clear record. You can check references, past results and how they handled similar roles. They also know what a credible offer looks like in Italy, so they will notice if your contract or onboarding is weak. That can feel uncomfortable, but it protects you from mistakes.

The risk with a senior hire is a wrong fit at a high level. If you hire someone with a strong network but weak execution, you may lose time before you see it. Senior people can also arrive with fixed habits. They may resist your reporting style or your tools.

**A junior hire** carries a different risk. You do not know yet how they will perform. Their record is short. If they struggle, there is nobody local to notice early or to help them.

A junior hire also depends more on your management. If your team is remote and busy, a junior person may drift. The damage is often quiet. Tasks get done slowly and you do not know why.

In short, a senior hire risks a costly mismatch. A junior hire risks slow failure without support.

## Autonomy

This is the main reason companies choose senior for a first hire.

A senior employee can work with little direction. They can open conversations with customers, partners or authorities without waiting for instructions. They can tell you what is realistic in the Italian market and what is not. For a company with no local presence, this is very valuable.

A junior employee needs a clear plan. They need a manager who is available, a defined set of tasks and regular feedback. If your headquarters is in a distant time zone, this is hard. A junior person alone in a new market has no peers to learn from.

Ask yourself one question. Who will teach this person? If the answer is nobody on your side and nobody in Italy, a senior hire is the safer route.

There is a case for junior hires too. If you already have a manager who can guide, or if the role is narrow and well defined, a junior person can grow into it. They often adopt your methods faster because they have no old habits to unlearn. Some companies hire a junior as a second step, after a senior has set up the basics.

## Cost

Senior salaries are higher. That is simple and expected. But salary is not the whole picture.

The total cost of an employee in Italy includes employer contributions and other mandatory items on top of salary. These scale with pay. A senior hire therefore costs more across the board, not only in the gross figure.

Still, cost per person is not the same as cost per result. A junior hire who needs heavy management consumes your own time and your managers' time. That time has a price, even if it never appears on an invoice. A senior hire who works alone may be cheaper in practice if they deliver faster.

The opposite can also be true. A senior hire in a role that does not need seniority is money wasted. If the work is mostly administrative or follows a clear process, a junior person may do it well at a lower cost.

Match the level to the work. Do not buy experience you will not use.

## A simple way to decide

Choose **senior** if:

- you have no one in Italy and no one who knows the market
- the role involves sales, partnerships or dealing with local institutions
- you need someone to shape the plan, not just follow it

Choose **junior** if:

- you have a manager ready to guide them
- the tasks are clear and repeatable
- you want to build a team over time and can wait for results

If you are unsure, lean senior for the first hire. A first employee who can stand alone gives you room to learn the market while you build your Italian operation.

## Do not forget the employment setup

Whoever you choose, the contract, payroll and compliance must be correct from the first day. Mistakes here create problems for the company and for the employee. This matters more with a first hire, because you have no internal Italian process to catch errors.

An Employer of Record (EOR) can employ the person in Italy on your behalf while you direct their daily work. It lets you test the market without setting up a local entity first. It also means the hire is handled correctly from the start, whether the person is junior or senior.

You hired your first people in Italy through an Employer of Record (EOR). The team grew. Now you are thinking about your own Italian entity. That is a sound step. It does not mean you should drop the EOR.

Many companies end up with a hybrid model. They run their own entity where they have scale. They keep an EOR where they do not. This article explains how that works and when it makes sense.

## Why companies set up their own entity

An entity gives you direct control. You hold the employment contracts. You run payroll or choose your own provider. You build a local brand as an employer. For a stable team with a clear future in Italy, this is often the right call.

It also brings fixed work. You need local accounting, payroll, tax filings, a registered address and someone who is accountable for compliance. That work has a cost whether you hire one person or many.

That is why the decision depends on volume and certainty. Where you have both, an entity pays off. Where you have neither, it does not.

## Why the EOR still matters

Your Italian entity solves Italy. It does not solve the next country.

When you test a new market, you usually do not know how it will go. You may hire one person to open sales. You may need a small engineering group for a short project. You may not yet know if the market will stay. Setting up a company in every country for that kind of uncertainty is slow and heavy.

An EOR lets you hire in that market right away. The EOR is the legal employer. You direct the daily work. You skip the entity setup, and you can scale up, scale down or move on without closing a company.

## How the hybrid model works

The idea is simple. Match the structure to the maturity of each market.

- **Mature market:** your own entity. Italy fits here once the team is stable.
- **New market:** an EOR. You hire fast and learn before you commit.
- **Growing market:** start on an EOR. When the team and revenue justify it, move to an entity.

Each country is judged on its own. You do not need one rule for the whole company.

## What this gives you

**Speed.** A new hire in a new country can start without waiting for incorporation, bank accounts and registrations.

**Lower risk.** If a market does not work out, you end the arrangement. You are not left with a dormant company to wind down.

**Focus.** Your internal team spends its time on the markets where it has depth. It does not need to learn employment rules in every country at once.

**A clear path.** You can move from EOR to entity later. Plan for it from the start so the switch is orderly.

## Where the model needs care

A hybrid setup is not automatic. A few points need attention.

**Keep one view of your people.** With some staff on your entity and some on EOR providers, data can scatter. Decide early where headcount, cost and contract records live. A simple shared sheet is better than none.

**Be consistent on terms.** Employees in different countries will compare notes. You do not need identical packages. You do need a logic you can explain.

**Watch for permanent establishment questions.** If staff in a country start acting like a local branch of your company, tax authorities may take notice. This is a real topic for team size and role type. Take local advice before a team grows beyond a pilot.

**Plan the transfer.** When you move a market from EOR to entity, employees change employer. This needs clear communication, correct paperwork and respect for the rights each person has built up. Start early and tell people why.

## Choosing your provider

If you use an EOR in several countries, you have two broad options. One is a single global provider. The other is a local specialist in each market. A single provider gives you one contract and one invoice. A local specialist usually knows the national rules, collective agreements and practice in more depth.

For Italy, depth matters. Collective agreements, contribution rules and visa steps vary by sector and by role. A provider who works in Italy every day will see problems before they reach you. The same logic applies in other countries.

## A practical way to decide

For each market, ask these questions:

- Do we know the team will be there for the long term?
- Is the headcount large enough to carry the fixed cost of an entity?
- Do we need to hold the employer relationship ourselves?
- Can we support local compliance in house or through advisers?

If most answers are yes, plan the entity. If most are no or not yet, stay on an EOR and review later.

## The short version

Setting up in Italy is a milestone, not a finish line. Keep your own entity where you are settled. Keep an EOR where you are still learning. Review each market as it grows.

Foreign companies hiring in Italy often ask the same language questions. Do we need an Italian contract? Can the team work in English? Who handles the paperwork? This FAQ gives direct answers.

## Does the employment contract have to be in Italian?

In practice, yes. Italian employment relationships sit inside an Italian legal framework. The contract, the hiring notices and the payroll records are normally prepared in Italian.

Many employers also give the employee an English version. This is common and helpful. The employee understands what they sign, and your headquarters can read it too.

The key point is which version prevails if the two differ. Decide this in advance. The usual choice is that the Italian text controls and the English text is a courtesy translation. Ask your Employer of Record (EOR) to confirm how they handle this before the offer goes out.

## Can we hire someone who does not speak Italian?

Yes. Many international companies hire English-speaking staff in Italy, especially in technology, sales and management roles. The employee does not need to speak Italian to be employed.

The employee will still receive some documents in Italian. Examples are payslips, tax and social security forms and official letters. Your EOR can explain these in English. Make sure this is part of the service before you sign.

## Can the team work in English day to day?

Yes. You choose the working language of your team. Meetings, tools, code, reports and internal chat can all be in English. Italian law does not force a company to run its daily work in Italian.

Some areas are different:

- Written policies that the employee must understand and follow should be provided in a language they can actually read.
- Safety instructions and training must be clear to the worker. If someone does not read Italian well, give them materials they can understand.
- Formal notices about the employment relationship, such as disciplinary matters, should go through your EOR and follow Italian form.

A simple rule works well. Daily work can be in English. Anything with legal weight should be in Italian, with an English copy for the employee.

## Which collective agreement language applies?

Most Italian employment is shaped by a national collective agreement for the sector. These agreements are published in Italian. They set rules on pay levels, working hours, leave and notice.

You do not need to read them in full. Your EOR should tell you which agreement applies and what it means for your role in plain English. Ask for a short summary, not just the document.

## What about payslips and payroll documents?

Payslips are issued in Italian. Employees who do not read Italian often ask for help the first time they see one. A good EOR provides a short guide that explains each line in English. Ask for it at onboarding.

## Do foreign documents need translation?

Often they do. If a new hire brings diplomas, certificates or records from another country, Italian authorities may ask for an Italian translation. In some cases the translation must be certified.

This matters most for work visas and residence procedures. The authorities work in Italian. Application forms, supporting papers and appointments are handled in Italian. Your EOR or relocation partner should prepare and check these documents so the candidate does not face the process alone.

If you are bringing talent from abroad, ask early which papers need translation. It is better to find out before the start date than after.

## Who talks to the Italian authorities for us?

Your EOR does. They register the employment, run payroll and deal with social security bodies in Italian. You get updates in English. This is one of the main reasons companies use an EOR instead of opening a local entity.

## Can we send our own templates and policies?

Yes, as inputs. Share your code of conduct, IT policy or handbook in English. Your EOR can tell you what can be used as is and what needs to be adapted or translated. Do not assume a global template will fit Italy without a check.

## Quick checklist before you hire

- Agree which contract version prevails.
- Ask for an English copy of the contract.
- Ask for an English guide to payslips.
- Confirm that safety and policy materials are understandable to the employee.
- Find out which foreign documents need translation.
- Confirm that all contact with Italian authorities goes through your EOR.

Language is rarely a blocker. With the right setup, your team works in English and the Italian paperwork stays out of sight.

Italy has a deep life sciences base. It has large manufacturing sites, contract manufacturers, research hospitals and universities with strong science faculties. For a foreign company, the question is not whether the talent exists. The question is where it is, which roles are tight, and how to hire quickly.

This article covers the main clusters and the roles that are hardest to fill.

## Where the talent is

### Lombardy

Milan and the surrounding area form the largest hub. Many multinational pharma subsidiaries have their Italian offices here. So do biotech start-ups, CROs and medical device firms. Several research hospitals and universities feed the pool.

This is the place to look for commercial, medical affairs, regulatory and market access profiles. Competition is high. Candidates in Milan know their value and often hold several offers.

### Lazio

Rome and the area south of it, towards Latina, host a long-standing pharma manufacturing and distribution presence. You find production, quality and supply chain people here. Rome also has public research bodies and hospitals, which supply clinical and scientific profiles.

### Tuscany

Florence and Siena are known for vaccines and biotech. The talent pool is specialised: process development, quality control, and research scientists. The region is smaller than Lombardy, so senior specialists are harder to find, but they tend to stay longer.

### Emilia-Romagna

Bologna, Parma and Modena combine strong universities with a large biomedical and packaging equipment industry. This is a good area for engineers who work at the border of medical devices, automation and manufacturing.

### Veneto, Piedmont and Campania

These regions add smaller clusters. Veneto and Piedmont have manufacturing and diagnostics activity. Campania has a university base and growing biotech and manufacturing interest. Hiring here can mean less competition, but you need to be realistic about the size of the local pool.

## Roles in demand

Some roles are scarce in every cluster.

- **Regulatory affairs.** Italian submissions, labelling and interaction with the national authority need local knowledge. Good regulatory specialists are always in demand.
- **Quality assurance and qualified persons.** Manufacturing and release roles require specific training and experience. Few people hold them, and they do not change jobs often.
- **Pharmacovigilance.** Safety teams need people who know the rules and the tools. The pool is limited.
- **Clinical operations.** Clinical research associates, study coordinators and trial managers are sought by sponsors and CROs alike.
- **Biostatistics and data science.** Italy produces strong quantitative graduates. Many are pulled towards other sectors, so life sciences firms must compete on project interest as well as pay.
- **Process and manufacturing engineers.** Plants need people who can run, validate and improve production. Skilled technicians are especially hard to find.
- **Medical science liaisons and medical affairs.** Doctors and PhDs who can speak with specialists are valued and scarce.
- **Market access and pricing.** Italy has regional health systems, so people who understand how access works across regions are useful.

## What this means for a foreign employer

Three points matter before you start.

**Hire for the cluster, not the country.** A role based in Milan, Siena or Parma draws on a different pool and a different salary expectation. Decide where the person needs to sit. Many roles can be remote, but lab, plant and site-facing jobs cannot.

**Expect long notice periods for senior people.** Senior specialists often have to give extended notice to their current employer. Plan your start dates around this and do not promise an early start you cannot control.

**Get the contract right from day one.** Italian employment is governed by national collective agreements. Pharma and chemical sectors have their own agreements, and these set pay floors, working time, leave and notice rules. They also add benefits that candidates expect. A generic template from another country will not work.

## Hiring without a local entity

Most foreign life sciences companies do not want to set up a subsidiary just to employ a few people. An Employer of Record (EOR) lets you hire in Italy through a local employer. The EOR holds the contract, runs payroll, pays social contributions and applies the right collective agreement. You direct the daily work. You do not need a local legal entity.

This suits several situations:

- a biotech that needs a regulatory lead in Italy before it files
- a CRO that needs clinical staff for a single study
- a manufacturer testing a market before it commits to a site
- a company that needs to hire a candidate who is already in another country and needs a visa and relocation support

If the hire works out, you can later move the team into your own entity. If it does not, you have limited exposure.

## A practical way to start

1. Define the role and the city. Check that the cluster has the profile you need.
2. Find the applicable collective agreement and the likely pay range for that profile.
3. Agree the notice period and start date with the candidate.
4. Set up the contract and payroll through your EOR.
5. Plan onboarding, equipment and compliance training from the first week.

Italy rewards employers who respect local practice and move with clear terms. The talent is there, and it is concentrated in a few places. Know those places and you can hire well.

You have decided to hire in Italy. Now you need candidates. The first question is where to post the role. LinkedIn is the default for most international companies. Local job boards are the default for many Italian employers. They do not reach the same people.

This article compares them on reach and quality. It does not give market statistics. It gives a way to choose.

## What reach means here

Reach is not the size of a platform. Reach is how many suitable people in your target profile see your post and respond.

A large audience of the wrong people is noise. A smaller audience of the right people is a pipeline. Judge each channel by the people it puts in front of you for this specific role.

## LinkedIn: strengths

LinkedIn works well for roles that already live in an international setting.

- **Professional profiles.** You can see work history, skills and seniority before you contact anyone.
- **Direct search.** You can find people who have not applied and who are not looking actively.
- **English-language candidates.** If the role needs fluent English, LinkedIn is a natural filter.
- **Familiar to your team.** Your hiring managers abroad already use it, so the process is easy to run.

It suits software, product, finance leadership, sales leadership, and any role where the person will work with colleagues in other countries.

## LinkedIn: limits

LinkedIn does not cover the whole Italian labour market.

Many candidates in operational, technical, trade and administrative roles keep thin profiles or none at all. Some sectors rely on other channels. If you only post on LinkedIn, you may never see a large part of the people who could do the job.

Seniority also skews the picture. Experienced managers are well represented. Early-career and hands-on roles are less so.

Another risk is volume without fit. A visible post in English can attract many applicants who did not read the requirements. Screening takes time, and your time is the cost.

## Local job boards: strengths

Italian job boards are built for the local market and the local way of applying.

- **Local candidates.** People looking for work in Italy often start there, in Italian.
- **Wider range of roles.** Roles that are rare on LinkedIn, such as plant, field, retail and back-office work, are common on local boards.
- **Regional focus.** Many boards let candidates search by city or region. Italy is a country of regions, and people often want to stay in theirs.
- **Clear intent.** Someone browsing a job board is usually looking now.

## Local job boards: limits

The interface and the expectations are Italian. Your posting should be in Italian, and it should follow local conventions for job titles, contract type and working hours. A literal translation of a foreign job ad often reads strangely and gets fewer good responses.

Profiles are also less detailed than on LinkedIn. You often get a CV and a short form, and not much else. That means more work to judge fit.

Some boards attract a high number of unfiltered applications. Others are narrow and sector-specific. You need to know which is which before you pay or post.

## Quality: what to look at

Quality is not about which platform is better. It depends on the role.

Use these checks:

- **Language.** If daily work is in English, test English early. If daily work is in Italian, write the ad in Italian and expect Italian CVs.
- **Seniority.** Senior and specialist roles often come through LinkedIn search and referrals. Junior and operational roles often come through local boards.
- **Location.** If the person must be on site in a specific city, a board with regional search helps. If the role is remote within Italy, LinkedIn's wider net helps.
- **Passive vs active.** If the best people are already employed and not looking, you must search and approach them. That is LinkedIn work. If the pool is mostly active job seekers, boards perform well.

## A practical way to combine them

Most companies do better with both channels, each used for what it does best.

1. Write the role in Italian and in English. Keep the content consistent.
2. Post the Italian version on a local board that fits the sector.
3. Post the English version on LinkedIn, and search actively for profiles that match.
4. Use the same screening questions on both, so you can compare candidates fairly.
5. Track where each good candidate came from. After a few hires you will know which channel earns its place for each type of role.

## Do not forget the hiring side

Finding the person is only the start. In Italy you also need a compliant contract, the correct national collective agreement, payroll, social contributions and onboarding. A candidate who accepts an offer will expect these to be handled properly and on time.

If you do not have an Italian entity, an Employer of Record (EOR) can employ the person on your behalf while you direct their work. That lets you move from a good interview to a signed contract without setting up a company first.

## Summary

LinkedIn gives you reach among international, senior and English-speaking professionals, and the ability to approach people directly. Local job boards give you reach among local, active and regional candidates, especially for roles that are not visible on LinkedIn.

Choose by role, not by habit. Use both when the profile is unclear.

You hired someone in Italy. The rest of your team is somewhere else. Now the real work starts: making the distance invisible.

Most problems in global teams are not about skill. They are about timing and clarity. This article covers how to set up communication so your Italian employees work well with colleagues in other regions.

## Start with the overlap

Italy sits in a European time zone. If your headquarters is in North America, the overlap is short and falls in the Italian afternoon. If your team is in Asia, the overlap is in the Italian morning. If you are in Europe, there is little to solve.

Do not guess. Map the working hours of every team member and mark the hours when most people are online. Treat that window as shared time. Use it for meetings, quick questions and decisions. Keep everything else asynchronous.

Do not rotate the pain. If one office always takes the early or late call, resentment builds. Share the inconvenience, or move the meeting to the middle of the overlap.

## Respect the local working day

An Italian employee works within local hours. Evening calls with a far-away head office should be rare, not routine. A call that runs late once in a while is fine. A standing meeting at the end of the evening is not.

Italian professionals also value a proper break in the middle of the day. Lunch is a real pause, not a desk meal. Do not book meetings through it. Avoid scheduling in the quiet holiday periods too. Many people in Italy take long breaks in summer and around the end of the year. Ask about planned leave early and put it in a shared calendar.

## Write things down

Asynchronous work only works if the writing is good. Set a few simple rules:

- Every request states the goal, the deadline and the owner.
- Every meeting ends with written notes and actions.
- Decisions live in one place that everyone can find.
- Handoffs at the end of the day say what is done, what is blocked and what is next.

This helps everyone, but it helps non-native English speakers most. Many Italian employees speak excellent English. Still, reading is easier than listening on a fast call. Notes let people check details at their own pace.

## Be direct, but check understanding

Italian business culture can be warm and relationship-driven. People often like to build trust before they dive into tasks. A short personal chat at the start of a call is not wasted time. It is how rapport is built.

At the same time, politeness can hide disagreement. An Italian colleague may soften a concern, or say it is "complicated", when they mean it will not work. Make it easy to be honest. Ask open questions such as "What could go wrong?" or "What would you change?" Follow up in writing so there is no confusion about what was agreed.

If you give feedback, give it in private and with specifics. Public criticism lands badly in most cultures, and Italy is no exception.

## Choose the right channel

Not every message needs a meeting. A simple split works:

- **Chat** for quick, low-stakes questions.
- **Email or a shared document** for decisions and anything that needs a record.
- **Video** for sensitive topics, planning and one-to-ones.

Avoid urgent messages outside local hours. If your tools allow scheduled sending, use it. A message that arrives at the start of the Italian morning is better than one that pings in the middle of the night. Make it clear that people are not expected to answer outside their hours.

## Include Italian staff in the whole team

A remote employee in a small country office can feel far from the centre. Fix this on purpose:

- Invite them to team events and planning, not just task calls.
- Give them visibility with leadership.
- Rotate who presents, so no one office is always the audience.
- Plan an in-person visit now and then. It pays back many times over.

One-to-one meetings matter more when distance is large. Keep them regular and keep them in a time slot that suits the employee, not only the manager.

## Keep the employment side simple

Good communication is easier when the basics are handled. Your Italian employees need a contract, payroll and local compliance that work without you chasing them. An Employer of Record (EOR) takes on the local employer duties, so your managers can focus on the work and the people. Your team gets a clear point of contact for local questions, and you avoid setting up a local entity just to hire.

## A short checklist

- Map the overlap hours and protect them.
- Rotate meeting times fairly.
- Respect lunch, local holidays and leave.
- Write goals, owners and decisions down.
- Ask open questions and confirm agreements in writing.
- Use chat, documents and video for what each does best.
- Include Italian staff in team life, not only in tasks.

None of this is complicated. It takes discipline. Teams that do it well find that location stops mattering.

Italian employees care about take-home pay. When you hire in Italy, a higher gross salary is not always the best way to give them more. Meal vouchers are one of the most common tools to raise net value at a lower cost to you and a better result for the employee.

This article explains the tax-free limits and how to use them well.

## What meal vouchers are

A meal voucher is a benefit the employer gives to cover the cost of lunch on working days. In Italy it is a standard part of many compensation packages. Employees expect it, and candidates often ask about it in interviews.

The benefit has a tax advantage. Up to a daily limit, the value of the voucher is not treated as ordinary salary. Below that limit, the employee receives the full value without income tax on it. The same value paid as cash salary would be taxed.

## The tax-free limits

The limit depends on the format of the voucher.

- Electronic meal vouchers: up to EUR 10 per day.
- Paper meal vouchers: up to EUR 4 per day.

These figures come from a secondary source that summarises the latest budget law changes. Check them with your Italian payroll provider before you set up the plan, because the rules can change.

The difference between the two formats is large. The electronic limit is much higher than the paper one. For a foreign company, the practical lesson is simple: choose electronic vouchers.

## Why the format matters

If you give a voucher worth more than the daily limit, the part above the limit is treated as taxable income. It is then taxed like salary, and it may also attract social contributions. You lose the efficiency you were looking for.

So the goal is to stay at or below the limit. A voucher worth exactly the limit gives the employee the most tax-free value per day. A voucher worth more than the limit gives little extra value for the cost.

With paper vouchers, the low limit means the tax-free benefit is small. With electronic vouchers, the same benefit can be much larger. For the employee, the net gain over a year is clear.

## How to use vouchers to raise net pay

Here is a simple way to think about it.

1. Decide the total package you want to offer.
2. Set the voucher at the electronic daily limit.
3. Keep the rest as base salary.

The employee gets a package that looks better in take-home terms. The voucher part is tax-free, so each euro in vouchers is worth a full euro to the employee. Each euro in salary is worth less after tax.

This is useful when you compete for talent. Candidates compare offers on what reaches their bank account or their wallet. A package with vouchers at the limit often beats a higher gross salary with no benefits.

## Points to check

Vouchers are paid per day actually worked, not per calendar day. They do not apply on days of leave or when the employee does not work. Your payroll must track this.

The limit is per day. It is not a monthly allowance you can spend in one go. Plan the benefit around expected working days.

Remote work needs a decision. Employees who work from home may still receive vouchers, depending on the contract, the collective agreement and company policy. Set the rule in writing from the start so there is no dispute later.

Your collective agreement may already define a meal benefit. Read it before you design your own. The agreement may require a minimum or set a specific format.

## What this means for a foreign employer

You do not need a local entity to offer this benefit if you hire through an Employer of Record. The EOR is the legal employer in Italy. It handles the voucher provider, the payroll treatment and the reporting. You set the budget and the policy. The EOR applies the limits correctly.

This removes a common risk. A wrong voucher value or format can create tax exposure for the employer. With a local payroll team that knows the current limits, you avoid it.

## Summary

Meal vouchers are a cheap way to raise net pay in Italy. Use the electronic format, because its tax-free limit is much higher than the paper one. Keep the value at or below the daily limit. Pay it only for days worked. Confirm the current figures with your payroll provider before you launch.

A mid-sized team in Italy works well under an Employer of Record (EOR). Then the company grows, and the question comes up: should we hire these people ourselves? Many companies reach this point. Few plan it well.

This article walks through a typical exit in the order it happens. It also covers what goes wrong when teams rush.

## Why companies leave an EOR

The reasons are usually simple.

- The team is stable and the hiring plan in Italy is long term.
- Leadership wants direct control over contracts and payroll.
- The EOR fee no longer fits the size of the operation.
- A local entity makes sense for sales, tax or customer reasons.

None of these is a problem. A planned exit is a normal stage of growth. The EOR model is built for it.

## Phase 1: Decide and prepare

Start before you touch any contract. Define what you want at the end. Do you need a new Italian company, or do you already have one? Who will run payroll? Who signs employment documents locally?

Read your EOR service agreement first. Check the notice terms and any handover duties. Ask the provider for a written exit process. A good provider will have one.

At this stage, build a full list of the people involved. For each person, collect the contract type, role, pay structure, benefits, leave balance and the collective agreement that applies. Missing data here causes most delays later.

## Phase 2: Build the legal home

You need an entity that can employ people in Italy. That means incorporation, tax and social security registrations, a bank account, and a payroll set-up. Each step depends on the one before it. This is usually the longest phase, and it is the one companies underestimate.

Do not start the employee transfer until the entity is fully ready. A half-ready entity leaves people without a clear employer, and that creates risk for them and for you.

## Phase 3: Choose the payroll route

Your entity needs a payroll process from the first day. Most companies outsource it to a local provider. Pick one early and run a parallel test using last month's data. Compare the results against what the EOR produced.

Differences will appear. Find out why before go-live, not after the first payslip.

## Phase 4: Talk to the team

People care about three things: will my pay change, will my benefits change, and is my service history safe. Answer these in writing and in plain language.

Hold individual conversations as well as a group meeting. Give people time to read their new documents and ask questions. A transfer that employees understand goes smoothly. One that feels sudden creates doubt, and some of your best people will start to look elsewhere.

Keep the terms at least as good as before. Changing pay, role and employer on the same day is a bad idea.

## Phase 5: Transfer and handover

This is the switch itself. The old employment ends with the EOR, and the new one starts with your entity. The details need care:

- Continuity of service should be agreed and documented.
- Accrued leave and end-of-service pay (TFR) must be settled or carried over in a clear way.
- Final payroll from the EOR and first payroll from your entity must not overlap or leave a gap.
- Benefits and insurance cover must continue without a break.

Ask the EOR to confirm each item in writing. Ask for payroll history, contracts and personnel files in a usable format.

## Phase 6: After the switch

The first payroll cycle under your entity is the real test. Check every payslip. Fix errors fast and explain them to the person affected.

Then close the loop. Confirm that registrations are in order, that the EOR relationship is formally ended, and that nothing is still billed. Review the first period with the team and with HR.

## Lessons that repeat

**Start with data, not law.** Clean employee records save more time than anything else.

**Do not shorten the entity phase.** Every shortcut here returns as a delay later.

**Run payroll in parallel first.** One test cycle finds most errors.

**Communicate early.** People forgive slow timelines. They do not forgive surprises.

**Keep the EOR on side.** A cooperative handover is worth more than a small saving on notice.

**Keep a fallback.** If the entity is late, extend the EOR arrangement for a short time. That costs less than a failed transfer.

## Is leaving always the right move?

Not always. If hiring in Italy is small or uncertain, staying with an EOR can be cheaper and simpler. The right time to leave is when the team is stable, growth is clear and you are ready to run a local employer yourself.

Whatever you decide, plan the exit as a project with an owner, a checklist and a clear order of work. Done this way, the move is quiet and the team barely notices it.

Most foreign companies hiring in Italy start in Milan or Rome. Naples and the South deserve a look too. Tech teams are growing there, universities feed local talent, and living costs are lower than in the northern cities. This article covers what to weigh before you open a hub or hire your first person in the area.

## Why the South is on the map

Naples is the largest city in the South. It has several universities, a large student population and a growing circle of software, digital and engineering companies. Other cities in the region follow a similar pattern: a strong academic base, a young workforce and fewer employers competing for the same people.

For an international company, this has practical effects:

- Candidates often stay longer with an employer that offers a serious technical role.
- Competition for senior engineers is less intense than in the large northern hubs.
- Remote and hybrid work is accepted, so you can hire from the South for a team based elsewhere.

None of this means hiring is easy. Some profiles are rare, and you still need a clear role, a fair salary and a plan for career growth. But the pool is real, and many companies have not looked at it yet.

## What kind of talent you can find

Expect strong profiles in software development, data, cybersecurity, embedded systems and industrial engineering. Many candidates speak good English and have worked with international clients or on remote teams. Some have studied or worked abroad and returned home. Others never left and prefer to build a career near family.

This last point matters. People who choose to stay in the South often value stability. A stable contract, clear terms and reliable payroll count for a lot. If you offer that, you can build a loyal team.

## Incentives: set expectations carefully

Southern Italy is often described as a region with generous public support for hiring and investment. Programs exist at national, regional and EU level. They change often, depend on the profile of the hire and the company, and have eligibility rules and deadlines. We do not publish figures for them here because we only quote verified data.

Our advice is simple. Do not build your business case on an incentive you have not confirmed. Treat any support as an upside. Check eligibility for your specific case before you commit, and ask the person handling your payroll to do the same.

## One local cost to know: the municipal income tax surcharge

One item is easy to verify. Italian employees pay a municipal surcharge on personal income tax, set by each city. According to a secondary source, Naples applies a single rate of 1%, with an exemption for income up to 12,000 EUR.

This is a cost for the employee, not for the employer. Still, it affects take-home pay, and it is part of the net salary conversation with candidates. When you compare Naples with another city, compare the net result for the person, not only the gross figure. Rates and exemptions can change, so confirm them against the current local rules before you quote a net salary in an offer.

## How to hire without a local entity

You do not need to set up a company in Italy to hire in Naples. An Employer of Record (EOR) employs the person on your behalf under Italian law. You choose the candidate and direct the work. The EOR handles the contract, payroll, social contributions and compliance with the national collective agreement that applies to the role.

This suits the South well, for three practical reasons:

- You can test the market with one or two hires before deciding on a larger presence.
- You avoid the time and cost of setting up a legal entity and local administration.
- You keep the option to move to your own entity later, when the team is large enough.

The EOR can also help with relocation and visas if you bring in talent from outside the EU, and with social security representation when needed.

## A practical way to start

Begin with the role, not the city. Define what the person will do, what seniority you need and which time zone overlap you require. Then decide whether the role can be remote, hybrid or based in Naples.

Next, look at the full package. Salary is one part. Italian employment also includes mandatory contributions, a severance provision, paid leave and a thirteenth month paid in many sectors. A good EOR will give you the full employer cost before you make an offer, so there are no surprises.

Finally, plan the first months. Give the new hire a clear point of contact, a defined onboarding and a real project. People in the South who join international teams often become the anchor of a local group, drawing in friends and former classmates over time. Treat the first hire as the start of something larger.

## Summary

Naples and the South offer talent, a lower-pressure hiring market and a growing tech scene. Public incentives may help, but confirm them case by case. Local taxes such as the municipal surcharge affect net pay, so check them when you set salaries. An EOR lets you hire quickly and compliantly without opening an entity.

You agree a gross salary with your Italian hire. They look at the net amount on the payslip. The gap between the two surprises many foreign employers, so it helps to know how it works before you make an offer.

This article covers what the employee pays. It does not cover what you pay on top as the employer. Two items matter for the employee: the pension contribution and income tax. A tax credit for employees then reduces the tax.

## Step 1: the employee pension contribution

The first deduction is the employee share of the pension contribution to INPS, the Italian social security institute. For employees the rate is 9.19% of the contribution base. This is the main IVS rate, which covers old age, disability and survivors.

The employer withholds it every month. The employee never handles it.

Other items can apply depending on the contract and the sector. We do not cover them here. The 9.19% is the core figure to plan around.

## Step 2: income tax (IRPEF)

Italian income tax is progressive. Each slice of income is taxed at its own rate. The rate does not apply to the whole salary. There are three brackets:

| Annual taxable income | Rate |
|---|---|
| Up to 28,000 EUR | 23% |
| From 28,000 to 50,000 EUR | 33% |
| Above 50,000 EUR | 43% |

So the first 28,000 EUR is taxed at 23%. Only the part between 28,000 and 50,000 is taxed at 33%. Only the part above 50,000 is taxed at 43%.

A common mistake is to see 43% and assume the employee loses that share of the whole salary. That is wrong. The top rate hits only the top slice.

The taxable income is the gross salary after the employee pension contribution is taken out. This is why the order of the steps matters.

## Step 3: the employment tax credit

After IRPEF is calculated, Italy gives employees a tax credit called the *detrazione per lavoro dipendente*. It lowers the tax due. It is largest for lower incomes and shrinks as income grows.

Here R is the reference income. The credit works like this:

- R up to 15,000 EUR: 1,955 EUR. There is a minimum of 690 EUR. For fixed-term contracts the minimum is 1,380 EUR.
- R from 15,000 to 28,000 EUR: 1,910 EUR plus 1,190 × (28,000 − R) / 13,000.
- R from 28,000 to 50,000 EUR: 1,910 × (50,000 − R) / 22,000.
- An extra 65 EUR if R is between 25,000 and 35,000 EUR.
- Above 50,000 EUR: zero.

The credit falls smoothly as income rises. There is no cliff where the benefit disappears overnight. Above 50,000 EUR it is gone completely.

## What this means for your offer

Three practical points follow.

**Net grows more slowly than gross.** Each extra euro of gross is taxed at a higher rate as the salary climbs. The tax credit also shrinks over the same range. In the 28,000 to 50,000 EUR range, a raise is taxed at 33% and also loses part of the credit. The employee keeps less of each raise there than the bracket rate alone suggests.

**Fixed-term contracts get a higher floor.** At low incomes the minimum credit is 1,380 EUR on a fixed-term contract, against 690 EUR otherwise. This only matters for lower salaries.

**Candidates think in net.** Italian candidates often compare offers by the net monthly amount. If you quote only gross, you may look weaker than a competitor who explains the net figure. Show the breakdown early.

## How to calculate it

The steps are always the same:

1. Take the gross annual salary.
2. Subtract the employee pension contribution at 9.19%.
3. Apply the three IRPEF brackets to what remains.
4. Subtract the employment tax credit from the tax.
5. What is left is the net annual pay.

Some employees have extra deductions for family members or other personal circumstances. These change the result and we do not model them here. For a standard employee with no special situation, the five steps above give a reliable estimate.

## Why this matters for an international employer

If your team is outside Italy, you may be used to simpler systems. In Italy, the payslip shows several lines and the employee will read each one. A clear explanation avoids disputes in the first months. It also helps you set a gross salary that matches the net the candidate expects.

Work out the net before you make the offer. Do not guess it.

If you plan to hire in Italy, you will soon learn that relationships matter. Contracts matter too. But in Italy, the relationship usually comes first.

This article explains how business networks work, why introductions carry weight, and what you can do as a foreign company to build trust.

## Trust comes before the deal

In many markets, a good offer and a clear price are enough to start a conversation. In Italy, that is often not enough. People want to know who you are before they decide what you offer.

This is not about being slow or difficult. It is a practical way to manage risk. If a partner, supplier or candidate does not know you, they look for a signal that you are reliable. That signal is usually a person they already trust.

So the first question is often not "What do you sell?" It is "Who sent you?"

## Why introductions work

A warm introduction transfers trust. When someone vouches for you, the other side assumes you have already passed a basic check. They will answer your message. They will take your call. They will give you time.

A cold email has none of this. It can still work, but it starts from zero. Many cold messages go unanswered, not out of rudeness, but because the sender is unknown.

An introduction also works as a filter in the other direction. The person who introduces you puts their own name at stake. They will only do it if they believe you are serious. That makes the introduction valuable, and it makes you careful about how you behave afterward.

## Where networks form

Business networks in Italy are usually local and personal. They grow in a few common places:

- **Professional advisers.** Accountants, labour consultants and lawyers know many companies. They often act as the first point of contact for a newcomer.
- **Trade associations and chambers of commerce.** These bring together firms in the same sector or region. Membership gives access to events and to people who know the local market.
- **Industry events and fairs.** These are useful, but the real value is in the follow-up conversation, not the stand.
- **Universities and schools.** Alumni links stay strong for many years and often lead to hiring contacts.
- **Existing clients and partners.** A satisfied partner is the best reference you can have.

Regions differ. A network in the north may not reach the south, and the reverse is also true. Think local first, then expand.

## How to behave once you are introduced

Getting the introduction is only the start. What you do next decides whether the trust holds.

**Be personal.** Take time for a call or a coffee before talking business. Ask about the other person's work and company. Do not rush to the point.

**Be consistent.** Do what you said you would do. Reply when you promised to reply. Small signals of reliability add up.

**Respect hierarchy.** Titles and seniority often matter. Address people formally until they invite you to do otherwise.

**Thank the person who introduced you.** Tell them how the meeting went. They will remember it, and they will introduce you again.

**Expect more than one meeting.** One call rarely closes anything. Plan for several conversations over time.

## What this means for hiring

The same rules apply when you recruit and employ people in Italy.

Candidates often learn about roles through people they know. A referral from a current employee or a trusted contact carries more weight than an anonymous job post. Candidates also want to see that your company is real and stable. A foreign company with no local presence can look uncertain, and good people may hesitate.

This is a common gap for international firms. You may have a strong product and a clear plan, but no local name behind you. Without a local reputation, you start without the trust that local competitors already have.

You can close that gap in several ways:

- Work with local advisers who already have standing in the market.
- Show a clear, legal and stable employment setup, so candidates see you as a real employer.
- Give candidates a named local contact they can speak to in Italian.
- Be open about who you are, where you are based and how long you plan to stay.

## Common mistakes

- Sending mass cold outreach and expecting fast replies.
- Pushing for a decision in the first meeting.
- Treating the introducer as a one-time tool and then ignoring them.
- Being vague about your company, your plans or your intentions.
- Assuming one regional contact opens doors across the whole country.

## A practical starting point

Start small. Pick one or two trusted local advisers. Ask them who in your sector is worth meeting. Accept the introductions you are offered, and follow up with care. Over time, your own name becomes the signal that others rely on.

Trust takes time to build. But once it exists, it makes everything else easier: hiring, partnerships and day-to-day operations.

Hiring in Italy is the easy part for many foreign companies. Letting someone go, or seeing them resign, is where surprises appear. This FAQ covers how people leave jobs in Italy and what you need to plan for.

## Do Italian employees have to give notice when they resign?

Yes. An employee who resigns must give notice. The length is not set by the company. It comes from the national collective agreement (CCNL) that applies to the role. The agreement usually sets longer notice for higher job levels and for people with more years of service.

Your employment contract cannot freely replace these rules. If you want to know the exact notice for a given hire, check the agreement that covers the sector and the job level.

## Who decides which collective agreement applies?

The sector and the type of work decide. A software engineer, a sales manager and a warehouse worker may fall under different agreements. Each agreement sets pay floors, leave, notice and other terms. Pick the right one before you hire, because it affects every exit later.

## How does an employee hand in a resignation?

Resignation must be submitted through an official online procedure. A letter or an email to the employer is not enough on its own. The employee files the resignation on a government platform, and the employer receives it. This rule exists to prevent forced or backdated resignations.

If your team is abroad, tell them about this early. Many managers expect a simple email and are surprised that it has no legal effect.

## Can the employee leave before the notice period ends?

Only if you agree. You can release the employee early. In that case the notice is shortened by mutual consent, and it is wise to put this in writing.

If the employee leaves without working the notice and without your agreement, the company can claim an indemnity for the missing notice. In practice, this is often deducted from final pay, within the limits the law allows.

## Can the company pay instead of letting the employee work the notice?

Yes, in many cases. The party who ends the relationship early can pay an indemnity in place of the notice. It is calculated on pay for the missing notice time. For the employer, this is a common tool when a departing employee has access to sensitive data or clients.

## Can an employer dismiss an employee freely?

No. Italy does not allow dismissal at will. A dismissal needs a valid reason. The reason can relate to the employee's conduct, to serious misconduct, or to genuine business needs. The process has formal steps, and mistakes can lead to reinstatement or compensation.

For a foreign company used to simple exits, this is the biggest difference. Plan any termination with local advice before you act.

## Is there a probation period?

Many contracts include a probation period. During probation, either side can usually end the relationship with less formality. The probation must be agreed in writing from the start. If it is missing from the signed contract, it does not exist.

## What does the employee receive when they leave?

Final pay is more than the last salary. Expect these items:

- Salary up to the last day worked.
- Pay for leave not yet taken.
- Any pro rata share of extra monthly pay set by the collective agreement.
- The accrued severance pay, known as TFR.

TFR builds up during employment. It is paid when the relationship ends, whatever the reason. Your payroll must track it correctly from the first month, because it can become a large amount over time.

## What happens if the employee is also a manager with special terms?

Executives often fall under a different agreement with their own rules on notice and dismissal. Their notice can be longer and their protection different. Do not assume the standard rules apply. Review the executive agreement before you sign.

## What paperwork follows an exit?

The company must report the end of the relationship to the authorities within the set deadlines. It must also close the payroll and social security position and issue final tax documents. Missing a filing can create fines, so these steps should have an owner.

## What should foreign companies do before hiring?

- Identify the correct collective agreement.
- Write the notice and probation terms clearly in the contract.
- Brief managers abroad on the online resignation procedure.
- Set aside budget for TFR and unused leave.
- Get local advice before any dismissal.

## How can an Employer of Record help?

An Employer of Record (EOR) becomes the legal employer in Italy. It applies the right collective agreement, handles the resignation procedure, calculates final pay and files the exit paperwork. You keep day-to-day control of the work. The EOR carries the local employment compliance.

This lets you hire in Italy without building a local entity first, and exit cases are handled by people who do this daily.

An offer letter in Italy is read closely. Candidates compare it with the contract they will sign later. They also compare it with what peers in the same sector receive. If your letter is vague, you lose trust early. If it is clear, you look like a serious employer.

This guide lists what Italian candidates expect to see, and what to avoid.

## Start with the contract type

Say plainly whether the role is permanent or fixed-term. Most candidates expect a permanent contract unless there is a clear reason for a fixed term. If the role is fixed-term, state the reason in simple words. If it is part-time, say so and describe the schedule.

Candidates also want to know the start date and the place of work. If the role is remote or hybrid, write down what that means in practice. Do not leave it for later.

## Name the collective agreement

This is the point foreign employers miss most often. In Italy, most employment relationships follow a national collective agreement (CCNL). It sets minimum pay levels, working time rules, leave, notice and many other terms. Candidates know this. Many will ask which one applies before they ask anything else.

Your letter should name the collective agreement that governs the role. It should also state the job level or grade under that agreement. The level drives the minimum pay, so candidates treat it as a core term. A letter that skips it will prompt questions, and some candidates will assume the worst.

The right agreement depends on your sector and the work. Choose it before you write the offer, not after.

## State pay on a gross annual basis

Italian candidates think in gross annual salary. Give the figure in euros, gross, per year. Then say how it is paid.

Many Italian contracts pay the annual amount across more monthly payments than the twelve calendar months. Candidates expect this. Say clearly how many payments the annual figure is split into, so nobody does the wrong mental maths. A candidate who compares your number with a local offer will do it either way. Make it easy.

If you quote a monthly amount, label it gross. Never mix gross and net in the same letter.

## Separate fixed pay from variable pay

If there is a bonus, commission or equity, describe it apart from base salary. Say who decides it, how it is measured and when it is paid. Say whether it is guaranteed or discretionary. Candidates will not count a vague bonus as part of their pay, and they should not have to.

If you grant equity from a foreign parent company, say that the plan rules apply and that the full terms come in a separate document. Do not bury this in a single line.

## List benefits in concrete terms

Candidates expect a short, specific list. Typical items include:

- meal vouchers or a canteen allowance
- supplementary health cover
- a company car or phone, if relevant
- supplementary pension contributions
- training budget
- flexible working arrangements

Only list what you will actually provide. If a benefit comes from the collective agreement, say so. If it is on top of the agreement, say that too. That distinction shows candidates you understand the local system.

## Be clear on working time, leave and notice

Working time, paid leave and notice periods are largely set by law and by the collective agreement. You do not need to restate every rule. You do need to refer to them correctly. A good letter says that these terms follow the applicable agreement and gives the candidate a way to read them.

If you offer more than the agreement requires, say so. That is a selling point, and it deserves a clear line.

Probation is also worth a line. State that a probation period applies, if it does, and that it follows the agreement and the contract.

## Explain who the employer is

Candidates will ask who signs their contract and who pays them. If the employer in Italy is a local entity or a service provider hiring on your behalf, name it. Explain that day-to-day work is directed by your team, while the contract, payroll and social security filings sit with the legal employer.

This matters for trust. A person leaving a stable job wants to know that salary, contributions and the severance entitlement are handled correctly. Say who handles them.

## Keep the language straightforward

Write the letter in English if the team works in English, but offer an Italian version for the contract. Candidates often want to read the binding document in Italian. Make sure the two match on every key term.

Avoid vague phrases such as "competitive package" or "salary to be discussed". Avoid conditions hidden in the last paragraph. Do not make the offer depend on terms that are not yet defined.

## Set out the next steps

End with a short list of what happens next:

- how and by when to accept
- which documents you need from the candidate
- when the formal contract will be sent
- who to contact with questions

Give the candidate a named person and a reasonable time to decide. Italian candidates usually need to handle notice with their current employer, so they value clarity on the start date.

## A short checklist

Before you send an offer to a candidate in Italy, check that it states:

- contract type and start date
- place of work and working pattern
- the collective agreement and the job level
- gross annual pay and how it is split into payments
- variable pay, kept separate from base pay
- benefits you will actually provide
- the legal employer
- next steps and a contact

If any of these is missing, expect questions. Answer them in the letter first.

A new hire in Italy forms an opinion about your company very fast. The first week decides whether they feel welcome or feel like a file number. This is true everywhere, but a few local habits make it more pronounced in Italy.

This article covers what to prepare, what to do on the first day, and what to keep going through the rest of the week.

## Start before the first day

Italian employees often wait for the start date with some uncertainty. Many have left a stable job. Many have a notice period to serve, and some have family who ask how the new employer is.

Silence in this period hurts. Send a short, personal message from the future manager. Confirm the start date, the place or the remote setup, and who will meet them. Keep it human. A line about what they will work on first is enough.

Also send the practical items early:

- The signed contract, in Italian, with an English copy if the working language is English.
- The list of documents you need from them, such as tax code, bank details and identity papers.
- Information on how payroll and benefits work.

If your company hires through an Employer of Record (EOR), explain this clearly. The employee will have a contract with the local employer and will work day to day for you. Say who handles what: payroll questions go to one place, daily work goes to the manager. Confusion about this is a common cause of first-week frustration.

## Make the first day personal

Italian workplace culture values relationships. People want to know who they work with before they dive into tasks.

On the first day:

- Have the manager greet them live, by video if remote.
- Introduce the team one by one, with a sentence about what each person does.
- Assign a buddy, a peer who answers small questions without judgment.
- Share lunch or a coffee, even a virtual one. A shared coffee is not a small thing in Italy.

Do not fill the day with forms and compliance slides. Do the paperwork, but keep it short and separate from the welcome.

## Equipment and access must work

Nothing damages trust like a laptop that arrives late. Check that the hardware is delivered before the start date. Test accounts, email, chat and any tools. If something will be late, tell the person ahead of time and give a date.

For remote staff, send a small welcome item from the company if you can. It does not need to be expensive. It shows that someone thought about them.

## Give a clear plan for the week

Italian professionals dislike vague starts. They accept that learning takes time, but they want to see a structure.

Share a simple plan with:

- What they will learn each day.
- Who they will meet.
- What you expect by the end of the week.
- When the manager will check in.

Keep the targets modest. A first small deliverable by the end of the week gives a sense of progress. It should be something they can finish and be proud of.

## Explain the company, not only the role

Foreign companies often assume that the Italian hire already knows the culture of the head office. They do not. Spend time on how decisions are made, which hours people are online, how feedback works and what the mission is.

Be honest about time zones and meeting load. If the team works across several regions, explain how that affects the Italian workday. Respect for working hours and for time off matters to many employees in Italy. Showing that you understand this early builds credibility.

Also explain the benefits they have in Italy in plain terms. Payslips can look complex. A short walk-through of the payslip with someone from the payroll side prevents questions and worry later.

## Check in often and listen

The manager should speak with the new hire every day in the first week, even if only for a few minutes. Ask what is unclear. Ask what was good and what was not.

At the end of the week, hold a longer conversation. Cover what went well, what is missing and what will happen next. Write down any problem and act on it. People remember when their feedback leads to a change.

## Avoid common mistakes

- Leaving the new hire alone with a pile of documents.
- Starting without a manager present.
- Mixing up who is the employer and who is the manager.
- Late equipment or missing access.
- No contact between signing and start date.

Each of these is easy to prevent with a checklist and one person who owns the process.

## What people remember

Employees rarely remember the slide deck. They remember being greeted by name, having a buddy, working equipment, a clear plan and a manager who listened. These are low-cost habits. They depend on preparation, not on budget.

If you do them well, the first week sets a tone of trust. That tone carries into retention, performance and how your new hire speaks about you to others in their network.

Your team is spread across time zones. Your new hire sits in Italy. Meetings land early or late for someone, and messages arrive at all hours. This FAQ covers what you can expect, and what you cannot, when an Italian employee works in a global team.

## Does Italian employment law care about working hours?

Yes. Working hours in Italy are set by law and by the collective agreement (CCNL) that applies to the role. The agreement sets normal weekly hours, rest periods, and how extra hours are counted and paid. Your contract can add detail. It cannot remove protections the law or the CCNL gives.

This surprises many foreign employers. In some countries, salaried staff are simply expected to work until the job is done. In Italy, hours are a legal topic, and the applicable CCNL decides much of the detail.

## What counts as overtime?

Overtime is work beyond the normal hours defined by law or by the CCNL. The agreement usually says how much overtime is allowed, how it must be requested, and how it is paid or compensated, for example with extra pay or time off.

A call at the end of the day that runs long is overtime if it pushes the employee past normal hours. It does not matter that the work is remote or that the call is "just a quick sync".

## Can I ask my Italian employee to attend calls outside local office hours?

Sometimes. A few early or late calls, agreed in advance, are normal in global teams. Problems start when the pattern becomes regular and nobody tracks it.

Good practice:

- Agree the expected working window in the contract or in a written policy.
- Rotate inconvenient meeting times so one office does not carry the burden.
- Record the extra time and compensate it as the CCNL requires.
- Ask first. Do not assume availability.

## Is overtime always paid?

Not always in the same way. Some roles, especially senior or managerial ones, may be treated differently under their CCNL or contract. But you should not assume that a job title removes the right to compensation or rest. Check the applicable agreement before you decide. A payroll mistake here can turn into a claim later.

## What is the right to disconnect?

It is the employee's right to stop work and not be reachable outside working hours, without suffering consequences. In Italy, this idea is linked to remote and flexible work arrangements. The individual agreement for remote work should state the employee's rest periods and the technical and organisational measures that allow them to disconnect.

In practice, it means your Italian employee can switch off after hours. They can ignore a late message until the next working day. You cannot mark that down as a lack of commitment.

## Does this apply if the employee works fully from home?

Yes. Working from home does not cancel working time rules. If anything, it makes a written agreement more important. The agreement should say when the employee is expected to be available, how work is measured, and how rest is protected.

## What about urgent issues, like a production outage?

True emergencies happen. Plan for them, do not improvise.

- Define in writing what counts as urgent.
- Set up an on-call arrangement if you need one, and check how the CCNL treats it.
- Give compensation or time off for work done outside normal hours.
- Keep emergencies rare. If every week is an emergency, you have a staffing problem, not an urgency problem.

## How do I manage expectations across time zones?

Set the rules early and put them in writing. A few habits help:

- **Publish core overlap hours.** Choose a window when the whole team is online and keep meetings inside it.
- **Default to asynchronous work.** Use written updates, recorded demos and shared documents so decisions do not wait for a live call.
- **Mark message urgency.** Make it clear what needs a reply today and what can wait.
- **Do not reward constant availability.** If the fastest replier gets praise, others will copy them and burn out.
- **Respect local holidays and rest.** Italian staff expect real time off. Do not schedule work into it.

## Can I monitor my Italian employee's hours?

Tracking working time is reasonable and often useful, since it shows overtime. But tools that monitor employee activity are regulated in Italy, and remote control of workers is limited. Do not install monitoring software without advice. Simple self-reported timesheets or agreed work logs are usually safer than intrusive tracking.

## What happens if I ignore all this?

The risks are practical. The employee may claim unpaid overtime. They may challenge a dismissal tied to a refusal to work after hours. Morale also drops quickly when staff feel they are always on call. Good employees leave. Replacing them costs more than respecting the rules.

## How does an Employer of Record (EOR) help?

An EOR employs the person in Italy on your behalf, under the correct CCNL, with compliant contracts, payroll and working time records. You still direct the daily work. The EOR makes sure that overtime is handled correctly, that remote work agreements include disconnection terms, and that the contract matches what you actually expect.

This lets you build a global team without learning every local rule yourself.

## Quick checklist

- Identify the CCNL for the role.
- Write the expected working window into the contract.
- Agree how extra hours are requested and compensated.
- Add disconnection terms to the remote work agreement.
- Rotate meeting times across offices.
- Use asynchronous work as the default.
- Plan emergencies in advance.

You have registered your Italian entity. Now people need to be paid, correctly and on time. This is where many foreign companies lose weeks, because payroll in Italy is not a simple monthly transfer.

This article lays out the options for running payroll and the trade-offs of each. It does not tell you what to pick. It tells you what to ask before you choose.

## Why Italian payroll is different

Payroll in Italy follows the national collective agreement that applies to your sector. That agreement sets minimum pay, job levels, extra monthly payments, leave rules and notice terms. Social contributions and income tax withholding are calculated each month and reported to the authorities through set channels.

Your head office payroll will not map cleanly onto this. A payslip that looks fine at home can be wrong here. Errors tend to surface later, as a dispute with an employee or a request from an authority.

The rules also change. Contribution rates, thresholds and agreement terms get updated. Someone has to track those changes and apply them.

## Option 1: Build it in-house

You hire a payroll specialist, or train someone, and buy payroll software that handles Italian rules.

**What works:** full control. Data stays with you. It can make sense when you have a large and growing Italian team.

**What does not:** you carry the knowledge risk. If your one specialist leaves, payroll stops. You also need software, updates, and a person who reads the agreements and contribution changes. For a small team, this is a lot of fixed effort for little volume.

**Fits when:** you plan a sizeable local headcount and want a permanent local finance function.

## Option 2: A local accountant or labour consultant

Many Italian companies use an outside professional for payslips and filings. This is a normal, accepted model.

**What works:** local expertise, and a person who knows the filing channels. Cost scales with the number of employees.

**What does not:** you still run the employer side. You must send clean inputs on time: hires, absences, changes in pay. You also need to manage the relationship, often in Italian. Your own entity remains the employer, so legal responsibility stays with you.

**Fits when:** you already have an Italian entity, someone on your side who speaks the language, and a stable team.

## Option 3: A payroll software or service provider

A specialist provider runs the calculation and produces payslips and reports. Some offer a platform, some offer a managed service.

**What works:** structured process, clear input deadlines, and often English-language support. Easier to compare across countries if you hire in several.

**What does not:** you are still the employer. The provider calculates, but you approve and you are accountable. You also need to confirm that the provider covers the agreement that applies to your sector, not just the standard rules.

**Fits when:** you want a process instead of a person, and you have internal staff who can review the output.

## Option 4: Use an Employer of Record (EOR)

With an Employer of Record (EOR), the EOR is the legal employer in Italy. It runs payroll, handles contributions and withholding, issues payslips and manages the employment contract. Your team works for you day to day. The employment paperwork sits with the EOR.

**What works:** no payroll build, no local filing duties for you, and a single point of contact. It also removes the need for an entity in the first place, which is worth remembering if you have set one up only to pay a few people.

**What does not:** you pay a service fee on top of employment cost. You also give up some direct control over contract administration. If you plan a large local team over time, the economics change and you may want to move to your own payroll later.

**Fits when:** the team is small, you want to move fast, or you are testing the market.

## Questions to ask before you decide

- How many people will you employ here over the next year, and how fast?
- Who on your side will review payslips and send monthly inputs?
- Which collective agreement applies to your sector, and does the provider know it well?
- Who is accountable if a payslip or a filing is wrong?
- Can you change model later without disrupting employees?
- Do you need to keep the entity at all, for other reasons such as sales or a branch function?

## A practical way to choose

For a very small team, outsourcing the whole function is usually simpler than building anything. For a growing team with a local finance lead, an accountant or provider plus internal review works well. For a large, stable team, an in-house function can pay off.

Whatever you choose, put the process in writing. Agree input deadlines, approval steps and who answers employee questions. Most payroll problems come from unclear handovers, not from the calculation.
