Most foreign companies do not plan to "enter Italy". They start with a single hire. A sales lead, an engineer, a designer, a country manager. The reasons behind that first hire vary by sector, but a few patterns repeat.

This article describes those patterns. It does not promise a fit for every business. It shows what we see when companies decide to put a person on the ground.

## Access to talent

The most common reason is skills. A company needs a specific profile and finds that the best candidate lives in Italy.

This happens often in engineering, industrial design, fashion technology, food science, mechanical and automation work, and software. Italy has deep expertise in manufacturing, craft and design. Foreign companies that work in or near these fields want people who understand the product and the supply chain from the inside.

There is also a practical side. Many strong candidates prefer to stay in Italy for family or lifestyle reasons. A company that is open to hiring locally can reach people who would never relocate abroad. The company gets a good hire. The hire keeps their life where it is.

## Access to the Italian market

The second reason is customers. Italian buyers often prefer to deal with someone who speaks their language, knows local habits and can meet in person.

A remote team in another country can win some deals. But trust is built faster with a local face. A first hire in sales, business development or customer success gives the company a voice that Italian clients understand.

This matters most in sectors with long sales cycles or strong relationships. Think of industrial equipment, healthcare, professional services, hospitality technology and public sector suppliers. In these areas, local presence is often the difference between a reply and silence.

## Supplier and partner proximity

Some companies hire in Italy because their suppliers, manufacturers or partners are there. A quality manager or sourcing specialist near the factory can solve problems that email cannot.

This is common for brands that design abroad and produce in Italy. It is also common for technology firms that rely on Italian hardware makers. One person on site can check samples, follow deliveries and keep relations healthy.

## Testing the market before committing

Many companies want proof before they invest in a full local structure. Opening a subsidiary takes time and administrative work. It also creates ongoing obligations for accounting, payroll and compliance.

A first hire lets the company test demand with a small commitment. If sales grow, the team can grow. If the market is slower than expected, the company has not built a heavy structure around a guess.

This is where an Employer of Record (EOR) fits. The EOR employs the person in Italy on the company's behalf. The company directs the daily work. The EOR handles contracts, payroll, contributions and local rules. The foreign company does not need its own Italian entity to start.

## Speed

Timing often drives the decision. A company wins a client, sees an opportunity or finds the right candidate, and wants to move now. Waiting to set up an entity can mean losing the person or the deal.

A compliant way to employ someone quickly removes that bottleneck. The hire starts when the business needs them, not when the paperwork is finished.

## Following a key person

Sometimes the reason is simple. An existing employee or a trusted contractor lives in Italy, or wants to move there. The company wants to keep them, and a proper employment contract is the right way to do it.

In other cases, the company needs to bring someone from abroad to Italy. That adds visa and relocation steps. These are manageable, but they need planning. Companies that start early avoid delays.

## Moving from contractor to employee

Some businesses begin by working with freelancers in Italy. Over time the role grows. The person becomes central to the team. The company then wants a stable, clear employment relationship that protects both sides.

Converting a long-term contractor into an employee is a common step. It gives the worker security and gives the company clarity about the relationship.

## What these reasons have in common

In every case the company wants a real presence in Italy without a large upfront burden. The first hire is a bridge. It connects the company to people, customers and suppliers it cannot reach well from outside.

Before hiring, it helps to be clear on a few points:

- What the role must achieve in the first months.
- Whether the person will work from home, a shared space or a client site.
- Which collective agreement applies to the sector.
- How the company will manage and support someone in another country.

Good answers to these questions make the first hire smoother. They also make the second and third hires easier.

## The takeaway

Companies hire their first employee in Italy for talent, for customers, for proximity to partners, for speed and for low-risk testing. These reasons often overlap. What matters is having a clear goal for the role and a simple way to employ the person correctly.

Many founders start with one office in London, Berlin, New York or Singapore. Then the team grows, hiring slows, and costs climb. At that point they look for a second hub. Italy keeps coming up on the shortlist. This article explains why, in three parts: talent, lifestyle and cost.

## Talent

Italy has a strong tradition in engineering, design, manufacturing and applied sciences. Its universities produce graduates in technical fields every year. Many of them speak English well and have studied or worked abroad.

The country is also home to industries that need specialists. Fashion, automotive, machinery, food, pharma and industrial design all have deep local expertise. If your product touches any of these sectors, hiring near the source makes sense.

Software and data skills are growing too. Italian developers, analysts and product people work for local firms and for international teams remotely. Many would take a stable local role with a foreign company if the terms are clear.

There is another point. Competition for senior people is lower in many Italian cities than in the big tech capitals. A good company with a clear offer can stand out. Candidates often care about the work, the team and the contract. They do not only look at brand names.

## Lifestyle

Lifestyle sounds soft, but it affects retention. People stay where life works.

Italian cities offer a daily routine that many people value. Food is good and local. Public spaces are lively. Towns are walkable. Family and friends matter, and employees often want to stay close to them. Offering a job in the place where someone already lives or wants to live is a strong draw.

Italy also attracts people from abroad. Some are Italians who want to return home. Others are foreign professionals who want to relocate for the climate, the culture or personal reasons. A hub in Italy lets you recruit both groups. You can bring in a senior leader from your home market and hire local staff around them.

Founders themselves often like the idea. A hub in Rome, Milan, Turin, Bologna or another city gives the team a base worth visiting. Offsites are easy to plan. Clients and partners enjoy the trip.

Geography helps as well. Italy sits in the middle of Europe and the Mediterranean. Time zones work for teams in Europe, the Middle East and Africa, and overlap with the Americas and Asia for part of the day.

## Cost

Cost needs a careful reading. Italy is not a low-wage country, and employment costs include social contributions that you must plan for. Rules differ by role, sector and collective agreement. You should not assume a flat saving.

The real advantage is value. Salary levels in many Italian cities are often more moderate than in the most expensive tech hubs. Office space and living costs outside the largest centres can also be lower. That lets you build a strong team without matching the pay of the busiest talent markets.

The other cost is complexity. A new legal entity takes time to set up. You need registrations, payroll, benefits, local contracts and reporting. For a small team, this overhead can exceed the savings.

This is why many founders use an Employer of Record (EOR). The EOR hires your people in Italy on your behalf. It handles contracts, payroll, contributions and compliance. You direct the daily work. You skip the entity setup and the admin, and you can test the market before committing to more.

That model fits a second hub well. You can start with a few hires, see how the team performs, and decide later whether to open your own entity. If the pilot does not work, you can scale down without closing a company.

## What to check before you decide

A second hub works best when the reasons are clear. Ask yourself a few questions.

- Which roles will sit in Italy, and why there?
- Do you need people with sector knowledge that is strong locally?
- Will you relocate anyone from abroad? If so, plan for visas and the move itself.
- Who will manage the team day to day?
- Do you want an entity now, or a lighter start?

Write down your answers. They shape the contract type, the budget and the timeline.

## The short version

Italy offers skilled people, a lifestyle that keeps them, and a cost base that can suit a growing team when you plan for local rules. The way you hire matters as much as where you hire. An EOR lets you start quickly, stay compliant and keep your focus on the product.

A team member asks to work from Italy for a few months. The request sounds simple. For the employer, it is not.

The employee keeps the same laptop and the same job. But the legal setting changes. Tax, social security, immigration, and employment rules can all be affected by where the work is physically done. This article lists the points an employer should review before approving a temporary stay.

## Why a short stay can create real obligations

Many companies treat remote work abroad as a personal matter for the employee. It is not. The employer is the party that pays wages, reports income, and carries the risk if something is wrong.

A temporary stay can still trigger duties in Italy. Whether it does depends on the facts: how long the person stays, what they do, who they work with, and what authority they have. You should not assume that a short visit is automatically safe.

## Immigration comes first

The right to be in Italy is not the same as the right to work there. A tourist stay does not usually cover remote work for a foreign employer. Some nationalities need a visa or permit. Others can enter freely but may still face rules on work activity.

Before you agree, ask the employee to confirm their nationality, their planned entry route, and the permit they intend to use. Do not rely on a verbal answer. Ask for the document or the official guidance they are following. If the route is unclear, pause the request until it is clarified.

Italy has specific routes for remote workers and for people who relocate for work. Their conditions change over time. Check the current rules with a qualified adviser before you commit.

## Income tax and withholding

An employee who spends enough time in Italy may become tax resident there. Even before that point, Italy may claim the right to tax income earned for work done on its territory.

This matters for payroll. If your home payroll keeps withholding tax as if nothing changed, the employee may face double taxation or a later claim. If Italian tax applies and you did not withhold, the employer can face penalties and back payments.

Tax treaties between Italy and the employee's country may help. They do not remove the need to analyze the case. Get a written tax view before the stay begins, not after.

## Social security

Social security follows its own rules. In many cases the employee stays covered by their home system for a temporary posting. This usually requires proof, such as a certificate, and it depends on agreements between the countries involved.

If no agreement applies, contributions may become due in Italy. That can mean paying twice for the same period. Ask your adviser which rules apply to the employee's home country and request the right documents early. Delays here are common.

## Permanent establishment risk

An employee working from Italy can, in some cases, create a taxable presence for the company. The risk grows if the person signs contracts, negotiates deals, manages local staff, or acts as the face of the company in Italy.

A person doing routine tasks for a short period carries less risk than a sales lead closing deals from a Milan apartment. Define the scope of work in writing. Say clearly what the employee may and may not do while in Italy.

## Employment law and contract terms

Italian labor rules can apply to people who work in Italy, even if the contract is governed by foreign law. Working time, rest periods, leave, and health and safety rules may all matter.

Review the employment contract. Does it allow work from other countries? Does it set limits? A short remote work addendum is useful. It should state the location, the start and end dates, the approved activities, and who pays for extra costs.

## Insurance, equipment, and data

Check that health cover and accident cover work outside the home country. Confirm that company equipment is insured while abroad. Make sure your data security policy allows access from Italy, and that the employee uses secure networks.

## A practical checklist

- Ask for the employee's nationality, dates, and purpose.
- Confirm the right to work or the correct permit.
- Get a written tax opinion for both countries.
- Confirm social security coverage and gather certificates.
- Review permanent establishment risk and limit the scope of work.
- Sign a short remote work addendum.
- Check insurance, equipment, and data rules.
- Set a clear end date and a review point.

## When a temporary stay should become a hire

Some stays start as a few months and quietly turn into a long-term arrangement. If the employee wants to settle in Italy, or the company wants a lasting presence, a temporary workaround stops being enough. At that stage, a proper local employment setup is usually cleaner and safer than stretching a short-term solution.

An Employer of Record (EOR) can employ the person in Italy on your behalf. It handles local payroll, contributions, and compliance, while you direct the daily work. It can be a good fit when you do not have an Italian entity and want to avoid the risks above.

## Bottom line

Saying yes to a temporary stay is a business decision with legal effects. Review it early, document it, and keep the scope narrow. Most problems come from approving the request quickly and asking questions later.

If you hire in Italy, you will meet a different rhythm of work. Hours, leave and the summer break follow rules and habits that may not match your home market. Plan for them early and they cause no trouble.

## Where the rules come from

Working time in Italy is not set by the employer alone. It comes from national law, from the national collective agreement for the sector, and from the individual contract. The collective agreement matters most in daily practice. It sets the weekly hours, the amount of paid leave, extra permits and how overtime is paid.

So the first question is always the same: which collective agreement applies to this role? Your answer decides most of what follows. Do not copy a template from another country.

## Typical working hours

A full-time employee in Italy works a standard week set by law and by the applicable agreement. Many companies run a regular office schedule with a lunch break. Some sectors use shifts or reduced hours as part of the agreement.

A few points to expect:

- Overtime is allowed, but it has limits and it must be paid or compensated as the agreement says.
- Rest periods between working days and a weekly rest day are protected.
- Part-time contracts are common and are regulated in their own way.
- Remote and hybrid work is possible, but it needs a clear written arrangement.

Employees often expect a real separation between work and private time. Late messages and weekend requests are not welcome as a routine. If your team spans time zones, agree the contact window in writing from the start.

## Paid holidays

Every employee earns paid annual leave. The exact amount depends on the contract and the collective agreement. The law sets a floor, and many agreements go above it.

Two habits surprise foreign managers. Leave is taken seriously, and employees are expected to actually use it. Also, a long block of holiday in summer is normal, not a sign of low commitment.

Beyond annual leave, there are other kinds of paid or protected time off:

- Public holidays, which fall on fixed dates across the year.
- Small paid permits that some agreements grant for personal needs.
- Sick leave, with rules on notice and medical certification.
- Parental leave, which is protected and well established.

The employer must record leave properly. Unused leave cannot simply be ignored. It has to be managed and, in some cases, paid out under strict conditions.

## The August shutdown

August is the clearest example of the cultural gap. Many Italian businesses slow down sharply or close for a stretch in mid-summer. Suppliers, clients and public offices may all be hard to reach at the same time.

This affects you in three ways.

**Your own team.** Many employees will ask to take their main holiday in this period. Some companies close the office and require everyone to take leave together. If you do this, say so in advance and count it against annual leave in line with the contract.

**Your clients and partners.** If you sell to Italian customers, expect decisions to stall. Plan launches and renewals around it.

**Your payroll and admin.** Filings and payments still have deadlines. Your payroll provider must plan ahead so nothing is missed while others are away.

## How to plan around it

Ask for the leave calendar early in the year. Agree which weeks are team-wide closure and which are individual choice. Make sure someone can cover urgent matters. Put the rules in the contract or in a short written policy.

A good rule is to avoid surprises. Italian employees respond well to clear expectations set in advance. They respond badly to last-minute changes to leave they already booked.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Applying your home country's leave policy without checking the Italian rules.
- Assuming one agreement fits every role.
- Scheduling key meetings in the summer slowdown.
- Leaving hours and remote work terms vague.
- Forgetting that leave and overtime records must be kept.

## Why an Employer of Record helps

An Employer of Record (EOR) becomes the legal employer in Italy. It applies the right collective agreement, writes a compliant contract, tracks leave and runs payroll. You direct the daily work. The EOR handles the rules on hours, holidays and records, so you do not need your own Italian entity to get it right.

That is useful when you have one or a few hires and no local HR team. You get the rules applied correctly, and you still plan your business around the Italian calendar.
